📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of Ethereum's consensus clients has merged a fix for a validator pubkey cache poisoning attack, according to a pull request on GitHub.
  • Gloas is the consensus layer part of the upcoming Glamsterdam upgrade.
  • The issue lies in a mechanism where the client stores validator public keys and their indexes in a global cache.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of Ethereum's consensus clients has merged a fix for a validator pubkey cache poisoning attack, according to a pull request on GitHub. The patch addresses a vulnerability around the Gloas fork, which could result in some nodes rejecting valid signatures due to a bug in the global pubkey cache.

Gloas is the consensus layer part of the upcoming Glamsterdam upgrade.

The issue lies in a mechanism where the client stores validator public keys and their indexes in a global cache.

Technically, deposits that are already finalized should give the same validators on every chain, though it is a different story at the fork boundary.

Sources indicate that the attacker needs 3 pending deposits just before the fork. The first one is a large top-up for an existing validator. The other two are upcoming keys: A with builder credentials and B with regular validator credentials.

Industry observers note that on the canonical chain, the top-up consumes the balance churn, so A and B are processed after the fork. A becomes a builder, and B takes the next validator index.

Recent findings suggest that on the attacker's side chain, the topped-up validator gets slashed before the fork, and its deposit is skipped. This leads to A being processed earlier, essentially taking B's index.

The buggy cache assumed both chains would produce the same validators and imported A's key globally.

At the fork, affected nodes would reject all valid signatures from B on the canonical chain and fork off.

Realistically, the attack is somewhat complicated, as it needs a slashing at the right moment and a side chain, so it's unlikely to happen by accident.

According to the PR, the fix is to only add keys to the global pubkey cache once their activation eligibility epoch is finalized.

A new HeadPubkeys structure also combines keys from the head state and the global cache, so nodes don't miss keys if the chain finalizes without new blocks.

Whether other consensus clients had a similar glitch is yet to be confirmed. In other words, the closer Glamsterdam gets, the more edge cases around the fork boundary developers have to catch.

Industry News: EXCLUSIVE: California officials urged to examine Zillow Preview, referral model

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A coalition of consumer and advocacy groups is urging California housing regulators to investigate Zillow Group’s listing, agent referral and mortgage practices, arguing the company is distorting the state’s housing market and overcharging buyers and renters.
  • Demand Progress Education Fund, Revolving Door Project, Americans for Financial Reform, Children’s Advocacy Alliance and the Consumer Federation of America sent a letter to Californian officials alleging that Zillow has leveraged its position in listings, buyer representation and mortgage lending to “soak homebuyers” and renters, and call for enforcement under multiple state laws.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A coalition of consumer and advocacy groups is urging California housing regulators to investigate Zillow Group’s listing, agent referral and mortgage practices, arguing the company is distorting the state’s housing market and overcharging buyers and renters.

Demand Progress Education Fund, Revolving Door Project, Americans for Financial Reform, Children’s Advocacy Alliance and the Consumer Federation of America sent a letter to Californian officials alleging that Zillow has leveraged its position in listings, buyer representation and mortgage lending to “soak homebuyers” and renters, and call for enforcement under multiple state laws.

The letter, addressed to Rohit Chopra, secretary of the California Business and Consumer Services Agency, and Chika Sunquist, commissioner of the California Department of Real Estate, contends that “the California housing market is broken” and that Zillow is “one of the most aggressive actors in distorting the market, to its own profit and to the detriment of the public.”.

The groups focus heavily on Zillow Preview, the firm’s pre-marketing program debuted in March 2026 that allows major brokerages to promote listings on Zillow before they hit the broader market. Keller Williams, REMAX, HomeServices of America, Side and United Real Estate were among some of the first firms to sign on to the program. More than 400 brokerages have entered exclusive agreements with Zillow, the letter states, arguing that the arrangement locks “freshest inventory” on Zillow and, more recently, Realtor.com, while sidelining competing platforms. The coalition urges California regulators to scrutinize these vertical agreements and what it characterizes as “monopsonistic capture of pre-market listings.”.

The coalition also targets Zillow’s long-running agent referral model. The letter alleges that when consumers click “Contact agent” or “Request a tour” on many listings, they are often routed to Zillow-affiliated buyer agents rather than the listing agent, citing prior academic research and litigation.

A Wharton School study found most consumers believed those buttons would connect them to an agent associated with the property and that “almost none” could correctly identify who would contact them based on Zillow’s interface, according to the letter.

The groups highlight Zillow’s Flex program (now known as Zillow Preferred), which charges participating buyer agents a “success fee” reportedly as high as 40% of the buy-side commission. They argue that this structure reduces incentives for agents to compete on price and aligns agent incentives more closely with Zillow than with consumers.

The letter notes that Zillow has faced class action litigation over these practices, including claims that its referral and commission structures constitute a racketeering “enterprise.” The case, filed in federal court in Washington state, challenges both the referral flows and undisclosed fees as deceptive under federal and state law.

It has been revealed that on the listing side, the group says Zillow offers listing agents a 10% share of the buy-side commission on deals that close from Preview leads, including when the buyer ultimately purchases a different property. They argue that this unilateral setting of referral compensation could conflict with the spirit or letter of the National Association of Realtors’ (NAR) commission lawsuit settlement, which sought to decouple listing and buyer-broker compensation.

Recent findings suggest that on the financing side, the letter accuses Zillow of using its agent network to steer borrowers toward Zillow Home Loans. It cites allegations in the amended complaint in the renewed Taylor lawsuit that affiliated buyer agents risk losing leads or expulsion from Flex if they do not prioritize Zillow’s lending arm.

Recent findings suggest that most buyers do not shop widely for financing. Zillow’s own research has found that roughly 72% of buyers submit just one mortgage application, according to the letter. Separately, Zillow research has shown that rate shopping can save borrowers thousands of dollars over the life of a loan.

Recent findings suggest that the coalition points to an empirical analysis by Georgetown University Law Center professor Steven Salop, which concluded that Zillow Home Loans borrowers paid about $4,600 more on average than comparable borrowers at other lenders between 2025 and 2027. Salop’s work estimates $186 million in projected overcharges over that period, with even higher average costs for military veterans and Black and Asian borrowers.

In a recent development, the letter compares the alleged steering to the in-house mortgage referral arrangements that drew a 2024 lawsuit from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) against Rocket Homes. That case, brought under the Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act, focused on alleged kickback and referral schemes between affiliated real estate and mortgage businesses and has since been dismissed.

The advocacy groups also raise concerns about Zillow’s expansion in rentals. They note that renters tend to have lower incomes and less bargaining power than buyers, and argue that Zillow has long tried to prioritize its own rental listings while limiting rivals’ visibility.

The letter references Zillow’s $100 million multifamily rental syndication deal with Redfin, claiming that it paid Redfin to shutter its multifamily rental advertising business and transfer clients to Zillow. That agreement later triggered an antitrust complaint by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and five states, which alleged Zillow illegally paid a competitor to exit the rental listings market.

Industry observers note that FTC staff estimated that landlords using Zillow paid an average 14.5% more per listing after the deal, according to public statements cited in the letter. The coalition says renters ultimately bore those higher marketing costs.

Industry observers note that zillow and Redfin settled with the FTC in August 2026 without admitting wrongdoing. The order requires changes to certain agreements but allows the companies to maintain some form of partnership through at least 2030.

The coalition urges California officials to deploy what it calls the state’s “strongest toolkit in the nation” against Zillow’s business model. Specifically, the letter asks Chopra and Sunquist to use the Department of Real Estate’s licensing and rulemaking authority to investigate alleged steering by licensees that may violate fiduciary duties, and to consider rules requiring privately marketed properties to be listed concurrently on public platforms, drawing on legislation passed in Connecticut and Fresh York.

Additionally, they ask officials to investigate and, where warranted, bring actions under the state’s Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law against Zillow Preview’s exclusive agreements, Zillow’s arrangement with Realtor.com and any “re-coupling” of commissions after the NAR settlement.

They also want officials to pursue enforcement under the Consumers Legal Remedies Act and Unfair Competition Law targeting Zillow’s “Contact agent” and “Request a tour” interfaces, alleged nondisclosure of Preferred referral fees and failure to disclose that agent recommendations can be driven by Zillow’s financial interests and to coordinate with the multistate coalition that brought the Redfin rental action, to avoid jurisdictional gaps that could allow similar conduct to persist in California.

The groups argue that while the FTC settlement with Zillow over its Redfin agreement “closed one case,” it did not address what they describe as a broader pattern of conduct spanning purchase, financing and rental markets. They frame California, the nation’s largest housing market, as a critical venue for testing newly introduced state-level responses.

Industry observers note that if regulators accept the coalition’s framing, California could move to restrict or reshape referral fee structures and pre-market listing programs, directly affecting how agents source leads and are paid. In addition, a California investigation into Zillow’s referral flows could set latest guardrails on when and how real estate professionals can recommend affiliate lenders, particularly around disclosure and independence requirements.

Zillow did not immediately respond to HousingWire’s request for comment on the letter.

The first line of code for the core of what would become the XRP Ledger (XRPL) was written about 15 years ago, on November 11, 2011, by David Schwartz.

According to the official XRP account on X, the date 11/11/11 marked the beginning of Schwartz's work on what would later support one of the cryptocurrency industry's established payment-focused blockchain networks.

Schwartz, now Ripple CTO Emeritus, was one of three engineers, alongside Jed McCaleb and Arthur Britto, who began developing the XRP Ledger in 2011. The three were inspired by Bitcoin to build an alternative that would address some of its problems, especially in the areas of sustainability and payments.

In June 2012, the XRP Ledger went live. Shortly after Chris Larsen joined the group in September 2012, a manufacturer called NewCoin was formed; it soon changed its name to OpenCoin before becoming Ripple. The founders of the XRPL donated 80 billion XRP, the network’s native digital asset, to the company.

Ripple has locked up most of its XRP in escrow, about 55 billion XRP, and releases 1 billion XRP on the first day of every month.

The anniversary on November 11 marks the start of the XRP Ledger’s development, as what began with Schwartz's first code in 2011 eventually morphed into a blockchain network designed to enable value transfers.

Industry observers note that november is also a big month for XRP as U.S. spot XRP ETFs celebrate the first anniversary of their landmark launch.Canary Capital’s XRP exchange-traded fund, listed under the ticker XRPC, began trading on November 13, 2025, and is the first spot XRP ETF on a U.S. exchange.

In upgrade news, XRPL version 3.5.0 is scheduled for December 3, 2026. This release includes only improvements and fixes, including a permanent fix for occasional slow ledger close times.

With $5M in funding, Pretxt rolls out runtime oversight layer to supervise AI agents in real time

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Artificial intelligence supervision pioneer Pretxt AI is launching with $5 million in seed funding today as it tries to contain the very real risk of unleashing autonomous agents in production environments.
  • It has created a upcoming kind of “AI Supervision” tool that applies oversight at runtime to ensure those agents follow a company’s rules at all times.
  • Industry observers note that the startup is pitching the idea of a continuous runtime supervision layer that monitors AI agents as they’re getting work done, contrasting their behavior with the parent organization’s rules and policies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 03:00 EST / NOVEMBER 17 2026.

Artificial intelligence supervision pioneer Pretxt AI is launching with $5 million in seed funding today as it tries to contain the very real risk of unleashing autonomous agents in production environments.

It has created a upcoming kind of “AI Supervision” tool that applies oversight at runtime to ensure those agents follow a company’s rules at all times. Today’s round was led by Deciens Capital and saw participation from Howdy Partners, Service Provider Capital and NSV Wolf Capital.

Industry observers note that the startup is pitching the idea of a continuous runtime supervision layer that monitors AI agents as they’re getting work done, contrasting their behavior with the parent organization’s rules and policies. If it spots an agent is starting to drift off-course, it will immediately intervene to put it back on the right track, before it can make a critical mistake that hurts the business.

Sources indicate that real-time guardrails like Pretxt has designed are likely going to become a priority for enterprises as they begin to trust AI agents with more consequential work than simply drafting emails or creating images. For instance, if agents are to be trusted with handling customer refunds and accessing mission-critical databases and modifying records within them, companies will need the strongest reassurance that they’re not going to mess up those tasks.

But those assurances are few and far between. AI is notorious for “hallucinating” responses when it doesn’t know the answer to a question, and autonomous agents have shown erratic behavior time and again. They don’t need a malicious prompt injection to start missing critical required steps in a workflow or invent policy exceptions to simplify a task they’re trying to complete. They’ve shown they can do this in both labs and in the real world.

In response, most security tools take a heavy-handed approach, blocking agents outright, but this means that work slows down. The other approach is to flag errors after the fact, but by the time that happens they could have already caused massive damage.

Pretxt’s co-founders Brian Soby (pictured, left) and Aaron Costello (right) realized that companies need a more balanced approach to agentic security and oversight. Soby, who serves as the startup’s chief executive, previously held senior security roles at Salesforce Inc. and Mitre Inc. before founding the software-as-a-service security startup AppOmni Inc.

It was there that he met Costello, who now serves as Pretxt’s chief technology officer. During their time at AppOmni, they uncovered several major vulnerabilities in AI agents developed by Salesforce and ServiceNow Inc. and began to understand what’s required to ensure those agents can still work safely.

Recent findings suggest that many traditional agent monitoring tools use a second large language model as a “judge” to monitor the behavior of the main LLM that’s doing the work. But Pretxt’s co-founders shunned this idea because it creates latency, increases compute costs and involves too much guesswork.

Instead, their AI Supervision platform is powered by a near-deterministic engine that evaluates agent’s actions in milliseconds in order to spot those that break the rules and intercept them in progress. The tech giant reckons it can do this up to 60 times faster than LLM-as-a-Judge-based security tools.

It has been revealed that the approach is effective. In tests on Zapier’s AutomationBench, Pretext was able to reduce agent policy violations from around one in five to zero. The tool is designed to be easy to implement, so teams don’t need a thorough understanding of the models or agents they’re trying to supervise.

Recent findings suggest that instead, they simply choose which policies, standards and guardrails should apply to an agent, and then they can keep track of them in real time. The platform allows users to track approvals, roll back plan versions and escalate any tricky edge cases to human decision-makers.

Sources indicate that that last capability is especially useful, because many organizations’ security intends have gaps when agents encounter situations that were not previously envisaged. In such cases, Pretxt halts the agent and asks a human to decide what the rules should be.

“Supervising an AI agent shouldn’t mean becoming an expert in everything it touches or in how it’s built,” Costello noted. “Teams tell us in plain language how it should behave and where the boundaries are, and we supervise and steer the agent to stay within them. So there’s no untangling permissions or digging into the agent’s internals.”.

In a recent development, pretxt’s AI Supervision tool is available in early access now. It’s primarily targeting high-stakes regulated industries where mistakes and hallucinations simply cannot be tolerated.

For financial services and insurance companies, it can enforce borrower verification rules and route complex claims to humans, while in healthcare and life sciences it ensures that agents don’t step outside of strict boundaries. In customer support applications, it can prevent agents from offering unapproved discounts or refunds to customers.

Recent findings suggest that AI Supervision can provide a lot of different benefits to a lot of different people. Chief information officers and other senior executives will be able to scale higher-value AI projects safely, while security teams, compliance officers and platform engineers can address gaps in risk management and ensure low-latency policy enforcement without needing to stack additional models.

Enterprise Management Associates analyst Chris Steffen noted the thing that really sets Pretxt apart is its focus on the basics. Not only does it check that agents are behaving themselves, but it also makes sure they’re doing the work they’ve been assigned without breaking any rules or cutting any corners, creating what is effectively a latest category of AI supervision tool.

In a recent development, “Most tools ask if an agent is secure, compliant or observable, but far fewer can show if the agent is correctly doing the job it was given,” Steffen remarked. “Most tools can only report what went wrong after the fact, when it’s too late. Pretxt intervenes while the outcome can still change to get agents back on track.”.

AWS gives developers a free local stand-in for its cloud, built from scratch by AI agents

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 10:51 amNovember 11, 2026 at 10:51 am.
  • AWS claims its engineers didn’t write or review a single line of code in its newest developer tool, and the tech giant is touting that as a selling point.
  • AWS Emulator, released Wednesday, simulates AWS services on a developer’s own machine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 10:51 amNovember 11, 2026 at 10:51 am.

AWS claims its engineers didn’t write or review a single line of code in its newest developer tool, and the tech giant is touting that as a selling point.

AWS Emulator, released Wednesday, simulates AWS services on a developer’s own machine. It’s built from more than 400 API models covering more than 200 AWS services. Developers and AI coding agents can use it to test code without a network connection and without paying for the real cloud.

Recent findings suggest that the tool addresses a problem that coding agents such as Amazon’s Kiro and Anthropic’s Claude Code have made worse. Agents can write code faster than teams can test it against the real cloud. Agents check their work by running the code and reading the results, over and over, and doing that in the cloud adds delays and costs.

The emulator lets them run that loop on a developer’s own machine.

In an ironic or perhaps appropriate twist, AWS used AI agents to build the emulator. Agents also maintain it, testing it against real AWS and fixing the gaps they find.

Sources indicate that “The emulator was written entirely by autonomous agents. Our team hasn’t written or reviewed any of the code,” wrote Matt Goldberg, the AWS senior principal engineer behind the project, in a blog post.

Recent findings suggest that goldberg compared his agents to himself as a kindergartner, too young to hold a crayon properly, who got yelled at by classmates for ruining a group drawing of dinosaurs. The problem wasn’t bad intent, he wrote, just a lack of competence. The answer, for agents, is clearly defined areas to fill in.

“I think agents also need coloring books,” he wrote.

The agents work from AWS’s public API models, which describe how each service should behave, and check their work against the real AWS cloud.

Recent findings suggest that the agents run on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore in three teams. One writes “fidelity tests” — real-world scenarios such as creating a queue, sending a message and deleting the queue — and checks each against real AWS. A second runs those tests against the emulator and files issues for failures, and a third fixes them, one agent per issue.

Industry observers note that every change passes through an automated gate where other agents check coding standards and security. Goldberg wrote that hundreds of agents now fix thousands of challenges a day.

The project started as a weekend experiment, inspired by Anthropic’s demonstration earlier this year in which a team of Claude agents built a C compiler. Goldberg gave Kiro a three-step prompt and got a passable first version of Amazon SQS, AWS’s message queuing service, in 15 minutes.

By the end of the weekend, Goldberg wrote, Kiro had built a rough version of the rest of AWS, with obvious gaps, and his team started using it to test its software that Monday.

Sources indicate that swami Sivasubramanian, AWS vice president of agentic AI and emerging tech, tied the project to a lesson he described to GeekWire in June. He spent four nights babysitting Kiro as it tried to rebuild a replication engine he and Allan Vermeulen built by hand nearly 20 years ago.

Once he gave the agent a spec and a way to test its work, the job took about two hours.

“When agents write the code and check their own work, the engineer’s job is to give them room to work on their own and to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when that work is correct,” Sivasubramanian wrote in a guest post on CTO Werner Vogels’ blog.

It’s the same idea behind Amazon’s recent move to rewrite its engineering playbook for an era when AI writes the code.

The emulator has limits. Devin Pratt, an IDC analyst, told InfoWorld that it doesn’t yet simulate throttling, outages or differences in which services and features are available by region, and that it doesn’t sandbox the code it runs. The agents’ backlog of known gaps is public, in a GitHub folder called “things-that-do-not-work.”.

Other AWS emulators exist, most notably LocalStack, which this year put its free version behind an account requirement and limited it to noncommercial use. AWS released its emulator for free under CC0, a public domain dedication, with the full commit history on GitHub.

The manufacturer claims it will share more at its upcoming re:Invent conference.

As Bitcoin’s price continues to fall further, sparking a fresh wave of panic across the broader crypto market, renowned Bitcoin advocate Anthony Pompliano has issued a statement to investors.

In a recent X post published by the pro-Bitcoin advocate on November 13, Pompliano urged investors to remain calm even as Bitcoin revisited $67,000 for the first time since August.

While Pompliano acknowledged the current market weakness, pointing out that Bitcoin was falling to price levels last seen just three months ago, he urged Bitcoin investors to remain calm.

While addressing Bitcoin's price decline, Pompliano related the situation to AI, another fast-growing technology, drawing attention to the growing relationship between the two sectors.

Pompliano considers the ongoing market movements as evidence that both Bitcoin and AI have become part of one major investment trade.

Although he did not explicitly explain how Bitcoin and AI have become one big trade, it appears that Pompliano is raising awareness of how closely investors may now view the two major investment products in the technology and financial markets.

As such, Pompliano is urging investors to remain positive about Bitcoin’s long-term potential, suggesting that the same market forces driving interest in AI could also influence a potential recovery for Bitcoin.

Pompliano’s comment has come as Bitcoin faces renewed selling pressure, retesting its three-month low at around $67,000 after declining over 5% in the last 24 hours.

Bitcoin’s current price movements have raised questions about whether the decline signals a deeper market correction or simply another temporary setback, causing commentators to disagree with Pompliano’s call for confidence.

How buyer objections shape listing strategy in 2027

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (827 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The longer I work in real estate, the more convinced I become that some of the most vital work in selling a home happens before the first photograph is taken.
  • It has been revealed that photography, descriptions and online exposure matter.
  • Sources indicate that before listing a home, I try to answer a simple question: What might cause a qualified buyer to hesitate, negotiate aggressively or walk away?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The longer I work in real estate, the more convinced I become that some of the most vital work in selling a home happens before the first photograph is taken. I’ve represented sellers through very different housing markets, and one thing hasn’t changed: Even the best marketing campaign can’t overcome every concern a buyer may have.

It has been revealed that photography, descriptions and online exposure matter. But they’re only part of the equation.

Sources indicate that before listing a home, I try to answer a simple question: What might cause a qualified buyer to hesitate, negotiate aggressively or walk away? I’d rather uncover those concerns before losing a good buyer.

According to recent reports, earlier this year, I listed a four-bedroom pool home in Oakland Park, Florida, that needed considerable updating. Frankly, I was concerned about how buyers would react to its condition. It wasn’t turnkey, but it had real strengths: an attractive location and a walkable neighborhood.

According to recent reports, we priced the property at $660,000. Within four days, we received five offers, and the home sold above asking price. The transaction was reported by Paul Owers for Homes.com in May 2026.

Sources indicate that that experience reinforced something I’ve observed repeatedly: Buyers will accept imperfections when they believe the overall value makes sense. Not every home needs extensive improvements before selling. Conversely, a desirable neighborhood doesn’t excuse unrealistic pricing. Our job is to recognize a property’s strengths and shortcomings, then help sellers decide how to proceed.

I wonder whether our focus on marketing sometimes crowds out essential preparation. We can produce photographs, videos and descriptions quickly. But if we haven’t researched the property, understood the competition or identified potential insurance concerns, we may be beautifully marketing a problem we should have investigated first.

Today’s buyers face affordability challenges, costly financing and, in many markets, more competing homes. Here in South Florida, insurance costs, property taxes, maintenance and condition can significantly influence purchasing decisions. A house may appear affordable, but the monthly cost of ownership can tell a different story.

In a recent development, as listing agents, we need to look at properties through the buyer’s eyes. Could an older roof create insurance or financing problems? Are improvements properly permitted? What might surface during an inspection? What else could buyers purchase for the same money?

Industry observers note that we won’t always have every answer. But we should know which questions to ask.

I like to start with the property itself.

That doesn’t necessarily mean expensive improvements are needed. But it calls for an honest conversation about price, condition and expectations. I don’t pretend we can anticipate every problem. Yet experience helps us recognize what might give buyers second thoughts.

One of the harder parts of representing sellers is telling homeowners something they’d rather not hear. Perhaps their anticipated price isn’t supported by the market. Maybe an expensive renovation won’t produce the return they expect. Those conversations aren’t easy.

For many sellers, their home represents years of memories, hard work and financial investment. We owe them empathy, but also honesty. I’d rather have that conversation before listing than watch a seller become discouraged after weeks of limited activity and repeated price reductions.

Technology can help with this preparation. I use artificial intelligence to research properties, study competing listings and organize information. But technology doesn’t replace walking through a property, asking difficult questions or recognizing when something deserves further investigation.

Sometimes you have to put the computer aside, visit the property and bring in someone who knows more about a particular problem than you do.

In a recent development, there’s wisdom in acknowledging another professional’s expertise. As we approach 2027, I believe listing agents should spend less time emphasizing how widely they can advertise a home and more time explaining how they’ve prepared it for the market.

Industry observers note that good marketing gets buyers through the door. What we’ve done before they arrive can make a real difference in what happens next. Even a well-prepared listing can encounter unexpected problems. There are no guarantees in this business. But sellers deserve to know we’ve done our homework, considered the competition and anticipated difficult questions.

For me, it comes down to this: The best listing strategy doesn’t begin by asking how we can make a home look more appealing. It begins by understanding what might keep a buyer from saying yes.

Recent findings suggest that gary Lanham is a broker associate with LoKation Real Estate and an AI-certified Realtor specializing in residential listings in the Fort Lauderdale area. With 22 years of real estate experience, he founded Lanham & Associates, acquired by Coldwell Banker Realty in 2014. A member of the Master Brokers Forum, Lanham writes and teaches about listing strategy, real estate technology and professional representation.

It has been revealed that CRANBERRY TOWNSHIP, Pa., Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Annexus Health, the infrastructure behind patient financial assistance, today announced that it has been awarded Gold for Best Healthcare Information System in the HealthTech category of the 2026 Merit Awards for Healthcare.

Merit Awards recognize achievements across industries including healthcare, technology, business, and communications. In healthcare, the awards honor organizations addressing industry needs through their technology, services, and innovations.

This recognition highlights Annexus' work to help patients receiving specialty therapeutics access and afford treatment, while reducing the operational complexity healthcare providers face in securing and managing financial assistance.

Through connected technology, automation, and intelligence, the Annexus Platform helps providers identify available financial assistance, improve financial performance, and maintain support throughout treatment. The Platform also helps life sciences organizations extend patient support programs into provider workflows, connecting more eligible patients with available assistance.

In a recent development, "Financial assistance can make a meaningful difference in a patient's ability to access treatment, but the complexity of securing and managing that support creates challenges across healthcare," mentioned Brad Frazier, Co-Founder and CEO of Annexus Health. "We've spent years developing the technology and operational expertise to make that process more connected and effective at scale. There's more work ahead, and we're focused on bringing these capabilities to more providers so they can connect more patients with the financial assistance available to them.".

In a recent development, annexus has helped secure more than $11 billion in financial assistance and supported more than 400,000 patient enrollments. Its nationwide network spans more than 735 healthcare organizations and 32,000 sites of care.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 11, 2026 at 11:21 amNovember 11, 2026 at 11:21 am.

If the eventual release of “The Snackbar at the End of the World” is a full-on meal for video game fans, news this week of the game’s first trailer should at least suffice as an appetizer.

It has been revealed that seattle-based Snackbar Studio, co-founded by SparkToro founder Rand Fishkin and his wife, writer Geraldine DeRuiter, unveiled its debut title and Steam page on Tuesday. The hand-drawn narrative adventure RPG puts players in the role of a chef trying to save a struggling family restaurant in a magical version of 1960s Italy.

The studio now plans to launch the game late next year, after originally targeting the second half of 2026. Snackbar raised $2.15 million from 38 angel investors two years ago, and the project began four years ago, according to Fishkin. The team includes five co-founders (Fishkin, DeRuiter, game designer Nicolas Kraj, lead programmer Miriam Cabrera and art director Francesco Mazza) plus about 10 contractors.

Industry observers note that in the studio’s description on Steam, players forage for ingredients in the “forbidden wilds” outside town, battling explosive tomatoes, chaotic zucchini and vendetta-driven poultry. They then cook dishes back at the restaurant before a tyrannical mayor known as the Sindaco can shut it down. The game mixes combat and stealth with cooking mini-games based on real-world recipes.

The trailer is set to “’O surdato ’nnammurato,” a classic Neapolitan song performed by professional musicians recruited by the studio’s music director. Fishkin said he and DeRuiter both cried the first time they heard it.

Fishkin is best known in Seattle tech circles as co-founder of SEO software company Moz and audience research startup SparkToro, and he more recently launched Alertmouse, a tool for tracking online mentions. DeRuiter, a writer and author, is Snackbar’s head writer.

In a recent development, in a LinkedIn post this week, Fishkin recalled telling DeRuiter during the COVID lockdown that he wanted to fulfill a childhood dream of making a video game. Her reply: “Don’t wait. Do it now. I’ll do it with you.”.

In the same post, he noted the game’s themes include found family and fighting fascism “even when there’s no hope you’ll win.” He called it a love letter to DeRuiter’s small family village in the mountains outside Naples, to that era of Italy, to video games, and to the many people both of their families have lost in recent years.

Industry observers note that moments like hearing that song come often in the work, Fishkin noted, such as when a latest feature clicks or a new animation brings DeRuiter’s characters to life. He has always loved art without being good at any form of it. “I may not be able to create art, but I can enable it,” he said. “What a wonderful feeling.”.

There have been lows, too. The team spent its initial 18 months on the project with a contract agency that didn’t work out, losing money with nothing to show for it. Fishkin is glad they kept going, “even when it felt financially irresponsible.”.

In a recent development, the game is entirely human-made, and Snackbar’s no-AI stance is firm. “Geraldine hates AI with the fury of a thousand suns,” Fishkin said. He once suggested, just once, that she use Google’s AI Mode to find a synonym, and she was mad at him for the rest of a six-hour flight home from Philadelphia. Even if players, the rest of the team and the games media were fine with AI (and they’re not), DeRuiter alone would make it a no-go, he said.

Still ahead are 10 to 12 months of finishing the game’s content, playtesting, bug fixing, marketing and launch prep. Fishkin called it daunting, but stated team members have done it many times before, “even though it’s our first rodeo.”.

Recent findings suggest that fishkin is still juggling Snackbar with SparkToro and Alertmouse, and describes his role at the studio as mostly oversight and management. SparkToro is growing again, and Alertmouse recently hit a big milestone in annual renewals with high retention. He and his Alertmouse co-founders are putting more money into the company to fund growth.

Balancing the three roles is a challenge, he stated, but only rarely completely overwhelming. “Like this week.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that HSBC Holdings sold about $300 million of an $18 billion construction loan for an Oracle $ORCL-linked data center in New Mexico at a discount, according to Bloomberg. The sale followed a force majeure notice that Oracle sent to the project's developer, a unit of Blue Owl Capital.

It has been revealed that the slice changed hands at mid-80s levels, according to Bloomberg. The campus is in Doña Ana County. An HSBC representative declined to comment, and an Oracle representative did not have an immediate comment.

About 20 banks provided the loan, which goes by the name Project Miner and is divided into tranches that correspond to individual buildings on the campus, according to Bloomberg.

Sources indicate that in the syndicated loan market, lenders can typically offload their positions on the secondary market, according to Bloomberg. Banks that fund construction projects usually hold the debt on their own books, and some are barred from selling until a pooled sell-down agreement runs out. A bank that leaves before the build is finished often has to accept a price cut that outweighs the upfront fees it collected.

The sale comes as lenders reconsider how much AI debt they hold amid fresh regulatory resistance after a Democratic sweep, according to Bloomberg. Jensen Huang’s departure as Nvidia $NVDA CEO has also fed worries over how quickly AI can keep expanding.

In a recent development, oracle sent the force majeure notice in September, a move that would allow it to delay payment on the campus if it does not come online as expected in 2028. Oracle said at the time that the project remained on its planned schedule. Blue Owl said the notice did not change the financial commitments to the project.

Recent findings suggest that the project has also faced a pipeline setback. The gas pipeline serving the site had to be rerouted after state regulators rejected its original path, which pushed the targeted in-service date to next year.

Sources indicate that the campus, known as Project Jupiter, forms part of the Stargate AI infrastructure build-out, which leaders of Oracle, OpenAI and SoftBank Group joined President Donald Trump in announcing in early 2025. The campus is planned to have a capacity of 2.45 gigawatts, and slow approvals of its air and pipeline permits have set it back, according to Bloomberg.

Yield-Bearing eZAR Blurs the Line Between Stablecoin and Investment Product

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1355 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation.
  • Most stablecoin introduces promise a token that never moves.
  • According to recent reports, according to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to upcoming institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Sources indicate that eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation. Its reserve yield is the feature that puts the stablecoin label to the test.

Most stablecoin introduces promise a token that never moves. eZAR's disclosures say its holders can make money or lose it. The rand-pegged token went live to the public on November 2, and its fine print reads more like an investment product than a payments coin.

According to recent reports, according to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to upcoming institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations. The company says R303 million worth of tokens had been issued and were in circulation as of October 30.

The project is a partnership between eZAR Ltd, asset manager Ninety One and AVBOB Financial Services, with AVBOB acting as lead institution and liquidity partner. CEO Sean Emery said the team put "getting it right" ahead of "getting it major" during the pilot. The message now is that eZAR is ready to scale.

The model also departs from the typical single-issuer coin. Neobanks, retailers, insurers and payment firms can plug the token into their own branded wallets and share in the economics. Transfers between participating wallets settle within seconds at any hour and, according to the tech giant, cost nothing.

The reserves backing eZAR are invested through a money market strategy run by Ninety One, mainly in the Ninety One Money Market Fund. Returns are distributed daily to partners after partnership fees, and each partner then decides on what terms its own customers receive a share.

Ninety One's head of digital assets, Adam Duxbury, described it as fresh rails under an old discipline. His firm has run money market strategies for 25 years, he noted, and South Africa should build its own digital rand rather than import a dollar coin.

The framing is clever, since it presents the yield as a feature of "digital cash that can grow." Yet that same feature makes the classification question hard to avoid.

Industry observers note that the risk language is the most revealing part of the launch. eZAR describes itself as a crypto asset issued by the eZAR En Commandite Partnership. It states that the token is not legal tender, not a bank deposit and not a banking product, and that it carries no guarantee.

In a recent development, the details that follow set it further apart. The R1 redemption value depends on available liquidity. Money market returns can be positive or negative, so capital is at risk. Holders also own no units in the underlying fund and have no direct claim on it.

"Capital at risk" rarely appears in stablecoin terms. A payments token is meant to hold its value and let users redeem at par, yet eZAR's own documents hedge on both counts. Back in March, a market survey from Blockhouse had already noted that eZAR doesn't qualify as a stablecoin under most regulations. The live launch now tests that observation against a real product.

Industry observers note that in the major rulebooks, the yield is the sticking point. The US GENIUS Act bars permitted payment stablecoin issuers from paying holders any form of interest or yield solely for holding, using or retaining the token. The EU's MiCA framework takes a similar line on interest. The logic is that a payment token paying a return starts to function like an unregulated deposit.

Industry observers note that the OCC issued its final GENIUS Act rules on October 21, and they confirmed that ban for covered issuers. The contested ground lies elsewhere, in who sits between the issuer and the holder. Earlier OCC proposals set a rebuttable presumption against yield arrangements run through affiliates and related third parties, whereas the statute itself names only issuers.

In a recent development, eZAR's design lands squarely in that gray zone. Returns flow to partners, and the partners decide how customers share in them. Whether that amounts to an issuer paying yield or a partner passing on profit is precisely the kind of question US regulators are now wrestling with, and it would be a difficult one to argue before the OCC.

Sources indicate that eZAR doesn't operate under the US or EU regimes, so none of those rules apply to it directly. eZAR Ltd is described as an authorised financial services provider responsible for the main technology and services behind the partnership. That technology also draws on the South African Reserve Bank's Project Khokha 2, where eZAR's parent manufacturer, Block Markets Africa, was a technical contributor.

It has been revealed that this background signals a serious, institution-backed build rather than a speculative launch. Even so, the rand stablecoin field is getting crowded. ZARU released earlier this year as an institutional-grade rand coin, and a pattern is emerging of different models competing for the same local payments niche.

Industry observers note that the bigger question is whether South Africa will define stablecoins narrowly, as the US and EU do, or leave room for hybrid products like this one. Because the network is permissioned, the reported circulation figure also rests on manufacturer disclosure rather than a public ledger, which makes the regulatory and disclosure framework matter even more.

For everyday consumers, the appeal is easy to see. A rand token that moves in seconds, costs nothing to send and might earn a daily return makes an attractive pitch. For partners, shared infrastructure with a revenue share offers a way into digital payments without building a coin from scratch.

The trade-off sits in the disclaimers. A holder who treats eZAR like a bank balance could be caught off guard by liquidity-dependent redemption, or by a money market return that dips below zero. That gap between how the product feels and how it is legally defined is where regulators tend to step in.

Recent findings suggest that eZAR is best understood as a hybrid: a payments token with an investment return attached. It may well succeed on those terms. Still, as more jurisdictions tighten the stablecoin definition around no-yield, par-redemption tokens, products like this will increasingly be judged on what they are rather than what they are called. How South African regulators treat eZAR in the coming months will show which way that debate is heading.

In a recent development, major crypto exchange Coinbase is set to suspend trading in 12 crypto trading pairs as part of an effort to improve overall market health and consolidate liquidity on the platform. This decision affects two trading pairs involving Cardano (ADA) and Stellar (XLM): ADA/ETH and XLM/BTC.

Coinbase remarked it regularly monitors the markets on its exchange and, in line with this, trading will be suspended on the named markets on November 25, 2026. In an effort to improve overall market health and consolidate liquidity, Coinbase will be removing a number of non-USD trading pairs for supported assets.

According to an announcement, Coinbase will suspend trading on the following markets on November 25, 2026, at or around 12 PM ET: APE-USDT, ATOM-USDT, ALGO-BTC, CRV-BTC, ETC-BTC, ICP-BTC, XLM-BTC, APE-EUR, ADA-ETH, 1INCH-GBP, CHZ-GBP, SNX-GBP.

However, Coinbase Advanced Trade owners in eligible regions can still trade these assets in the USD order books.

In light of this, APE-USDT, ATOM-USDT, ALGO-BTC, CRV-BTC, ETC-BTC, ICP-BTC, XLM-BTC, APE-EUR, ADA-ETH, 1INCH-GBP, CHZ-GBP have been moved to limit-only mode on Coinbase Exchange and Coinbase Advanced.

In recent delistings, Coinbase has disabled trading for Balancer (BAL) and Tensor (TNSR), but users will continue to have the ability to withdraw their funds at any time.

In a recent development, the suspension of trading for Stargate Finance (STG) and Vulcan Forged (PYR) has also been postponed to November 20, 2026, at or around 2 PM ET. Based on recent reviews, Coinbase will suspend trading for Ampleforth Governance Token (FORTH) on November 23, 2026, at or around 2 PM ET. Trading for Neon EVM (NEON) and Syndicate (SYND) will be suspended on November 16, 2026, at or around 2 PM ET.

Sources indicate that spot trading for Pearl (PEARL) will go live on November 13, 2026. The opening of the PEARL-USD trading pair will begin at or after 9 AM PT, if liquidity conditions are met, in regions where trading is supported.

Perpetual futures trading for GRAM, GRASS, QNT and ZRO will go live on November 13, 2026, at or after 12:00 PM UTC.

ebm-papst DiaForce, AxiForce, and RadiCal series fans help mitigate rack-level hot spots, minimize harmonic vibration, reduce parasitic power draw, and improve energy efficiency in critical data center infrastructure.

FORT WORTH, Texas, Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- RS, a high-service global product and service solutions provider for industrial customers, offers high-performance ebm-papst air-moving products engineered to solve rack-level thermal management challenges in high-density data centers, including several series of robust, compact, and versatile fans. As processing demands soar, these proven fan technologies allow data center operators, system builders, and thermal engineers to optimize airflow, overcome high static pressure resistance, minimize harmonic vibration, reduce parasitic power draw, and reliably protect critical assets from thermal damage and mechanical stress.

Rapid growth in artificial intelligence, machine learning, and high-performance computing has pushed server rack power densities from 3â5kW a decade ago to 40â100kW or more per rack today. Because server chips convert nearly all electrical energy into heat, unmitigated thermal energy creates localized hot spots that facility-level air conditioning cannot effectively dissipate, risking component degradation, silicon melting, and unplanned downtime that averages around $9,000 per minute. While liquid cooling adoption is growing, fan-based forced-air cooling remains the global standard for roughly 90% of data centers due to lower capital costs, easier maintenance, legacy facility compatibility, and zero risk of fluid leaks near high-voltage electronics.

According to recent reports, effectively cooling these densely populated server chassis requires specialized fans engineered to overcome extreme aerodynamic resistance from PCBs, power supplies, and cabling without introducing excessive noise, harmonic vibration, or energy penalties. ebm-papst offers a variety of precision engineered fans through RS that directly resolve these common rack-level thermal and mechanical constraints. Key product lines include:.

In a recent development, "As data centers scale to handle generative AI and high-performance computing, thermal management has shifted from a facility-wide consideration to a precise, component-level engineering discipline," stated Steve Berestecky, Director of Information Technology & Clean Room Air Technologies at ebm-papst. "Evaluating fans strictly on total volumetric airflow is no longer sufficient when dense internal components create intense aerodynamic impedance. By matching static pressure requirements, optimizing air velocity at critical component sites, and utilizing intelligent PWM control loops, ebm-papst solutions like our DiaForce, AxiForce, and RadiCal series fans allow engineers to master thermal density, curb parasitic power consumption, and protect operational uptime.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 11, 2026 at 2:31 pmNovember 11, 2026 at 2:31 pm.

Lila Bio, a startup spun out of Nobel laureate David Baker’s lab at the University of Washington, has received a $3.65 million grant from the National Institutes of Health to develop a treatment for pulmonary hypertension.

The condition causes high blood pressure in the arteries that carry blood from the heart to the lungs. It forces the heart to work harder and can lead to heart failure.

The Small Business Innovation Research fast-track award supports Lila’s efforts to develop a protein-based treatment for pulmonary hypertension that could be given by injection a few times a year.

“Most approved therapies only manage symptoms, such as vasodilators,” Lila CEO Jake Kraft said in a LinkedIn post, referring to drugs that widen blood vessels. “Lila Bio is pursuing clinically-validated, disease-modifying mechanisms that treat the underlying disease.”.

The funding comes from the NIH’s National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and is divided into two phases. The initial $605,981 will support early testing in mice, rats and non-human primates. The second phase, totaling $3,049,462, will support further animal testing and studies using lung tissue from patients.

Kraft and chief scientist Anindya Roy co-founded Lila in 2023. Both worked as postdoctoral fellows at UW’s Institute for Protein Design, which Baker directs. Lila raised $10 million in seed funding the year it was founded. Last year, it revealed a collaboration with pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly to develop treatments for solid tumors.

The startup uses AI and machine learning to design therapeutic proteins through two platforms. One supports the pulmonary hypertension project, creating long-acting injectable drugs designed to remain active in the body for weeks or months. The other focuses on targeted radiotherapy, using proteins to deliver radioactive isotopes to tumors.

It has been revealed that “We want to bring medicines to patients,” Kraft told GeekWire in an earlier interview. “We don’t want to just say we’ve designed a protein, but we actually want to be able to say we’ve saved lives.”.

Latest Update: SuperDial revamps its healthcare voice agent platform to stop AI bots wasting time calling each other

💡 Key Takeaways
  • SuperDial Inc., the creator of voice-first artificial intelligence agents for automating healthcare workflows, is overhauling its platform with a upcoming Agent-to-Agent RCM architecture.
  • The goal is to eliminate the compute inefficiencies that have arisen as autonomous workers become more prevalent in the industry.
  • The startup, which raised $15 million in a Series A funding round last year, is best known for its voice agents that automate payer operations, revenue cycle management and administrative outreach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 08:00 EST / NOVEMBER 17 2026.

SuperDial Inc., the creator of voice-first artificial intelligence agents for automating healthcare workflows, is overhauling its platform with a upcoming Agent-to-Agent RCM architecture.

The goal is to eliminate the compute inefficiencies that have arisen as autonomous workers become more prevalent in the industry.

The startup, which raised $15 million in a Series A funding round last year, is best known for its voice agents that automate payer operations, revenue cycle management and administrative outreach. It aims to alleviate the time-consuming burden of having to call health insurance providers, waste time on hold, navigate phone trees and check online portals for information. Traditionally, SuperDial has seen itself as a voice-first platform that’s focused on call automation, but the shift to its Agent-to-Agent RCM architecture suggests it wants to deemphasize phone calls as much as possible.

The manufacturer is addressing the friction that has emerged from the slightly dystopian reality that both healthcare providers and insurance payers have largely replaced humans with AI agents in order to automate routine calls. But the fact that agents are handling the calls on both sides creates huge inefficiencies, resulting in those bots wasting time and compute resources as they engage in unnecessary robotic conversations. Rather than streamline insurance eligibility checks, claim follow-ups and prior authorizations, those agents find themselves stuck in multi-minute phone exchanges to relay structured data verbally that both sides already possess.

SuperDial founder and Chief Executive Sam Schwager refers to these scenarios as the “bot wars,” and claims they’re increasingly engaging in relentless and destructive battles with one another that cost both healthcare providers and insurance companies money.

In a recent development, “One side deploys AI to secure approvals and payment for care,” he mentioned. “The other deploys AI to review those requests and, at times, deny them. Neither has a reason to stop. Every extra round costs more in AI spend, pulls in staff on both sides to handle what the bots can’t settle, and can delay payment and care. The result is more friction, not less.”.

In a recent development, with Agent-to-Agent RCM, SuperDial is trying to sidestep the bot wars by no longer defaulting to outbound calls. Instead, it acts as a kind of omnichannel orchestration layer, where success is determined by the number of requests resolved, rather than completed phone calls. When a revenue cycle team initiates a request, SuperDial’s agents will first check the relevant electronic data interchange feeds and application programming interfaces to find the information they need.

In a recent development, if they find it, great, but if not, they will then try the payer’s web portals. If they’re still out of luck after exhausting all options for digital retrieval, only then will they proceed to place a voice call. Those calls are more efficient too, since SuperDial’s agents will retain all of the context from their initial search, so they only need to query the agent on the other side of the line for the information that’s missing.

Schwager noted Agent-to-Agent RCM puts more emphasis on resolution, allowing a provider’s agent and a payer’s system to connect and work together to resolve administrative requests with less work on both sides.

Recent findings suggest that “The difference between this and the bot wars is the definition of done,” he stated. “Two agents were optimizing for their own side of the exchange, but now those two agents are optimizing for a usable answer — that is, the information the provider needs to move the account forward, delivered in response to a request the payer can actually answer.”.

For customers, life becomes much simpler. All they have to do is tell SuperDial what it needs to know, and its agents will work to get the answers in the fastest time and most efficient manner possible. “How we get the answer is our problem, not theirs,” Schwager said.

Schwager mentioned the industry needs to move away from the idea that healthcare administration can be improved by having two bots argue with each other faster. “If an agent already has the information, that context should travel with the request,” he explained. “If a digital channel can answer it, there should be no call. The goal is fewer exchanges, not faster ones.”.

Recent findings suggest that the company’s long-term goal is to create an AI-native network that facilitates seamless, automated payer-provider communications. The goal is to eliminate repetitive inquiries and cut down on the administrative delays that can negatively impact patient outcomes, Schwager added.

According to recent reports, superDial states it’s already having a significant impact. Since it founded its platform in 2021, it has handled more than 10 million automated calls between healthcare providers and insurance firms – interactions that would once have been made by humans. Had humans made those calls, it would have been much slower, because SuperDial says its agents average about four minutes per call when dealing with insurers’ automated voice systems, compared with 17 minutes or more when reaching a human representative.

With its architectural overhaul, SuperDial is now targeting insurers, in addition to the healthcare providers it already serves. Earlier this year, it announced it had signed a key deal with Guardian Life Insurance Co. of America to modernize its dental provider data attestation workflows.

Sources indicate that the daily trading volume of the NVDA-USDC perpetual contract on the decentralized exchange Hyperliquid has reached a record $2.14 billion, according to CoinGlass. The contract is provided by the Trade.xyz protocol, and only Bitcoin had higher trading volume on Hyperliquid over the same period.

Nvidia futures also surpassed Ethereum, Solana and XRP in trading volume, and the combined volume of Nvidia derivatives across all tracked crypto exchanges reached $9.51 billion, according to CoinGlass.

Sources indicate that the latest surge in trading comes amid the resignation of Jensen Huang, the co-founder of Nvidia and the only CEO in the history of the company. Huang stepped down on Nov. 12 amid an internal investigation, and Nvidia CFO Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO.

On Nasdaq, the price of NVDA went down by as much as 14% during the day, but the stock later recovered most of the loss and closed at $166.19, down 4.34%.

In a recent development, sharp price moves cost leveraged traders on crypto exchanges $40.86 million, according to CoinGlass. Of that amount, $26.23 million came from the on-chain ticker XYZ:NVDA, and $14.63 million came from the base NVDA contract. The largest single liquidation on Hyperliquid was a $1.54 million long position.

Sources indicate that in the base NVDA contract, $8.87 million in long positions and $5.89 million in short positions were liquidated. During the same period, the price of Nvidia futures on crypto exchanges went up by 5.6% to $171.17.

Industry observers note that liquidations in the NVDA contracts were almost twice as large as those in XRP, where traders lost $20.75 million over the same period. The price of XRP went down by 2.5% to $1.0192, and long positions accounted for 94.5% of XRP liquidations, or $19.6 million.

The liquidations came amid a sell-off across major cryptocurrencies. The price of Bitcoin dropped below $70,000 to $69,450.50, down 5.3% over 24 hours, and Ethereum fell 4.1% to $1,958.71.

Over the past 24 hours, crypto exchanges liquidated 187,389 traders for a total of $1.65 billion, and 88% of that amount came from long positions, according to CoinGlass. Bitcoin traders lost the most at $919.56 million, followed by Ethereum traders at $297.24 million.

Sources indicate that finally, Nvidia is expected to report its quarterly earnings on Nov. 17.

DataOne's VIN Decoding Now Incorporates OEM Build Data for Mercedes-Benz Vehicles.

Recent findings suggest that BEVERLY, Mass., Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- DataOne Software, a Dominion Enterprises manufacturer and a leading provider of automotive data and software solutions, today announced a new OEM build data licensing agreement with Mercedes-Benz USA (MBUSA). This agreement enables DataOne's VIN decoding services to provide OEM-sourced, option-level data for MBUSA's complete portfolio of vehicles, which includes Mercedes-Benz, Mercedes-AMG, Mercedes-Maybach and Mercedes-Benz Vans.

Sources indicate that dataOne customers will now have the option to utilize Mercedes-Benz build data when decoding a vehicle with DataOne's VIN Decoder API. OEM build data is instrumental in identifying all the optional features and equipment present on the vehicle, including transmission, color, and trim level, in addition to factory-installed options, marketing packages, and safety features.

According to recent reports, "We are extremely excited to announce this data collaboration with Mercedes-Benz USA, which will provide immediate benefits to our customer base across the automotive industry," states DataOne Software President Jake Maki. "DataOne users are now empowered to more easily identify the innovative vehicle technology and customization incorporated into Mercedes-Benz vehicles and to utilize this insight to better support their organization's needs.".

DataOne Software's option-level VIN decoding returns both the manufacturer-specific terminology as well as DataOne's standard vehicle descriptors. The manufacturer-specific terminology is optimized for use in generating OEM marketing-compliant vehicle descriptions, while DataOne's standard vehicle descriptors make this information easy to integrate and use across all brands.

For more information about obtaining Mercedes-Benz build data through DataOne's VIN decoder web service, contact DataOne at 877.438.8467 or e-mail [email protected].

DataOne Software (www.dataonesoftware.com) is a premier automotive data source providing the data and software solutions needed to power modern businesses across all segments of the automotive industry. DataOne's comprehensive data solutions cover everything from VIN decoding and vehicle descriptions to specifications, optional equipment, and market pricing. With the acquisition of Cross-Sell in 2026, DataOne has expanded our product offering to include PII-free vehicle sales and registration data. Our high-quality solutions are delivered with industry-leading support, making them easy to integrate and scale.

Mercedes-Benz USA (MBUSA), headquartered in Atlanta, is responsible for the distribution, marketing and customer service for all Mercedes-Benz products in the United States. MBUSA offers drivers the most diverse lineup in the luxury segment with 18 model lines ranging from the sporty GLA SUV to the flagship S-Class and the dynamic all-electric vehicles from Mercedes-Benz. MBUSA is also responsible for Mercedes-Benz Vans in the U.S. More information on MBUSA and its products can be found at www.mbusa.com and www.mbvans.com. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 2:56 pmNovember 11, 2026 at 3:19 pm.
  • WellSaid, the AI voice company that spun out of Seattle’s Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence in 2019, is reinventing itself for the era of AI agents.
  • The firm this week rolled out WellSaid Producer, which connects its voiceover direction tools directly to AI assistants such as Claude and Microsoft Copilot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 2:56 pmNovember 11, 2026 at 3:19 pm.

WellSaid, the AI voice company that spun out of Seattle’s Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence in 2019, is reinventing itself for the era of AI agents.

The firm this week rolled out WellSaid Producer, which connects its voiceover direction tools directly to AI assistants such as Claude and Microsoft Copilot.

Instead of logging into WellSaid’s app, corporate consumers can ask the AI assistant for a voiceover to accompany a training or marketing video, for example. The assistant then sends the script to WellSaid, which generates the audio using its licensed voices.

It’s part of a broader overhaul and refocusing of WellSaid’s business. The manufacturer has spent the past two years moving away from individual users to focus on businesses. It now has about 30 employees, down from more than 70 in late 2024.

Along the way, WellSaid has turned profitable, CEO Benjamin Dorr told GeekWire.

Recent findings suggest that “We’ve been calling this adventure Act II, so I guess Producer is Scene I,” Dorr remarked. Extending the metaphor, he acknowledged that “the cast is a lot smaller,” and noted that many of the tech giant’s leaders are new, recruited from his own network.

Dorr joined WellSaid as CFO in 2024 and became CEO in spring 2025. He was previously chief operating officer of Cordial, a San Diego marketing software manufacturer, and earlier worked in tech investing and banking at The Carlyle Group, Morgan Stanley and Citi.

In a recent development, he succeeded Brian Cook, the former Nintex CEO who led WellSaid for about 16 months. Co-founder Matt Hocking, who was CEO until early 2024, remains on WellSaid’s board and is now chief product officer at Type, an AI startup for creative writers.

Dorr’s leadership team includes three executives who also worked at Cordial and joined WellSaid since last fall: Natalia Holts, senior vice president of finance and accounting; Jeni Bishop, vice president of marketing; and Bryan Keefer, vice president of product.

Chris Johnson, the chief product and technology officer, and co-founder Mixail Petrochuk, the chief technology officer, remain from the earlier leadership team.

The tech giant is maintaining its longstanding practice of building its AI voices from recordings of professional voice actors, who are paid royalties when businesses use their voices to narrate training courses, marketing and other videos.

WellSaid drew widespread attention in 2023 when it created a spot-on synthetic version of former NPR “Planet Money” host Robert Smith’s voice, with his permission, as part of a special series by the popular radio show and podcast.

Recent findings suggest that its customers include nearly half of the Fortune 100, according to WellSaid. The tech giant’s licensing approach stands out in a sector that remains a wild west, with models trained on audio scraped from the internet and tools used to fake the voices of public figures.

According to recent reports, how it works: Producer uses Model Context Protocol, or MCP, a standard way for AI assistants to connect to other software. It works with Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot and Atlassian’s Rovo, and Dorr mentioned AI agents that work on their own will be able to use it by the end of the year.

Companies using WellSaid Producer can set up style guides so brand names, acronyms and technical terms are pronounced the same way in every file. When a product name or script changes, Producer can update every affected voiceover in one pass, and each finished file carries a record of its license.

Industry observers note that wellSaid also says it’s the first voiceover platform to generate audio natively at 48 kHz, the standard for film and video. WellSaid will continue to offer its Studio app for customers who want to work there directly.

Sources indicate that producer is sold as a platform, with customers committing to buy credits for minutes of finished, licensed audio. WellSaid’s licenses today are mostly one-time buyouts, but Dorr said the company wants to price more like the traditional voiceover industry, where an ad voiceover is priced by its length, reach and how long it runs.

Sources indicate that the strategy: Dorr said voiceover is just one step in a larger production process, and many creative tools now include basic AI speech that is sometimes good enough. He sees AI agents letting companies combine specialized tools from vendors they trust, instead of settling for one all-in-one app.

“We view MCP, and agents in general, to be as disruptive to software as the Web once was twenty years ago,” he said.

Voice actors: Actors’ revenue share rates won’t change when their voices are used through AI assistants, Dorr remarked. One of his first moves as CEO was to open the tech giant’s stock option pool to its top 20 voice actors, and WellSaid is building a voice actor advisory board, with more details expected to be released in December. Dorr said WellSaid prepares to add custom royalty structures, “potentially all the way up to union rate cards.”.

According to recent reports, customers will also be able to use voice models from other companies alongside WellSaid’s own, for features its models lack, such as one voice speaking several languages. The voices still come from WellSaid’s actors under its licensing terms. “We’re not moving from our position on commercial licensing,” Dorr noted.

The business: WellSaid has about 1,000 business customers, and its top 25 customers each spend more than $100,000 a year, Dorr stated. Moving away from individual consumers “did flatten our growth compared to a lot of AI companies growing at astronomical rates,” he said.

By comparison, rival ElevenLabs, which has offered voice generation through Claude since 2025, was valued at $22 billion in a recent employee tender offer.

Recent findings suggest that wellSaid raised venture debt from Multiplier Capital in March but didn’t disclose the amount. Its most recent disclosed equity funding was a $10 million Series A round in 2021 that valued the company at $65 million, according to PitchBook.

Dorr remarked debt was a better fit than equity for a “modestly growing and, now, profitable firm,” at a time when investors’ growth expectations “have become extreme.” He said WellSaid will consider other financing in 2027 “if our ambitions outstrip our ability to reinvest.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that the survey draws on responses from 753 strategy sponsors about how their aims performed during 2025.
  • Sources indicate that “The Roth era is here.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Plan Sponsor Council of America reported in its 69th annual survey that 42.4% of organizations have already adopted, or will adopt, a Roth option for employer contributions in their 401(k) plans, compared with 19.7% a year earlier.

Recent findings suggest that the survey draws on responses from 753 strategy sponsors about how their aims performed during 2025. Another 11% are considering the option, according to CNBC.

Sources indicate that “The Roth era is here. SECURE 2.0’s mandatory Roth catch-up made Roth essential for nearly every plan, and sponsors aren’t stopping there,” Will Hansen, the council’s executive director, said in a statement.

Roth use is also growing among employee contributions, the survey found. Among the surveyed looks, 96.9% give participants a Roth option, and 24.5% of participants now use it, compared with 22.1% before. Among plans with Roth deferrals available, 65.0% let participants shift existing balances into Roth money without leaving the plan, compared with 61.0% before.

Workers used to receive their employer's matching dollars solely on a pretax basis, according to CNBC. The SECURE 2.0 law, signed in 2022 by then-President Joe Biden, allows employers to provide a Roth match if they choose. A strategy that offers one does not apply it automatically, and workers must opt in.

Hattie Greenan, the council's research director, told CNBC she expects the share of employers offering the option to keep rising. "Roth is becoming mainstream," she said.

Industry observers note that financial advisers told CNBC the choice between Roth and pretax savings varies by person. Roth contributions carry no up-front tax break, but qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free. “It’s personal preference,” mentioned Philip Chao, who holds the certified financial planner designation and serves as chief investment officer at Experiential Wealth, in comments to CNBC.

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 12, 2026 at 5:51 amNovember 12, 2026 at 5:51 am.

DeltaGen, an AI startup that got its start in Seattle before moving to San Francisco this year, has been acquired by Worker.ai, a upcoming small-business software organization backed by Veeam founder Ratmir Timashev.

Worker, which launched Thursday, acquired all of DeltaGen for an undisclosed price that included a substantial cash component and equity in Worker, DeltaGen co-founder and CEO Rene Bystron told GeekWire.

Bystron joins Worker as co-founder and COO, and nine other DeltaGen employees are coming with him, including co-founders Michal Studnicka and Matus Ondreicka.

According to recent reports, worker, led by co-founder and CEO John Roberts, a former private equity operator based in Raleigh, N.C., is building software that lets small businesses hand off recurring work to AI agents. DeltaGen’s voice technology captures decisions made in conversations and turns them into assigned tasks.

Roberts had been a DeltaGen customer before Worker needed voice technology, Bystron remarked. “We could have raised another round and kept building independently, but this gave us the capital and experience to move faster with people we trusted,” he said.

Launched in 2024, DeltaGen raised a $1.2 million pre-seed round in early 2025 to build generative AI tools for financial professionals, with a focus on streamlining mergers and acquisitions. The organization relocated from Seattle to San Francisco earlier this year.

Recent findings suggest that “I still love Seattle and miss it like crazy,” said Bystron, who is keeping his apartment in Belltown. “But being closer to the AI founders, customers and investors in San Francisco makes a real difference at this stage. It also didn’t help that Washington has been chipping away at its tax advantage.”.

Timashev, who co-founded data backup giant Veeam, is backing Worker to help small businesses such as manufacturers, service companies and family businesses grow.

Recent findings suggest that “AI can now give small businesses more capacity without asking already stretched owners to work longer days,” he said in a statement. “Worker is my bet on that shift.” The size of his investment was not disclosed.

Sources indicate that deltaGen’s current product is an AI voice platform, which will continue as it’s integrated into Worker. DeltaGen’s AI voice platform will continue as it’s integrated into Worker, which is opening access gradually through a waitlist.
