📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 09:00 EST / NOVEMBER 17 2026.

It has been revealed that vulnerability management startup Cogent Security Inc. today launched DefenseOS, an operating system designed for artificial intelligence agents that carry out defensive cybersecurity work inside the enterprise.

Sources indicate that arriving with DefenseOS are two new capabilities, Agent Policies and Agent Automations. The first is designed to give Cogent’s AI agents a deep understanding of the enterprise environment, while the second puts recurring security work on an automated schedule.

Recent findings suggest that cogent is pitching DefenseOS at security teams that are struggling to keep up as AI speeds up the discovery of vulnerabilities. In October, Microsoft Corp. fixed more than 1,400 security flaws in a single Patch Tuesday release, more than it fixed in all of 2025. The window between disclosure and exploitation has also shrunk, by Cogent’s count, from months in 2024 to only hours this year.

Recent findings suggest that prioritizing at that pace requires context such as which assets are business-critical, which are exposed to the internet and who owns them. According to the company, that information is spread across documents, teams and tribal knowledge, and most organizations see only a fraction of it.

In a recent development, in its role as the context engine for Cogent, DefenseOS ingests data from scanners, business systems and other security tools. Once the data has been normalized and deduplicated, DefenseOS encodes how the enterprise functions to deliver accurate risk scoring, prioritization and remediation. The platform serves as the AI harness that sets the working environment and limits for Cogent’s agents.

It has been revealed that the first of the two new capabilities, Agent Policies, is described by Cogent as creating a context layer that builds and grows via agents, turning how an enterprise works into rules. Those rules then shape how the Cogent platform handles asset context, risk scoring, prioritization and remediation. The firm claims the feature strips out much of the operational overhead that enterprises formerly had to put into running a vulnerability management program.

The second, Agent Automations, acts as the execution layer within DefenseOS. Using it, security teams can build agentic workflows that run automatically to generate alerts and reports, investigate vulnerabilities and deliver remediation guidance on a consistent basis.

In a recent development, co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Geng Sng said recurring reports, known investigations and routine alerts take up a large share of a security team’s week. With Agent Automations, he said, teams can “define that work once” and have Cogent’s agents run it on their schedule.

In a recent development, “Every enterprise runs its security program differently, and moving at machine speed means grasping those differences,” stated co-founder and Chief Executive Vineet Edupuganti. “DefenseOS unifies the context of an enterprise environment, surfacing rules into Agent Policies that a customer can codify, and creating the runtime environment for continuous cyber defense led by AI agents.”.

The launch follows the release earlier this month of VR-1.1, a new version of Cogent’s frontier reasoning model that writes fixes for newly disclosed software vulnerabilities.

DefenseOS and Agent Automations are available now to all Cogent customers. Agent Policies has launched in beta for newly introduced Cogent deployments ahead of general availability at a later date.

It has been revealed that founded in 2025 and staffed by former researchers and operators from Google DeepMind, Abnormal AI Inc. and Coinbase Global Inc., Cogent states Fortune 500 security teams using its platform have cut the exposure window for critical vulnerabilities by 97%. The tech giant has raised $53 million to date, including a $42 million Series A led by Bain Capital Ventures in February.

1 Chase outage and 6 bank failures in 2026 reached customers' money differently

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3677 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 16 Chase software bug disrupted banks and Zelle, and the FDIC listed 6 failures in 2026.
  • When people say their bank is down, they can mean two very different things, and in 2026 Americans saw both.
  • According to recent reports, the November disruption felt bigger than it was partly because of when it came.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Nov. 16 Chase software bug disrupted banks and Zelle, and the FDIC listed 6 failures in 2026. Here is what each meant for customers' money.

When people say their bank is down, they can mean two very different things, and in 2026 Americans saw both. With the loud kind, customers could not reach their money, but none of it was lost. Customers trying to sign in during the November disruption met login errors. Chase mentioned those customers still had access to their accounts and their money, according to TIME. The fear of loss and the reality did not match. The quiet kind is a bank closing for good. Such closures were rare going into this year, with just two bank failures in the U.S. in all of 2025, according to the Chicago Sun-Times. Closures picked up in 2026 but stayed uncommon. How much noise a banking problem makes and how much harm it does are two separate questions, and the answers often differ.

According to recent reports, the November disruption felt bigger than it was partly because of when it came. It followed a Microsoft $MSFT outage on the Thursday before and an air traffic control outage on the Friday, then bank customers ran into trouble on Monday, according to The Associated Press. Nothing ties those three breakdowns to a common cause. What they share is timing. Still, a frozen login screen at the end of a week like that feels like a system in danger, while a small bank quietly changing hands on a Friday feels like nothing at all. People's instincts about which trouble is serious can easily run backward, and sorting the two kinds apart is the useful work.

USA TODAY set out to explain the Nov. 16 bank disruption that began at JPMorgan $JPM Chase and to list the year's bank failures, with entries ranging from Zelle to Nano Banc and Tioga-Franklin Savings Bank. The FDIC listed six bank failures in 2026, and none of them had any link to the November disruption. Each was a bank closed over its finances, not a technology breakdown. Read together, the two kinds of trouble show where the real cost of a banking problem falls. Sometimes it is a customer's lost afternoon. Sometimes it is a charge to the insurance fund that backs deposits. The question for any bank customer is which kind of trouble ever reaches their money, and why.

The November 16 bank disruption had a single source, JPMorgan $JPM Chase, and not a breakdown across the whole banking industry. The cause sat inside one institution's own systems, yet customers felt it at once and in large numbers. At the peak, nearly 4,800 to 5,000 reports of problems with Chase reached Downdetector, according to USA TODAY. That many people speaking up in the same stretch of time makes an outage feel like an assault, and the natural first guess is a hack.

In a recent development, the outage had no attacker behind it, which places it among the ordinary failures that have disrupted large banks before. Chase and DHS officials found no evidence of a cyberattack. Major banks have lost their systems to mundane faults in the past. At one large bank, smoke set off an automatic shutoff that cut power to a data center, and in 2016 Bank of New York could not send or receive SWIFT payment messages for 19 hours, according to a Federal Reserve analysis published in 2022. A fault with no villain behind it can still drag on for hours. Ruling out an attacker removes the villain from the story, but it does not remove the risk. A bank's own systems can fail for long stretches without anyone breaking in.

Sources indicate that the fault began at one bank. Whether it stayed there is the next question.

In a recent development, on Nov. 16, customers of JPMorgan $JPM Chase were not the only ones who complained. TIME reports that people also flagged problems with Bank of America $BAC, Wells Fargo $WFC, Capital One $COF, Truist and Zelle that day. Bank of America, the next most reported, drew just over 2,000 reports on Downdetector, and Wells Fargo, Capital One, Truist and Zelle drew hundreds each. Those totals were far lighter than the flood of complaints at Chase, where the trouble began. A pattern that heavy at one bank and much lighter at the rest most likely reflects trouble spilling over from Chase, not six separate breakdowns at the same moment.

A bank can draw a flood of complaints while nothing inside it has broken. U.S. Bank customers filed 1,060 reports, according to TIME, yet the bank denied any fault of its own. "U.S. Bank systems are not directly impacted," a U.S. Bank spokesperson remarked. The likeliest explanation is that its customers were trying to send money to or through Chase that day. A reader who sees their own bank named in an outage report should expect that a payment might stall, not that the bank itself is in trouble.

Zelle was the most misunderstood name among the services customers reported. TIME reports that Zelle, according to its spokesperson, keeps no separate accounts for consumers and holds none of their money. A stalled Zelle payment is a stalled message between two banks, and the dollars stay at the bank on one end or the other. Zelle links many banks, so customers whose own banks were working could still find their transfers held up when Chase had trouble. When Zelle seems down, the banks on either end are the place to look. A delayed transfer could still leave someone waiting for money they needed that day, but the money itself stayed at a bank the whole time.

Customers made the November 16 disruption public through a flood of complaints. At the peak, nearly 4,800 to 5,000 people reported problems with Chase, according to Downdetector. That crowd was large enough to make the day feel like a national emergency, but it counts people who spoke up, not people who lost money. Reports about Zelle came in as well, though many people think of the payment app as separate from any one bank. Early Warning Services owns Zelle, The Associated Press reports, and that company's owners include financial institutions. Banks share that network, so customers who never opened Chase's app could still feel one bank's trouble. The people caught up in the outage were not only Chase customers. Anyone whose payment touched Chase that day could be caught up in it.

In a recent development, the disruption followed individual payments, not whole banks, and customers elsewhere slowed down only when Chase stood on the other side of a transfer. "This is not a systemic glitch — other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us," Joe Evangelisti, spokesman for JPMorgan $JPM Chase, told The Associated Press. That is the bank's own account of its own failure, and readers should weigh it as a claim, not a settled finding. It does fit the complaints about Zelle, whose job is moving money from one bank to another. For someone who banks elsewhere, the risk that day came from sending money to or through Chase, not from any fault at their own bank.

The complaints filled every board that Monday, yet people felt the outage only when their payments crossed the connections between banks, and those connections are the weak point worth watching.

Sources indicate that JPMorgan $JPM Chase had its own systems working again on the same day the trouble began. Users had started flagging errors by 11:30 a.m. ET, according to CNBC. While complaints were still arriving, the bank promised a fix before the day was out. "We're working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today," a JPMorgan spokesperson noted. USA TODAY reports that Chase said its transactions were processing normally on Nov. 16, so by the bank's own account it kept that promise. Both the promise and the all-clear came from Chase, and the all-clear covered only its own transactions.

Customers dealt with the trouble for longer than the bank's timeline suggests. People kept reporting problems through Monday night, and the reports largely subsided only in the early hours of Tuesday, Nov. 17. No one has given a separate time when service returned to normal at other banks or at Zelle. For anyone outside Chase, the clearest sign that the trouble had ended was the drop in complaints overnight.

The outage gave no sign of a threat to the money in customers' accounts. Chase and officials at the Department of Homeland Security found no evidence of a cyberattack. By Chase's account, ending the outage meant fixing a fault inside its own systems, not driving out an intruder. For customers, the documented cost was the wait for logins and payments to work again.

A larger question remains: whether the banking system is built to absorb this kind of failure.

In a recent development, the bank where a disruption starts claims little about whose payments end up stuck, because banks rely on the same few service providers and send payments to one another all day. The November 16 disruption began at JPMorgan $JPM Chase, according to USA TODAY, but the customers held up that day banked across the system. Federal Reserve Board analysts Chase Englund and Zach Modig report that in a scenario where one provider in their study, which they call Provider 2, was disrupted for an hour on a sample day, only one of the 23 firms most central to the payment network bought its service directly. Nearly all of the banks at the center of that scenario had no direct tie to the provider in trouble. A customer whose bank has no tie to Chase can still get caught in a Chase outage, and the more useful question is whether that bank sends payments along the same paths.

Community banks appear among the firms the payment network leans on most. In the hour the analysts studied, eight of those central firms belonged to a group of community bank holding companies, according to analysts at the Federal Reserve Board. Choosing a smaller bank does not, on its own, keep a customer away from the part of the network where trouble can spread.

For a household or a business, the real test of an outage is whether the rent, the payroll or the transfer due that day went through, not how long the login screen stayed frozen.

Sources indicate that the year's string of bank closings began at a modest lender in Chicago. Metropolitan Capital Bank & Trust closed on Jan. 30, the first of the six bank failures the FDIC recorded in 2026, according to USA TODAY. The Chicago Sun-Times reports that the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation shut down the bank, which was based in the city's River North neighborhood. A state regulator closed it over its finances, and none of its systems had broken. It was also too small to signal trouble in banking as a whole, with about $261.1 million in assets as of Sept. 30, a modest sum by banking standards. Its customers kept their money because First Independence Bank of Detroit took over all of the deposits, and their accounts continued at the fresh bank.

The failure did cost money, but the bank's depositors did not pay it. Acting as receiver, the FDIC put the price of this closing for its Deposit Insurance Fund at about $19.7 million, according to the Chicago Sun-Times. The FDIC keeps that fund to cover losses of this kind. "We want to be clear that no depositor will lose any money as a result of this action," noted Susana Soriano, acting director of the Division of Banking at the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation. A bank failure can carry a real price and still leave every customer's account whole, because the FDIC pays that price from its insurance fund.

Sources indicate that A failed bank is not latest to Chicago. The city has had 22 bank failures since 2000, according to the Chicago Sun-Times, and this closing adds one more to that long record. Soriano notes the state closed this bank because it was operating in an unsafe way and did not have enough capital. That broad finding is the only reason on record, and no specific cause has been made public, so the failure points to no particular danger for other banks.

Nobody has explained in public what went wrong inside the bank, but its customers' deposits were already safe at a fresh bank.

Community Bank and Trust - West Georgia closed so smoothly that its customers lost little more than a weekend. The bank became the second failure of 2026 on May 1, months after the year's first in January, according to the FDIC. That gap shows how rarely banks closed this year. The Georgia Department of Banking and Finance shut the LaGrange, Ga., community bank, and Anchor Bank of Palm Beach Gardens, Fla., took over its insured deposits. Customers ended up with a new bank rather than none, and the old branches reopened as Anchor Bank the following Monday, May 4. They saw none of the error screens that marked the November lockout.

According to recent reports, the quiet weekend hid an expensive failure. Community Bank and Trust was a small lender that held $288 million in assets at the end of 2025, according to the FDIC. The modest size of the bank helps explain why its closing drew so little notice. Yet covering the failure is expected to take approximately $97 million out of the Deposit Insurance Fund, a sum that is large next to the bank's own size. Readers can't judge the price of a bank failure from the size of the bank alone. Regulators can close a small bank with little public notice and still draw heavily on the fund that stands behind every insured account.

The only depositors who faced real risk were those with balances above the insurance limit. Approximately $27 million in deposits went beyond that limit, a figure likely to change, according to the FDIC. That money sat in the bank's largest accounts, and it was the only depositor money without insurance behind it. The pattern here runs opposite to the November disruption. In November, nearly everyone was inconvenienced and no one's money was at stake. In LaGrange, almost no one was inconvenienced, and the only money without a guarantee was the part of the largest balances that went past the insurance limit.

A bank on the federal failure list can be one that few people outside a single small town have ever heard of. Kentland Federal Savings and Loan Association, a savings and loan in Kentland, Ind., failed on July 10, 2026, according to an FDIC list of the year's bank failures reported by USA TODAY. It was a very small bank, with about $3.65 million in deposits as of March 31, according to Financial Regulation News. A count of failures treats a bank of that size the same as a much larger one, and the number of closings alone says little about how much money was at stake.

Kentland did not close because of a hack or a system crash. Its own finances gave out. Financial Regulation News reports that the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency shut the association after finding it critically undercapitalized. In plain terms, the bank no longer had enough capital of its own to stay open. Customers cannot check a bank's capital on an app, and trouble of this kind never demonstrates up as a frozen login screen. The problem that ends a bank can be the one its customers are least likely to see coming.

Industry observers note that kentland's depositors did not lose their money. Their deposits are now held at Kentland Bank and remain FDIC-insured, according to Financial Regulation News. Kentland Bank is a separate institution with no affiliation to the failed association. Customers' accounts changed hands, even though the name on their statements barely changed. The town's loss is practical rather than financial, because the association's only branch is closing for good. The FDIC expects to pay for the failure from its Deposit Insurance Fund, not from account holders, at an estimated cost of about $1.2 million, according to an FDIC estimate reported by Financial Regulation News.

A failure this quiet still costs real money, and Kentland's depositors were not the ones who paid it.

In a recent development, bank failures came closer together in midsummer 2026. Small Business Bank, a lender in Lenexa, Kan., shut on July 17 and became the year's fourth failure only seven days after the Kentland savings and loan closed, according to USA TODAY. The Kansas Office of the State Bank Commissioner closed the bank, and the FDIC took charge as receiver, according to the FDIC. Whether a bank's collapse ever reaches its customers' money depends on that handoff to a federal insurer more than on the failure itself.

For depositors, the failure changed little beyond the name on the sign. Customers got no warning, and the FDIC reports that the public receives no advance notice when a bank is closed. The Farmers State Bank of Oakley, Kan., took on substantially all of the deposits along with certain assets, so savers' money moved to the fresh bank together with their accounts. The old locations reopened as Farmers State Bank branches, and customers walked through the same doors under a new name. The November outage kept people away from money that was never at risk. This failure ended a bank, and its customers went on banking.

In a recent development, customers who already held accounts at Farmers State Bank have one detail to know. Their transferred deposits and their existing accounts at the bank are insured separately, according to the FDIC, so the two sets of balances do not fall under a single coverage limit. The rescue covered the depositors and stopped short of the bank's owner. Gardner Bancshares, Inc., the holding company that owned all of the bank's shares, was not included in the receivership.

The safety net carried the depositors through the failure and left the owner outside it.

Industry observers note that state regulators kept closing banks through the summer, and Tioga-Franklin Savings Bank in Philadelphia became the fifth of the year's six FDIC-listed failures, according to USA TODAY. The FDIC reports that Pennsylvania's Department of Banking and Securities closed the bank on Friday, Aug. 21, 2026. The federal agency counts the closure among the year's failures, but a state agency made the decision. The FDIC stepped in only after the state acted, serving as receiver to take over and wind down what was left of the bank. Anyone tracking the national tally of bank failures is therefore, at least in this case, tracking a state regulator's decision about one local bank.

Industry observers note that depositors at Tioga-Franklin kept the basic services they depended on, even though the closure came without any advance public notice, according to the FDIC. The public learned of the failure only after the bank had already shut. Direct deposits continued as usual through the change of ownership, so paychecks and benefits kept arriving on schedule. The physical bank stayed in place too. Customers can keep using the same locations, which now operate under the name of Second Federal Savings and Loan Association of Philadelphia, a bank based in the same city. They could walk into the same buildings and deal with a local institution rather than a distant one.

A bank closed in Philadelphia that summer, yet its depositors kept both their direct deposits and their branches.

Nano Banc, a lender in Irvine, Calif., failed on Sept. 25, the latest of the six bank failures in 2026, according to FDIC figures reported by USA TODAY. It was a state-chartered member of the Federal Reserve, so the Fed oversaw it directly, according to the Federal Reserve. Regulators had been watching the bank for years before it closed. As early as February 2021, the bank had agreed in writing to corrective terms set by the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco. Nano Banc did not break overnight. Its trouble had been on the public record long before September.

The warnings grew more serious as regulators moved from a written agreement to legal orders. The state of California ordered the bank to cease and desist in December 2021, and the Fed followed the next month with a consent order that became binding on Jan. 18, 2022, according to the Federal Reserve. By the time of the 2022 order, examiners had found unsecured loans to shareholders of Nano Financial Holdings, the bank's parent manufacturer. When a bank lends to its owners without collateral, it puts their interests ahead of the safety of depositors' money. Nano Banc also had no permanent chief executive or chief financial officer in 2022, while it still had to carry out the corrective steps its 2021 agreement with the Fed required. The bank faced a large repair job with no one permanently in charge. That was a plausible warning sign, though not a forecast of failure.

The 2022 order reached past the bank to the companies that controlled it, binding both of its holding companies, Allegiant United Holdings and Nano Financial Holdings, according to the Federal Reserve. That fits a problem that involved the bank's owners. Still, a record of warnings does not establish a cause, and no reason for the September closing has been made public. The orders from 2021 and 2022 are evidence of long-running trouble, not an explanation of why the bank failed.

It has been revealed that the warnings that mattered here never appeared as error screens. They were public orders from regulators, issued years before the failure, and for anyone worried about their own bank, those orders are a quieter and more telling place to look.

Strategy, the world's largest corporate Bitcoin (BTC) holder, has sent an crucial message regarding Bitcoin’s future resistance to quantum computing attacks.

The organization, which was co-founded by renowned Bitcoin champion Michael Saylor, recently posted on X that the Bitcoin network can implement new security measures as and when they are needed.

“Quantum-resistant upgrades can be adopted if & when it's needed,” wrote Strategy.

These comments come at a time when the crypto industry is debating whether the rise of quantum computing could, in the long run, threaten Bitcoin’s cryptographic security.

Given that Bitcoin leverages elliptic curve cryptography for transaction security, quantum computing could pose a significant threat to Bitcoin.

It has been revealed that A sufficiently powerful quantum computer has the potential to reverse-engineer private keys from exposed public keys. This could give attackers access to the Bitcoin holdings associated with those keys.

At this point, there is no known publicly available quantum computer that can successfully break Bitcoin’s cryptography in this manner.

While speaking at the World Bank in Washington in October, Saylor noted that the Bitcoin network would be able to defend itself against any realistic quantum computing threat by coming together and upgrading the software.

Saylor estimated that such an upgrade would take about 90 days once a worldwide consensus is reached on the need for quantum-resistant cryptography.

Saylor also warned against the hasty introduction of newly introduced cryptography. He reasoned that more complex security measures may themselves introduce weaknesses.

However, the 90-day estimate has come under scrutiny because such a network-wide shift would involve developers agreeing on technical changes and Bitcoin users moving their funds to new, secure addresses.

Interestingly, Strategy has also initiated efforts aimed at research and development for Bitcoin’s long-term security.

In July, Strategy was part of a group of seven major financial institutions and crypto companies, including BlackRock and Coinbase, that formed the Bitcoin Security Consortium.

Sources indicate that the Bitcoin Security Consortium has committed $15 million over three years. One of the areas of focus of the consortium is post-quantum cryptography.

In fact, Bitcoin developers are already working on ways to address the quantum computing concern.

One of the most prominent proposals is Bitcoin Improvement Proposal 360 (BIP-360). This BIP introduces a fresh type of transaction output, Pay-to-Merkle-Root (P2MR).

by Todd Bishop on Nov 12, 2026 at 12:15 pmNovember 12, 2026 at 12:16 pm.

Docugami, the Seattle-area startup led by XML co-creator Jean Paoli, has been acquired by Inveniam, a Detroit-area firm that uses blockchain to help investors verify the data behind assets such as commercial real estate and private loans.

The deal follows a partnership this summer in which the companies released DGML, Docugami’s open-source format for turning business documents into data that AI agents can use and check.

Financial terms of the acquisition weren’t disclosed. All of Docugami’s employees are joining Inveniam, a Docugami spokesperson mentioned. The team numbers about 50 including contractors. Paoli becomes Inveniam’s chief product and technology officer, and Docugami will keep operating from Kirkland, according to the announcement.

Paoli co-founded Docugami in 2018 after more than 20 years at Microsoft, where he helped create XML and the Office file formats.

The startup, based in Kirkland, Wash., raised a $10 million seed round in 2020 led by SignalFire, with backing from Bob Muglia, the former Microsoft executive and Snowflake CEO. Grammarly, the writing-assistant company now known as Superhuman, later disclosed that it had taken part in the round, its first investment in another company.

Prior to the acquisition, Docugami ranked No. 155 on the GeekWire 200, our list of the Pacific Northwest’s top independent, privately held startups.

In a recent development, DGML labels each piece of a document by what it is — a base rent, a loan payment, a liability cap — so a single figure can be traced back to the page it came from. Inveniam records a digital fingerprint of each of those data points on its blockchain, called NVNM Chain, so any later change demonstrates up.

Inveniam executives mentioned Thursday morning on a livestream with Paoli that DGML solves a problem they’ve had in bringing on fresh clients: every client’s documents are different, which required templates and standard formats before the data could be used.

“One promise I want to make personally: DGML stays open and its openness is strategic to Inveniam,” Paoli wrote in a LinkedIn post.

In a recent development, inveniam, led by CEO Patrick O’Meara, also acquired Mantra, a crypto tech giant that provided the original technology for NVNM Chain, earlier this year. Mantra co-founder John Patrick Mullin mentioned on the livestream that NVNM Chain will move to its own independent blockchain, with the main network expected to launch in the next few weeks.

Fees on that network will help fund buybacks of an NVNM cryptocurrency token, Mullin noted. O’Meara proposed a separate session on when that token will launch.

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

In a recent development, webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and indicates it tops Gemma 4 31B. The card's own footnotes show why the comparison deserves a re-run.

A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500. The most revealing line in its model card isn't a score, though. It's a footnote saying the competitor numbers were never re-run.

Industry observers note that webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers. The 8.8B-parameter reasoning model is post-trained from IBM's Granite 4.2 8B using full-parameter supervised fine-tuning, followed by GRPO/DAPO reinforcement learning. A final length-aware RL stage produces the "balanced" variant, which is the default.

Sources indicate that the card reports 98.2 on MATH-500 and 88.3 on AIME 2025. It claims TwIL-8B posts the highest MATH-500 and LiveCodeBench scores in its comparison group, which includes Gemma 4 31B at about 3.5 times its size. That claim is worth testing, because small models that beat larger ones are exactly what open-weight people want to hear.

On MATH-500, the card lists TwIL-8B at 98.2, Qwen3.5-9B at 96.6 and Gemma 4 31B at 87.9. On AIME 2025, TwIL-8B scores 88.3 against 87.1 for Gemma 4 31B. On LiveCodeBench, TwIL-8B scores 81.6 against 80.0, though that figure carries a dagger marking it as measured on the verbose variant, not the default balanced one.

The card is also more candid than most. It says TwIL-8B is not a knowledge model. GPQA Diamond comes in at 70.2, trailing Gemma 4 31B by 14.1 points, and the model also trails on MMLU-Pro and HLE. There is no safety or preference tuning beyond what Granite carries, and the license is non-commercial. That honesty makes the claims easier to weigh.

According to recent reports, here is where the headline gets complicated. TwIL-8B's scores come from webAI's own internal high-effort pass@1 runs. The card states that competitor scores are published figures and were not re-run.

In a recent development, gemma 4 31B's 87.9 on MATH-500 comes from Red Hat's evaluation of an FP8 build, using the lighteval harness, not from Google. The card itself notes that this figure is unusually low and may reflect answer extraction. In other words, the 10.3-point gap that anchors the headline compares one team's own harness against a third party's number that the card suspects may be understated.

None of this makes TwIL-8B's result wrong. It means the margin isn't established until both models run under the same harness, prompt and sampling settings. For reference, Google's Gemma 4 model card is the source for several of the other Gemma figures in the table.

It has been revealed that read the whole table and the picture is more balanced than the headline suggests. In the card's head-to-head summary, TwIL-8B beats Gemma 4 31B on 3 of 14 shared benchmarks and loses 11. It leads on MATH-500, LiveCodeBench and AIME 2025, but trails on AIME 2026 (88.3 against 89.2), HMMT Feb 2026 (68.2 against 77.2), GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and IFEval.

The AIME 2025 lead is the shakiest. The card indicates AIME and HMMT sets have 30 to 33 problems, so one problem is worth about 3 points, and gaps of that size sit within noise. A 1.2-point margin is well under one problem, so the result is best read as a tie.

Against the closest same-size rival, Qwen3.5-9B, the card demonstrates the models roughly level on contest math, with TwIL-8B using fewer tokens: about 19.5k per AIME 2026 problem against 31.2k. That efficiency claim may turn out to be the more durable one.

Industry observers note that the card makes replication unusually practical. The Q4_K_M balanced GGUF weighs 4.98 GiB and runs through llama.cpp, with a command given in the card. Larger Q8_0 and F16 builds exist only for the verbose variant. The model also needs a massive generation budget, since a short limit truncates its reasoning and scores far worse. The card suggests settings around 32,768 newly introduced tokens and a 40,960-token context.

Anyone planning a check should expect three catches. First, the card says all its scores were measured on bf16 weights, not the GGUF builds, so a CPU run tests a slightly different artifact, and the card expects small deviations, most likely at Q4_K_M. Second, MATH-500 is 500 problems and each answer can run to tens of thousands of tokens, so CPU testing will be slow. Third, the decoding setup matters, since the card says none of its numbers use low-effort or thinking-off modes.

For a fair comparison, the same prompt, answer extraction and sampling must be applied to Gemma 4 31B too, ideally at full precision.

In a recent development, the card also lists contamination caveats. Its training pools were decontaminated against AIME, HMMT Feb 2025 and 2026, MATH-500, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, HLE, IFEval, IFBench and LiveCodeBench using 13-gram matching. HMMT Nov 2025 and the HumanEval, MBPP and CRUXEval suites weren't in the decontamination set. The MATH-500 and AIME results fall inside the protected group, which counts in the model's favor.

According to recent reports, overall, TwIL-8B looks like a genuinely strong small model for contest math, code and instruction following, and the card is open about its weak spots. The claim to beat Gemma 4 31B is narrower than the headline suggests: a clear lead on one benchmark, a likely tie on another and a loss on most of the rest.

Industry observers note that the useful next step is a same-harness run of both models, with the bf16 weights as a control for the GGUF build. Until independent results appear, the 98.2 is best quoted as webAI's reported figure, and the size-beating framing is better described as unproven than wrong.

Amazon is the best firm in America, according to Forbes.

Industry observers note that the Seattle tech giant took the No. 1 spot on the publication’s 2027 “America’s Best Companies” list, moving up from No. 2 last year and edging out Apple.

Three other Washington state companies landed in the top 50: Microsoft at No. 6, Costco at No. 13 and Alaska Air Group at No. 39.

It has been revealed that last year’s No. 1, Berkshire Hathaway, slipped to No. 4. Nvidia ranked No. 3 on the same day CEO Jensen Huang resigned, following his admission of an extramarital affair. JPMorganChase, Alphabet, Royal Caribbean Group, Walmart and Marriott International round out the top 10.

Industry observers note that now in its third year, the ranking scores thousands of the largest public and private U.S. companies on factors including customer and employee sentiment, financial performance, creditworthiness, cybersecurity and innovation. Forbes said it worked with 12 data organizations to build the index.

It has been revealed that forbes said Amazon’s financial strength and size, its standing in news and social media, and the range of voices across the firm and its leadership lifted it to No. 1. Apple scored especially well on employee satisfaction, customer loyalty, financial strength and innovation.

Forbes also pointed to Amazon’s speed, citing a feature that lets customers shop by text message. An employee suggested it in October and it launched Nov. 6.

“Innovating for customers, doing it fast, working backwards from their needs, that’s really at our core,” Beth Galetti, Amazon’s senior vice president of people, experience and technology, told Forbes.

In its own blog post Thursday, Amazon highlighted everything from faster delivery and custom AI chips to warehouse robotics and higher pay for frontline workers.

The ranking comes after a year of workforce cuts at Amazon. The tech giant eliminated about 30,000 corporate jobs in rounds declared in October 2025 and January 2026, including more than 4,500 in Washington state. Smaller cuts followed throughout the year, including layoffs of fewer than 1,000 corporate employees in October, mainly in its Stores unit.

UPDATED 09:00 EST / NOVEMBER 17 2026.

In a recent development, enterprise identity protection and cyber resilience firm Semperis Ltd. today released the latest version of its Semperis Lightning identity security platform, which is designed to help organizations defend against identity attacks by artificial intelligence agents and conventional attackers alike.

In a recent development, delivered through a single console, the fresh version of Lightning is stated to combine exposure management, attack-path analysis and detection-and-response workflows. Along with Microsoft Corp.’s Active Directory and Entra ID, the new release supports Okta Inc.

In a recent development, semperis claims organizations using Lightning can adopt AI tools for productivity while reducing the risk of agents compromising critical resources. According to Chief Executive Mickey Bresman, identity systems have become “the main control plane” in the agentic age.

Though AI agents move at machine speed through the enterprise, Bresman said, they still depend on the identity fabric for access. With Lightning, organizations are said to be able to create, enforce and monitor what he called “agentic execution boundaries.”.

Chief Product Officer Alex Weinert, who joined Semperis in April 2025 after serving as vice president of identity security at Microsoft, noted security teams “do not need another flat list of identity findings.” Context on what can actually reach the identity control plane is what they need instead, he said. Agentic identities, he added, are opening fresh routes to privileged systems.

Sources indicate that on the exposure side, Lightning, which now comes with a growing catalog of more than 220 security indicators, continuously scans identity infrastructure for exposures in human and nonhuman identities. The results are then scored, according to Semperis, before being triaged in a single workflow.

According to recent reports, the platform’s live identity graph, which Semperis describes as a map of relationships and attack paths, covers routes to domain administrators, privileged accounts and other critical assets. According to the manufacturer, remediation guidance from the graph is prioritized by risk so that teams can respond faster.

Industry observers note that nonhuman and agentic identities are discovered automatically, Semperis says, and added to a searchable inventory of every identity in an environment. The company claims Lightning can scale to the largest multitenant, multiforest environments.

In a recent development, built-in rule templates are designed to detect suspicious activity in Active Directory and Entra ID, such as unusual logons over Kerberos and NT LAN Manager. The tech giant is also offering what it calls generative assistance alongside the templates.

Sources indicate that semperis introduced Lightning in April 2024 with Lightning Identity Runtime Protection, a machine learning-powered identity threat detection service. The firm extended its resilience offerings to Okta and Ping Identity Corp. environments in February, when it acquired MightyID Inc.

More than 1,200 organizations, including over 25% of the 100 largest U.S. companies, are stated to use Semperis. The company last raised $125 million in growth financing from JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Hercules Capital Inc. in June 2024. Earlier investors include Kohlberg Kravis Roberts & Co. LP, Insight Partners, Ten Eleven Ventures and Paladin Capital Group.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 12, 2026 at 2:41 pmNovember 12, 2026 at 2:41 pm.

Industry observers note that nick Huzar co-founded Juicer Energy in 2023 to make electric vehicle charging more widespread and reliable. Now the Seattle-area startup is pursuing a broader goal: helping buildings manage rising electricity demand and costs.

Industry observers note that juicer installs and operates EV charging systems at apartment buildings, hotels and other properties. It is also developing battery systems to store electricity on-site and help manage the power needed for charging and other building uses.

The push comes as data centers and the growing use of electricity for transportation, heating and other needs put more pressure on the grid. Batteries can help balance supply and demand by storing energy when electricity is plentiful and releasing it when demand peaks. In some cases, they can reduce the need for costly grid upgrades or latest power plants built to meet peak demand.

“We think there’s a big opportunity there,” Huzar said. He spoke at an event this week hosted by GeekWire and Bank of America at the Bellevue showroom of Ferrari of Seattle.

In a recent development, other companies are similarly pairing EV charging with battery storage. Fellow Seattle startup Electric Era has deployed battery-backed fast chargers at retailers including Costco and convenience stores. ADS-TEC Energy and XCharge also sell fast-charging systems with integrated batteries.

Huzar, OfferUp’s co-founder and former CEO, sees an opportunity to make buildings more self-sufficient by combining hardware and energy-management software. He said Juicer has a project scheduled to come online in 2027 with 70 chargers in one building.

His longer-term vision also includes tapping the energy stored in vehicles connected to those buildings.

It has been revealed that “Imagine you’re an apartment owner and you have 20 EVs, 40 EVs plugged in,” Huzar stated. “That is a huge amount of power. Like you’re a mini power plant at that point.”.

In a recent development, he described feeding excess electricity back to the grid as a possibility that remains years away. He also predicted that most businesses, apartments and homes would have on-site batteries within the next decade, in part because battery costs continue to fall.

Juicer started with EV charging, Huzar said, “but the more we’ve gotten into this, the more we realize that we actually can build an asset for buildings versus relying on the grid.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Four lessons from the Chargers' first win of 2026 in Baltimore, from a late forced fumble to a run defense that held the Ravens to 16 yards.
  • A team that keeps losing has to stop losing before anything else about it can be judged fairly.
  • Sources indicate that the team across the field was struggling, too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Four lessons from the Chargers' first win of 2026 in Baltimore, from a late forced fumble to a run defense that held the Ravens to 16 yards.

A team that keeps losing has to stop losing before anything else about it can be judged fairly. For the Chargers, the losing outlasted an entire offseason. Their last win before Monday came against the Cowboys in Week 16 of 2025, according to NBC Sports. The drought spanned two seasons, not just a bad start to one. Ending it was a genuine release for a team that had gone most of a calendar year without a victory. The relief also makes it tempting to treat everything that worked on that one night as the start of a turnaround, and that temptation is worth resisting.

Sources indicate that the team across the field was struggling, too. The game was Baltimore's fifth straight loss, according to NBC Sports, and ESPN reports that it dropped the Ravens to 4-6. Monday night matched two slumping teams rather than handing the Chargers an upset of a contender. Baltimore was also without its star quarterback. Lamar Jackson was out with a right thumb injury, according to ESPN, and Jacoby Brissett played his first game for the Ravens after Baltimore acquired him in a trade. The Chargers' defense faced a quarterback who was still new to his offense. The win counts in the standings, but it came in a softer test than a typical Monday night in the NFL. The useful question for each lesson from the game is whether it would hold up against a healthier, sharper opponent.

Industry observers note that the Los Angeles Chargers set out on the team's website to draw the key lessons from the Monday night win over Baltimore, from a defense that shut down the Ravens' running game to a late forced fumble and a ground attack that the offense relied on. Each of those lessons holds true for that one night. They differ in how much of each result the Chargers earned on their own and how much came from the condition of the team they played. Some rest on choices the coaching staff can make again next week, while others depended on what Baltimore could and couldn't do. The Chargers get their first chance to find out promptly, when they host the Jets at SoFi Stadium in Week 11.

The Chargers led the Ravens from start to finish on Monday night, according to NBC Sports, and still had to hang on for their first win of the season. A road win in Baltimore in prime time would usually point to a team that finally took control of a game. The Chargers instead won 23-20, according to chargers.com, and finished only one score ahead of an opponent that never once held the lead. They pulled ahead by double digits twice in the second half, and Baltimore kept closing the gap after each of those leads. The close finish did not come from a stronger team rallying late. It came from the Chargers failing to put away an opponent they were already beating.

Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh credited his offense, defense and special teams alike for the win, but Baltimore moved the ball better than his team did. The Ravens gained 347 yards to the Chargers' 287, according to NBC Sports, and the Chargers' offense did not carry the night. The defense helped make up for that gap by forcing two turnovers. Takeaways tend to rise and fall from week to week, while a yardage edge is a steadier sign of which team controlled play. The Chargers won without that steadier sign on their side. After eight straight losses, the result mattered more than the way the Chargers reached it. Whether a win built this way can hold up is the question the rest of the night's lessons have to answer.

The Chargers' first win of the season came down to one Baltimore possession, and their defense ended it by taking the ball away. Baltimore had the ball on its final drive with the Chargers up three, according to chargers.com. ESPN reports that Zay Flowers lost the ball with 2:03 left, after cornerback Tarheeb Still kept working for it following the catch and pulled it free. "That was huge. Tarheeb was able — the ball come away from the body, and he was right there to claw it out," Chargers coach Jim Harbaugh told ESPN. With the ball back, the Chargers' offense no longer needed to score. It only needed to keep possession, and Justin Herbert's pass to Charlie Kolar on the next play gave the Chargers the first down they needed to run out the clock.

The defense had to make that play because the offense had stopped scoring touchdowns after halftime. The Chargers managed only a field goal in each of the third and fourth quarters, according to ESPN, so the offense added nothing in the second half that could put the game out of reach. Baltimore's passing game was carrying its offense, with Jacoby Brissett finishing the night at 340 yards, and Flowers had just caught one of his throws when Still stripped him. Still took the ball away from the part of Baltimore's offense that had been working, at the last moment when Baltimore could still tie or win the game.

A single forced fumble, however well timed, does not yet make a pattern. Chargers safety Tony Jefferson indicates the defense discusses going after the ball every day and treats it as a habit to keep repeating. The coming weeks will show whether the defense takes the ball away from offenses that are moving it well. Until then, Still's strip saved one win but has not shown that this defense can produce more of them.

Industry observers note that A team trying to finish off its first win of the season needs a way to move the ball without giving it back, and the Chargers chose to run it. They ran for 160 yards at Baltimore, a total they had not reached in any earlier game this season, according to chargers.com. The offense also played its most careful game of the year and finished without a turnover. USA TODAY reports that it was Justin Herbert's first game of 2026 without an interception. By running the ball, the Chargers kept moving it without putting it at risk, which is what a winless team holding a lead needed most.

The big rushing night came from a decision about who would carry the ball. Mike McDaniel, who calls the Chargers' plays, stopped splitting carries among his running backs for this game, USA TODAY reports, and Omarion Hampton answered with the team's first 100-yard rushing game of 2026. Hampton finished with 105 yards on the full workload of a featured back. His longest run went only 19 yards, so he built his total from steady gains, not from a single breakaway. "The downhill runs were extremely good," Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh remarked. Runs like those depend on how the staff uses Hampton, not on luck, and the coaches can call them again as long as they keep giving him the ball.

It has been revealed that herbert also gave Baltimore a second runner to account for, and his scramble produced the Chargers' first touchdown. The run game did not build every score, though. Hampton's touchdown followed an interception of Jacoby Brissett that the Chargers turned into points, according to USA TODAY. The defense helped set up that score as much as the runners did, so the running game's clearest value on Monday was control and safety.

This lesson depends least on Baltimore's condition, because it rests on a choice the Chargers make for themselves.

Baltimore had no running game to fall back on at any point in the night. The Ravens finished with 16 rushing yards and gained none before halftime, the Chargers' best run defense of the season, according to chargers.com. That left Baltimore with an offense that could only throw. Stopping the run was the Chargers' plan from the opening snaps, and it worked before Baltimore had any chance to wear the defense down. "There was a heck of a run wall, big emphasis on that," Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh mentioned. The Chargers also stopped the back Baltimore trusted most. Derrick Henry gained 10 yards on 10 carries, according to ESPN, so Baltimore could not keep handing him the ball until he found room.

It has been revealed that the defenders who stopped the run also reached the quarterback when Baltimore threw. Jacoby Brissett faced 23 pressures from the Chargers, according to ESPN, on a night when his team could give him almost no help on the ground. Together, those results point to a Chargers front that won at the line of scrimmage on running plays and passing plays alike.

According to recent reports, one strong night does not yet show a lasting change. Holding Baltimore to 16 yards stands out against every earlier game this season, and a single game that stands out that much is hard to treat as the new standard. Harbaugh's emphasis on the run suggests the Chargers can bring the same effort again. They have not yet shown they can get the same result against other offenses.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 13, 2026 at 7:24 amNovember 13, 2026 at 4:23 pm.
  • 13 with additional Microsoft statements.
  • If emails sent by Outlook consumers on Thursday are just now landing in your inbox, no, you haven’t gone back to the days of the Pony Express.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 13, 2026 at 7:24 amNovember 13, 2026 at 4:23 pm.

Updated at 4 p.m. PT Nov. 13 with additional Microsoft statements.

If emails sent by Outlook consumers on Thursday are just now landing in your inbox, no, you haven’t gone back to the days of the Pony Express. Microsoft is still digging out from a nearly daylong outage that cut off email for businesses, schools and governments around the world.

As of early Friday, the company reported that email queues were “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels,” though some customers could still have trouble getting in or see delayed messages.

In a post on X Friday morning, Microsoft said it was “deeply sorry” for the disruption to customers and partners. The manufacturer said the outage was a technical matter, not related to a cyberattack or AI agents.

The problem was introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade and surfaced after a more recent network change, the organization said, adding that it has addressed the underlying glitch and is still restoring service to remaining customers and regions.

In a recent development, we are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services.This was a technical issue….

Industry observers note that in an upgrade on its status page at 5 a.m. Pacific, Microsoft stated it was seeing “broader improvements now observed in North America and sustained improvements across much of Europe,” along with early signs of recovery in Asia Pacific.

The problems started Thursday morning with Exchange Online, the Microsoft service that runs Outlook email for businesses, and spread to other Microsoft 365 services that depend on it, including Teams calendars, Copilot and SharePoint.

Microsoft mentioned servers were failing automated health checks and dropping out of service, which overloaded the ones that were left. The organization paused all deployments while it worked on a fix, and some of its repairs Thursday evening were “not taking as expected.” Microsoft said it restored service gradually, checking stability at each stage, which took longer but helped ensure a stable restoration.

Earlier, The Verge’s Tom Warren reported on X that his sources linked the outage to configuration changes in Azure Virtual Network, Microsoft’s cloud networking service.

Australia’s Home Affairs Minister, Tony Burke, told reporters in Sydney that Microsoft believes it is dealing with something similar in some ways to the 2024 CrowdStrike outage, “where there is an update that has gone awry,” the Associated Press reported.

“We know our customers rely on our services to get notable work done every day, and regret the impact these outages had on those who depend on us,” remarked Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, in a statement provided to GeekWire. He said Microsoft’s teams are reviewing what happened and how to prevent similar problems.

In a post on X Friday afternoon, Lamanna stated the investigation points to “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter,” which made recovery harder than normal. A thundering herd happens when large numbers of clients try to reconnect at the same time, overwhelming systems as they come back online.

He noted Microsoft will publish a post-mortem “shortly” with a step-by-step timeline and the repairs it looks to make to avoid similar outages.

Industry observers note that the outage reached well beyond email. Government offices in Japan, Singapore and the Philippines reported disruptions, according to the AP. Workhorse Group delayed its quarterly earnings call, and OpenAI and Anthropic both reported problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools.

Credit rating agency Morningstar DBRS estimated insured losses of $300 million to $500 million, well below estimates for CrowdStrike, which ranged from $400 million to $1.5 billion. Some cyber insurance policies cover only malicious attacks, the firm noted, though it said the toll could grow if the outage drags on for several days.

The disruption hit close to Microsoft’s home. Ansel Herz, a spokesperson for the Seattle mayor’s office, told the Seattle Times that the outage didn’t bring city government to a halt but knocked out the systems that move documents and messages around City Hall.

The newspaper quoted Herz calling the outage “a huge pain.” In a post on X, he chided the paper for not using his whole quote, which we presume was “a huge pain in the ass.”.

Industry observers note that we’ve followed up with him to confirm this important detail. Here’s hoping he gets the email.

Patch, 10 a.m.: Herz did receive GeekWire’s message and responded, confirming the quote and saying that, to his knowledge, nothing public-facing was affected at the city. Email appears to be back and working properly as of Friday morning, he said.

Grand Theft Auto history in 10 milestones, from DMA Design's 1997 top-down original through GTA V and GTA Online to the Leonida-set GTA 6.

Recent findings suggest that grand Theft Auto has changed its viewpoint and its format several times since 1997, yet it keeps returning to the same few fictional places. The series began as a top-down game made by DMA Design, a Scottish studio, and published by BMG Interactive on PC and PlayStation. Grand Theft Auto III, published by Rockstar Games, launched on PlayStation 2 in October 2001 and moved the series into a full 3D open world. Grand Theft Auto Online followed in October 2013 as a multiplayer mode, shortly after Grand Theft Auto V. It has been updated over the years. Those shifts in perspective and format form the backbone of the Grand Theft Auto history traced here.

The 1997 original was set in three fictional cities: Liberty City, San Andreas and Vice City. Each name came back later in a newly introduced form. Grand Theft Auto III rebuilt Liberty City in 3D. Grand Theft Auto: Vice City, released in 2002, used its name for a 1980s Miami-inspired setting. Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, released in 2004, used its name for a state with three cities: Los Santos, San Fierro and Las Venturas. Grand Theft Auto IV went back to Liberty City in 2008 and ran on the RAGE engine. Grand Theft Auto V, released in September 2013, was set in Los Santos.

Sources indicate that the series also moved through time. Grand Theft Auto: London, 1969, a 1999 expansion pack for the original game, placed the action in the London of 1969. Grand Theft Auto 2, another 1999 release, went the other way. That top-down sequel was set in a near-future city and used a gang-respect system. The San Andreas story was set in 1992.

The people at the center of the games changed as well. Tommy Vercetti led Vice City. Carl "CJ" Johnson led San Andreas. Niko Bellic, an Eastern European immigrant, led Grand Theft Auto IV. Grand Theft Auto V split its story across three playable protagonists: Michael De Santa, Franklin Clinton and Trevor Philips.

According to recent reports, grand Theft Auto VI, which Rockstar has revealed, is set in the state of Leonida, with Vice City as a setting. Its first trailer was released in December 2023.

The 10 slides below cover a selection of milestones from the series, not every game it includes. They run in chronological order, from the 1997 original to Grand Theft Auto VI.

Industry observers note that grand Theft Auto released in 1997 as a top-down game from DMA Design, a Scottish studio. BMG Interactive published it on PC and PlayStation.

According to recent reports, the top-down view defined how the original looked and played. Players watched the action from a camera positioned above the city.

That viewpoint did not end with the first game. The 1999 sequel, Grand Theft Auto 2, kept the same top-down approach.

Sources indicate that the 1997 game spread its action across three fictional cities. They were Liberty City, San Andreas and Vice City. All three appeared within that single release.

Those names outlasted the original. Each one returned in a later entry of the series.

The publisher also changed after the first game. BMG Interactive released the 1997 original. Grand Theft Auto III, released in 2001, was published by Rockstar Games.

It has been revealed that grand Theft Auto: London, 1969 is a 1999 expansion pack for the original Grand Theft Auto. It moved the action to London and set it in the year 1969.

Sources indicate that an expansion pack adds upcoming content to an existing game. It is not a new numbered entry in the series. London, 1969 built on the 1997 original, the top-down game that started Grand Theft Auto.

The expansion arrived two years after that first game.

Recent findings suggest that its setting broke with the original. The 1997 game took place in three fictional cities. London, 1969 used a real city instead.

It also tied the action to a specific year in the past. That year falls 30 years before the expansion's own release.

Grand Theft Auto 2, released in 1999, was a top-down sequel to the original Grand Theft Auto. It was set in a near-future city called Anywhere, USA, and used a gang-respect system.

In a recent development, the sequel kept the overhead perspective of the 1997 game. Players still saw the city from above.

Recent findings suggest that the setting changed. The original game spread its action across three fictional cities: Liberty City, San Andreas and Vice City. Grand Theft Auto 2 placed its story in one city set in the near future.

Sources indicate that the sequel came out in the same year as Grand Theft Auto: London, 1969. That expansion pack for the original game looked back to 1969 London, while Grand Theft Auto 2 looked ahead.

Grand Theft Auto III moved the series from a top-down view to a full 3D open world. Rockstar Games published it on PlayStation 2 in October 2001.

Liberty City was its setting. That made Liberty City the first location in the series built as a three-dimensional open world.

In a recent development, the main games before it demonstrated their cities from overhead. The 1997 original used that top-down perspective. Grand Theft Auto 2, released in 1999, kept it. Grand Theft Auto III dropped the overhead map for a world built in three dimensions.

The city's name went back to the start of the series. Liberty City first appeared in the 1997 Grand Theft Auto as one of its three fictional cities.

Recent findings suggest that the publisher had changed too. BMG Interactive published the 1997 original on PC and PlayStation. Rockstar Games filled that role for Grand Theft Auto III.

It has been revealed that grand Theft Auto: Vice City, released in 2002, set the series in a fictional city inspired by 1980s Miami. Its protagonist is Tommy Vercetti.

It has been revealed that the game came out the year after Grand Theft Auto III, which was set in Liberty City. Vice City replaced that location with one drawn from Miami.

The setting combines a place and a period. The place takes its cues from Miami, a real U.S. city. The period is the 1980s, a past decade rather than the present day.

Tommy Vercetti is the character players control in that 1980s world.

Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, released in 2004, casts players as Carl "CJ" Johnson in a story set in 1992. Its map is a fictional state that holds three cities: Los Santos, San Fierro and Las Venturas.

The state itself is called San Andreas, and the game takes its title from it. Los Santos, San Fierro and Las Venturas each have their own name, but all three sit on the same map.

It has been revealed that the 1992 setting puts CJ's story 12 years before the game came out in 2004. The game is set in the recent past, not the present day.

It has been revealed that carl Johnson is the game's protagonist. He goes by the nickname CJ.

Grand Theft Auto IV, released in 2008, took the series back to Liberty City and ran on the RAGE engine. Its protagonist is Niko Bellic, an Eastern European immigrant.

Sources indicate that the RAGE engine is the technical marker for this entry. Grand Theft Auto IV used it to build its version of Liberty City.

Liberty City was not a fresh location for the franchise. It was one of three fictional cities in the original 1997 Grand Theft Auto. The other two were San Andreas and Vice City. That first version of the city was shown from a top-down view.

Grand Theft Auto III used Liberty City again in 2001. That game moved the series into a full 3D open world. Grand Theft Auto IV came back to the same city seven years later.

Across this timeline, Liberty City is the setting for three entries: the 1997 original, Grand Theft Auto III and Grand Theft Auto IV. The 2008 game is the one in that group built on the RAGE engine.

Niko Bellic gives the game its point of view. He is an Eastern European immigrant. The two entries just before this one in the timeline each had a different lead. Grand Theft Auto: Vice City, from 2002, followed Tommy Vercetti. Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, from 2004, followed Carl "CJ" Johnson.

In the GTA timeline, the 2008 game arrived four years after Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas. It came five years before Grand Theft Auto V, which was released in September 2013 and is set in Los Santos.

In a recent development, grand Theft Auto V, released in September 2013, gives players three protagonists instead of one. They are Michael De Santa, Franklin Clinton and Trevor Philips, and all three are playable.

That structure departs from the entries that came before it. Grand Theft Auto: Vice City cast players as Tommy Vercetti. Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas followed Carl "CJ" Johnson. Grand Theft Auto IV centered on Niko Bellic, an Eastern European immigrant.

It has been revealed that each of those games was built around one named lead. Grand Theft Auto V divides its story among three characters instead. The design moves the series from a single point of view to several within the same game.

The game is set in Los Santos. That name already had a place in the series. Los Santos was one of three cities in Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, alongside San Fierro and Las Venturas.

Grand Theft Auto V came out nine years after San Andreas, which was released in 2004. San Andreas spread its story across a fictional state with three cities. Grand Theft Auto V is set in one of them.

The release also followed Grand Theft Auto IV by five years. That 2008 game was set in Liberty City. Grand Theft Auto V moved the numbered series from Liberty City to Los Santos.

Grand Theft Auto Online is a multiplayer mode that debuted in October 2013. It arrived shortly after Grand Theft Auto V, which was released in September 2013.

Sources indicate that that timing puts the two releases side by side in the GTA timeline. Grand Theft Auto V came out first, and the multiplayer mode went live soon after.

Grand Theft Auto Online has been updated over the years since that 2013 debut. The mode players reach today is not the same as the one that first launched.

That pattern sets it apart from the entries before it. It has a single launch date, followed by years of further updates.

It has been revealed that grand Theft Auto VI is set in Leonida, a fictional state, and Vice City is one of its settings. Rockstar has declared the game, and its first trailer was released in December 2023.

Leonida frames GTA VI around a state rather than a single city. Vice City is one location within that state, not the whole setting.

Sources indicate that that structure has a precedent in the series. Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, released in 2004, was also set in a state rather than in one city. GTA VI takes up that wider framing again with Leonida.

The Vice City name runs deep in the GTA timeline. It first appeared in the 1997 original Grand Theft Auto, as one of that game's three fictional cities. In GTA VI, the name returns as part of a larger state.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Working around the clock, the new service analyzes context from customer conversations, emails and customer relationship management data to identify opportunities, prepare personalized outreach and complete work before reps realize it needs doing.
  • Scout is aimed at addressing a limitation of most AI assistants, which still require people to tell them what to do, according to Spara.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 09:00 EST / NOVEMBER 17 2026.

Artificial intelligence sales agent startup Spara Inc. today introduced Scout, an AI assistant designed to act on sales opportunities before salespeople know to look for them.

Working around the clock, the new service analyzes context from customer conversations, emails and customer relationship management data to identify opportunities, prepare personalized outreach and complete work before reps realize it needs doing.

Scout is aimed at addressing a limitation of most AI assistants, which still require people to tell them what to do, according to Spara. The service instead works within the daily workflows of salespeople, providing an always-on partner that keeps track of customers and helps move work forward without constant direction.

Signals analyzed continuously by Scout include job changes, organization news, buying signals and CRM activity across a salesperson’s accounts. From there, the service determines when to engage customers and prospects, as well as who to contact. Instead of requiring another platform to manage, Scout delivers its findings through Salesforce Inc.’s Slack and text messages.

Over time, Scout retains what it learns about each account, along with the salesperson’s preferences and previous outreach. Doing so is remarked to allow the service to anticipate next steps and deliver more relevant recommendations.

Outreach messages are drafted in the salesperson’s voice, with reps kept in control of what gets sent. Going beyond recommendations, Scout can join customer calls and contribute to conversations in real time, helping salespeople move opportunities forward.

According to recent reports, “Sales has always been a game of speed, timing and relationships, but there’s only so much one person can keep track of in a day,” mentioned David Walker, co-founder and chief executive of Spara. “Even the best sales organizations can’t realistically give every rep the support they need to act on every opportunity at exactly the right moment.”.

Spara also released early results from users of the new service. Salespeople using Scout were found to have increased the number of personalized emails sent eightfold in their first two weeks of use. Outreach generated by Scout drew a 10.5% reply rate, against 3.5% for traditional sales sequences, according to the company. Early users also booked 29% more meetings.

Chris Brown, a partner at Spara investor Inspired Capital who has worked with the team since the beginning, stated Spara has built agents that go-to-market teams trust with their most important customer conversations. Scout is now “putting that trust to work for individual sellers,” he added.

Scout is available for free starting today at spara.com/scout.
