Uncommon Thinkers: Alexis Harroun aims for space with a latest engine — and stays grounded

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1430 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 13, 2026 at 7:46 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:19 am.
  • According to recent reports, editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec.
  • A few weeks after learning that her tiny startup had won a NASA prize to fly its engine in space, Alexis Harroun was camping in Yellowstone, sitting around a fire and looking up at the stars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 13, 2026 at 7:46 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:19 am.

According to recent reports, editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

A few weeks after learning that her tiny startup had won a NASA prize to fly its engine in space, Alexis Harroun was camping in Yellowstone, sitting around a fire and looking up at the stars. Satellites kept drifting past overhead — and the news finally sank in.

In a recent development, “I’m like, oh, we’re going to be sending something up and we’re going to be able to see it,” she mentioned. “That was very humbling in a lot of ways and very exciting.”.

Recent findings suggest that harroun is co-founder and CEO of Juno Propulsion, a Tukwila, Wash.-based startup building a new kind of rocket engine. Instead of burning fuel in a steady flame, Juno’s engines use detonation, a supersonic combustion wave that releases more energy from the same amount of propellant.

“It’s essentially like a higher MPG rocket engine,” Harroun noted.

The technology has been studied for decades but has never flown in orbit. Juno aims to change that next year, when its engine is set to fly aboard a Momentus satellite in a mission called Project Iris.

That’s a significant goal for a firm that, when the July 2025 NASA call came, was just Harroun, co-founder and CTO Ari Martinez and a summer intern working out of a one-room office.

Sources indicate that if Iris succeeds, Juno’s engines could let satellites run on non-toxic fuel and maneuver far more freely in orbit, something both commercial and defense customers increasingly want. For Harroun, who earned her Ph.D. studying these engines, it would be the payoff of years of work.

Industry observers note that harroun sees the technology as a long-overdue leap. The basic physics behind today’s rocket engines dates to the 1930s and has been refined about as far as it can go, she said, calling it a constraint that’s “been a glass ceiling for too long, in my opinion.”.

Harroun grew up south of Seattle in Federal Way. She didn’t come from an aerospace family or spend her childhood dreaming about space. Her dad was a physician and her mom a flight attendant and flight instructor.

What she did pick up at home was an entrepreneurial streak. Her dad ran his own practice for about 20 years, and her mom is now a real estate agent. Harroun remarked watching them make “something out of completely nothing” has shaped her own path, especially in building Juno.

Industry observers note that she calls herself a “late bloomer” who fell for engineering as she was finishing high school and heading to the University of Washington. Sci-fi became an inspiration along the way, and it’s now one of her favorite genres.

She spent all four years at UW working with professor Carl Knowlen, who leads the Aeronautics & Astronautics Department’s Detonation Engines Lab, and she joined the student rocketry team, eventually leading its propulsion group.

Recent findings suggest that knowlen “sees the potential in everyone,” Harroun said, and the two built a strong relationship that’s still going. Juno’s $1.2 million National Science Foundation grant, awarded this summer, is a partnership with his research group.

Knowlen was also the faculty adviser for the student rocketry team, where he spent “many hot, and sometimes rainy, days” with Harroun and her teammates, test-firing motors and launching high-powered rockets.

Industry observers note that “She always was level-headed and led by example,” Knowlen said. “No one worked harder than her to see these tests and releases go off as planned.”.

He called her “an exceptional student, natural leader, creative thinker, and very independent,” and stated it’s been a great satisfaction to see the engineer she has become.

During college, Harroun interned at NASA, Boeing and Blue Origin. That first stint at Blue Origin, in 2016, set her next move.

“I realized that everyone who had the job that I wanted had gone to Purdue,” she said.

According to recent reports, she spent the next six years at Purdue University in West Lafayette, Ind., earning a master’s degree and a Ph.D. Her doctoral research was on the technology Juno is now building. She also met Martinez there. The two shared an office for years.

Harroun never planned to stay in academia.

“That just didn’t feel like my calling,” she said. “I wanted to use that very unique experience to get the technical chops to do the type of engineering that I wanted to do.”.

Her doctoral advisor, Purdue professor Stephen Heister, still advises her and the company.

It has been revealed that “He was one of the people who really pushed me to think about starting this tech giant,” Harroun mentioned. “I think he saw the potential that I had as a founder, both from a technical and a leadership perspective.”.

Heister recalled their first technical discussion, when Harroun arrived as a latest master’s student. He went deep on nozzle flows, her thesis topic, and the complications of building a nozzle for a detonation engine.

“At the end of my diatribe, she sat quietly and said, ‘You’ve given me a lot to think about,’” Heister said. “I can’t think of any other 22-year-old student with such a response but I knew she was indeed a special talent.”.

He described Harroun as having “the unique ability to think deeply and at length,” and noted it’s “terribly gratifying” to watch her commercialize the technology she worked on as a grad student.

It has been revealed that after finishing her Ph.D. in 2023, Harroun came back to the Seattle region and started Juno. She knew the territory: her UW lab work and the rocketry team had put her in touch with local industry, and Juno now works with some of the same companies she did as a student.

It has been revealed that interning at Blue Origin was the first time she could say “there’s literally a rocket company in our backyard,” Harroun said. Its presence helped build a regional talent pool, which she described as “a contingent of rocket scientists that just live here.”.

Starting a tech giant comes with many unknowns, and coming home crossed one off the list.

It has been revealed that “I knew how to go start doing stuff immediately,” she noted. “So it made that calculus really easy.”.

Harroun’s ambitions reach well beyond one demo flight.

“Our mission is to be the rocket engine provider for the U.S.,” she mentioned. “Think of a Rocketdyne.”.

According to recent reports, that firm built engines for the Saturn V and the space shuttle, and it’s now part of L3Harris. Juno wants to play a similar role with a upcoming technology. It’s starting with in-space propulsion for satellites and plans to expand into engines for upper stages, orbital transfer vehicles and, eventually, the boosters that lift rockets off the pad.

It has been revealed that the first step is Project Iris. NASA paid Juno about $500,000 through its TechLeap program to build the payload, and it’s also covering the Momentus spacecraft and the flight. There’s no paying customer yet, but the mission is designed to mimic the maneuvers a real satellite would make.

In a recent development, japan’s space agency has flown rotating detonation engines on suborbital research rockets, but going to orbit is “a whole ‘nother game,” Harroun stated. “Going to space is hard. I can attest to that.”.

Industry observers note that building a manufacturer has taught Harroun things her Ph.D. didn’t. Handling toxic propellants is so complicated, she learned, that operators can spend more fueling a satellite than on “the propulsion system itself, which is kind of crazy.”.

It has been revealed that the bigger draw is mobility. For decades, satellites have mostly stayed in the orbit a rocket left them in, she stated, and “that’s not really acceptable anymore in today’s world.”.

To get there, Juno has raised a $1.4 million pre-seed round led by SOSV, on top of its NASA and NSF awards.

As for going to space herself, Harroun admits it would be hard to say no if she got the opportunity.

But the avid hiker and backpacker is partial to terra firma. Her best-case future is one where Earth is the place humanity gets to enjoy and space is what makes that possible.

“I don’t know that I would be the traveler,” Harroun mentioned, “but I’d definitely like to be the enabler.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that could Ripple’s XRP, Dogecoin, and Solana eventually lose their place in the crypto market as Bitcoin strengthens its dominance? Billionaire investor Tim Draper believes the future of cryptocurrencies could look very different, predicting that altcoins will eventually be absorbed by Bitcoin.

Draper’s bold forecast raises fresh questions about the long-term survival of major digital assets and whether BTC’s growing influence could ultimately leave even established altcoins struggling to remain relevant.

Tim Draper has drawn a striking comparison between Bitcoin’s potential dominance and Microsoft’s rise to power in the software industry, arguing that the OG crypto could eventually absorb innovations pioneered by competing digital assets.

In a recent post on X, Draper suggested that Bitcoin could follow a similar path to Microsoft, which built its dominance not necessarily by inventing popular software applications but by incorporating successful innovations into its broader ecosystem.

According to recent reports, to illustrate his argument, Draper pointed to Microsoft’s handling of early software pioneers such as Lotus 1-2-3 and WordPerfect. Although these companies helped establish demand for spreadsheet and word-processing applications, Microsoft eventually introduced Excel and Word and integrated both into its operating system. The company also acquired PowerPoint early on, turning the presentation software into another core part of its productivity suite.

According to recent reports, according to Draper, this strategy allowed Microsoft to absorb successful ideas while the companies that initially popularized them gradually lost their competitive edge. He believes Bitcoin could follow the same playbook, with alternative cryptocurrencies serving as testing grounds for innovations that could eventually migrate to the Bitcoin network.

“Altcoins are the Lotus 1-2-3s and WordPerfects of this era,” Draper wrote, arguing that competing blockchain projects may demonstrate the value of latest technologies before Bitcoin adopts them. In his view, Bitcoin’s powerful network effects and growing ecosystem could give it the gravitational pull needed to attract innovations from across the broader cryptocurrency industry.

It has been revealed that draper further supported his argument by highlighting Bitcoin’s expanding share of the overall cryptocurrency market. The billionaire recalled watching the flagship cryptocurrency’s market dominance climb from approximately 40% to 50% and eventually reach 61%. He views this steady increase as evidence of Bitcoin’s growing influence and its ability to strengthen its position despite the emergence of thousands of competing digital assets.

“Bitcoin is that platform,” Draper asserted.

If his prediction proves accurate, established altcoins such as Ripple-linked XRP, Dogecoin (DOGE), and Solana (SOL) could face an increasingly challenging competitive environment. Each has built its reputation around distinct use cases and communities, but Draper’s argument suggests that Bitcoin could eventually incorporate innovations that currently give these competing networks their appeal.

For instance, XRP is best known for its focus on cross-border payments and the expanding financial ecosystem built around the XRP Ledger. Dogecoin, meanwhile, has evolved from an internet meme into one of the cryptocurrency market’s most recognizable assets, backed by a dedicated community. Solana, on the other hand, has established itself as a major smart contract platform, attracting developers with its high transaction speeds and relatively low fees while supporting a diverse ecosystem of decentralized finance (DeFi), NFTs, meme coins, and tokenized real-world assets.

Ultimately, Draper’s thesis is that these innovations could be a boon for BTC rather than guarantee the long-term dominance of the altcoins that pioneered or popularized them.

#18361. Base Switches Off Flashblocks as Denim Goes Live: The Migration Risks Behind 200ms Blocks

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1236 w)
📖 Baca

Base Switches Off Flashblocks as Denim Goes Live: The Migration Risks Behind 200ms Blocks

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1236 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, base's Denim upgrade replaced Flashblocks with five canonical blocks per second.
  • For about sixteen months, Base's fastest blocks were only promises.
  • Denim went live on Base mainnet on November 5, after activating on Sepolia on October 21.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

According to recent reports, base's Denim upgrade replaced Flashblocks with five canonical blocks per second. What that means for sequencers, RPC providers and smart contract developers is where the real story sits.

For about sixteen months, Base's fastest blocks were only promises. Since November 5, they are the ledger itself.

Denim went live on Base mainnet on November 5, after activating on Sepolia on October 21.

According to the upgrade page, the chain now produces five complete canonical blocks every second instead of one every two seconds. Flashblocks, the preconfirmation layer that ran alongside the two-second blocks since July 2025, is retired.

Most coverage stopped at the speed figure. The sharper question is what separates a canonical block from a preconfirmation, because that gap decides what breaks and what improves for anyone building on the chain.

Those updates were the sequencer's early word on what the next block would contain. They were previews of pending state, and nothing in them had its own hash, state root or receipts until the two-second block was sealed. Developers therefore had to keep an early execution result mentally separate from a settled transaction.

It has been revealed that denim turns the 200ms unit into the real thing. Under Base's 200ms Native Blocks specification, every block carries its own number, hash, state root, receipts and forkchoice updates, and moves through the unsafe, safe and finalized stages like any other block.

Sources indicate that the sequencer's job gets heavier and stricter. Instead of streaming fragments of a larger block, it has to build and execute a full block for every 200ms slot. The header keeps its timestamp in whole seconds, so Denim adds a metadata transaction, the BaseTime deposit, placed second in every block. It supplies the sub-second portion: 0, 200, 400, 600 or 800 milliseconds.

Timing rules are tight. Slots can't be skipped, and each block's full timestamp must land exactly 200ms after its parent's. That timestamp comes from a schedule tied to the Denim activation and the block number, not from the sequencer's clock, so wall-clock time only determines when a build begins. Once execution finishes, the client rejects any block that breaks the 200ms progression.

Industry observers note that this removes a layer of ambiguity. A preconfirmation was only as strong as the sequencer's word, while a canonical block can be validated, replayed and challenged by any node running the same derivation rules.

Industry observers note that app developers face the biggest practical shift. Flashblocks streams ended at activation, so anything built on newFlashblocks, pendingLogs or the pending block tag has to move to canonical subscriptions like newHeads and logs. The migration guide lists the API changes required.

The seconds-based timestamp field stays as it was for compatibility. Block, header, transaction, log and receipt responses now include optional millisecond fields, timestampMs and blockTimestampMs, derived from authenticated BaseTime data. They are left out when that data has been pruned or is unavailable. One tooling detail deserves attention: the spec warns that the plain Alloy AnyRpcHeader type drops unknown fields, so anyone who needs millisecond timestamps must use a different type.

It has been revealed that node providers will see heavier traffic too. Dwellir's analysis notes that any service doing work on every block now does it ten times as often. Five fetches a second replace one every two seconds. Denim improves latency without adding capacity, so infrastructure bills are likely to climb.

Recent findings suggest that finality hasn't gone away either. Faster production doesn't erase the confirmation policy an application picks, and each 200ms block still passes through the same unsafe, safe and finalized stages. Bridges and exchanges that wait for a specific stage before crediting funds may need to rethink how many blocks they wait for, since a block count no longer equals the same stretch of time.

This is the area that deserves the most urgent attention. Base's spec warns that block.number now advances ten times faster in real time, while block.timestamp still ticks in whole seconds. A contract that treats a block count as a duration will see that duration collapse to a tenth of what its authors intended.

According to recent reports, the affected patterns are common ones. Timelocks and cooldowns measured in blocks expire in a tenth of the time. Vesting and emission schedules run ten times faster. Per-block rate limits reset five times a second instead of once every two seconds, which lifts the effective per-second limit tenfold. Governance voting windows set in blocks shrink the same way. Uniswap V3-style TWAP oracles stay accurate, but a fixed observation cardinality now covers less wall-clock history, so long lookbacks can revert sooner.

Contracts built on block.timestamp are unaffected. Where a block count can be adjusted through governance, teams proposal to divide it by ten. Where it is hardcoded into an immutable contract, the spec says it can't be retuned after activation, which leaves migration as the only fix. Denim also tightens transfer rules for Base's B20 token standard, and transfers to a token's own address now revert.

Recent findings suggest that the coming weeks will show how much of this stays theoretical. Three things are worth tracking: whether any immutable contract with block-count logic misbehaves, how providers cope with the jump in per-block requests, and whether apps built around Flashblocks have fully moved over.

Denim looks like a cleaner design than the layer it replaced. A preview mechanism gives way to a block anyone can verify, and developers pay for it with a real migration. Speed grabbed the headlines, but the lasting change is that Base's sub-second confirmations now stand on the same footing as the chain's ordinary blocks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 13, 2026 at 12:51 pmNovember 13, 2026 at 4:38 pm.

Araceli Biosciences, a Portland-area biotech manufacturer, has secured $4.5 million in funding to help commercialize technology and develop new products that support using human cells instead of animal studies to test new drugs.

According to recent reports, the Tigard, Ore., startup offers instruments and software for creating images of cells and automating analysis. Its technologies fall under the umbrella term “New Approach Methodologies,” which includes human-tissue models, computer simulations and AI-based approaches that reduce or avoid experimentation on animals such as mice, rats and monkeys.

It has been revealed that supporters of the methods, known as NAMs, argue that they can yield better outcomes because animals are not a perfect substitute for humans and can generate irrelevant findings. That can lead to costly, time-intensive development of drugs that fail to perform in people. Advocates also promote the alternatives as more humane.

The National Institutes of Health unveiled $84 million in September to build infrastructure for NAMs research at 10 sites nationwide.

“[T]he efforts signal a significant investment into human-based technologies as the future of preclinical science, aiming to make research faster, more predictive, and more directly relevant to human health,” the NIH mentioned in a release.

Araceli noted it has raised a total of $22.7 million from investors. The new round was led by William Cortelyou and included Fluke Venture Partners, according to PitchBook. The company disclosed Thursday that businessman and animal welfare advocate Jeff Swickard was also an investor.

Swickard owns 54 auto dealerships across Western states and is a commercial real estate investor with $250 million invested in Portland properties.

Shawn MacDonald, chief financial officer for Araceli, remarked Swickard’s “support reflects a belief that we share, which is that better science and more humane science go hand-in-hand.”.

Araceli introduced in 2023 as a spinoff from Phoseon Technology, which makes UV LED units for industrial curing and life sciences applications.

In a recent development, the manufacturer stated that companies and institutions using Araceli technology include the Max Planck Institute and Evotec in Germany, the Wertheim UF Scripps Institute in Florida, VALID Therapeutics in Boston, and Ginkgo Bioworks, as well as large pharmaceutical companies. It has 30 employees.

The project could also help Amazon navigate a shift in how people shop. Currently, some shoppers are using AI agents to research products and potentially make purchases. AI agents need reliable product information to make recommendations, which is something the World Product Graph could provide.

It has been revealed that if the proposal becomes reality, it could offer Amazon an advantage that goes beyond competitive pricing. The site could offer information that makes other shopping sites feel less useful by comparison.

In a statement to Reuters, Amazon stated it is “constantly working on new ideas and technologies.”.

“Draft, outdated documents often paint an incomplete picture and the existence of a brainstorming document such as this one doesn’t necessarily reflect our current prepares,” the company said in the statement.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As Dogecoin continues to struggle amid prolonged crypto market volatility, its ETF performance has remained muted for the past week, drawing attention from market participants.

Although Dogecoin has retained its position as the king of all meme tokens, institutional demand for the leading meme token has remained on hold as it continues to post deeper price corrections.

Sources indicate that latest data from SosoValue demonstrates that the U.S. Dogecoin spot ETFs have gone an entire month without recording any upcoming inflows or outflows.

More specifically, the two existing spot DOGE ETFs last recorded activity on October 13, when they experienced a combined net outflow of $138,570.

The ETFs became muted the following day, October 14, and neither of the funds has registered a single day of positive or negative flows since then, leaving daily net inflows at zero until November 13.

As such, the Dogecoin ETFs have posted zero flows all month, signaling fading institutional interest in the world’s largest meme token by market capitalization despite its leading position in the memecoin market.

While institutional interest in Dogecoin appears to have declined significantly, both Dogecoin ETF issuers, Grayscale and 21Shares, recorded zero daily net inflows on November 13, confirming that the prolonged period of inactivity remains unchanged.

However, Grayscale's Dogecoin ETF has retained its dominance in the U.S. spot Dogecoin ETF market, holding a total of $9.15 million in net assets, while 21Shares' Dogecoin ETF has held only $1.58 million since its launch.

As such, Grayscale accounts for about 85.3% of the combined $10.73 million in assets held across the Dogecoin ETF market.

10 infamous video game delays, from Duke Nukem Forever to Grand Theft Auto VI

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2138 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • These 10 infamous video game delays, from Duke Nukem Forever to Grand Theft Auto VI, show how game development can stretch across years, studios and console generations.
  • A release date in the video game business is a promise made before the product exists.
  • The announcements and target dates in this list run from 1995 to 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These 10 infamous video game delays, from Duke Nukem Forever to Grand Theft Auto VI, show how game development can stretch across years, studios and console generations.

A release date in the video game business is a promise made before the product exists. Studios often announce games years before the core work is finished. When development runs longer than planned, the date moves. Sometimes it moves again. In a few cases, the wait stretches past a decade.

The announcements and target dates in this list run from 1995 to 2026. In between are projects that changed engines, studios, names, directors and console generations before anyone could buy them. Some of the finished games were completed by teams that were not involved at the start. One shipped on a console that did not exist when it was first shown.

Sources indicate that these 10 infamous video game delays are a selection, not a complete record. They are ordered by announcement date, oldest first. The four earliest were shooters announced between 1995 and 1998. Among the later entries, one game was pulled from a digital storefront eight days after launch.

Each slide covers one game and one kind of delay story. Prey and Duke $DUK Nukem Forever were both confirmed by 3D Realms in the 1990s. They took different routes to release. Valve appears twice: once for a nine-year gap and once for a target date that fell in the same month its source code leaked. Square $SQ Enix also appears twice, with one project renamed midway and another revealed years before it shipped. Sony $SONY's The Last Guardian was revealed for one PlayStation and released on the next. Cyberpunk 2077 shows how a run of shorter postponements can add up. Grand Theft Auto VI remains an open case, with its schedule set by Take-Two announcements rather than a completed launch.

The aim is not to rank failure or to explain away every slip. Delays are a routine part of software development. What sets these examples apart is their length, their visibility or the specific chain of events that kept them from shipping on time. Taken together, they show how wide the gap between a first trailer and a finished product can grow.

Prey reached players in July 2006, 11 years after 3D Realms announced the game in 1995. Human Head Studios built the version that went on sale.

That makes Prey a case where the studio that finished the game was not the studio that first unveiled it. 3D Realms put the project before the public in 1995. Human Head Studios delivered the release that players could buy in July 2006.

Industry observers note that daikatana missed its Christmas 1997 target by about two and a half years. Ion Storm, the studio led by John Romero, released the game on PC in June 2000.

It has been revealed that ion Storm planned to have Daikatana on sale for the 1997 holiday season. That window closed without a release. The holiday seasons of 1998 and 1999 also passed before the PC version reached stores.

Romero led the studio throughout the project. The game shipped under the same studio that had set the original Christmas target.

The game's pre-release advertising campaign drew criticism. That campaign ran before the finished game was available to buy. Players were reacting to Daikatana's marketing years before they could play it.

In a recent development, daikatana's delay combines two separate threads. One is a specific holiday date that the studio did not meet. The other is an advertising campaign that met criticism well ahead of launch. The June 2000 PC release closed the gap between the two.

Team Fortress 2 reached players on October 10, 2007, nine years after Valve announced it in 1998. It did not arrive as a standalone release. Valve shipped it as part of The Orange Box.

Industry observers note that valve made the announcement in the late 1990s. Players could not buy the game until the late 2000s. The project was promised in one decade and delivered in the next.

The release format is the defining detail of this case. The long wait did not end with a launch date of its own. Team Fortress 2 instead reached the market as one part of a larger package.

Sources indicate that duke $DUK Nukem Forever was released on June 14, 2011, 14 years after 3D Realms revealed it in 1997. The studio that announced the game was not the one that finished it.

According to recent reports, the project changed technology in its first year. In 1997, the same year as the announcement, the team moved development to Quake II technology.

According to recent reports, A second switch followed in 1998, when the team moved to Unreal technology. Within two calendar years of the announcement, the project had changed its technical foundation twice.

Recent findings suggest that the next major event on the record came in May 2009, when 3D Realms laid off staff. That was 11 years after the move to Unreal technology.

The layoffs did not end Duke Nukem Forever. Gearbox Software took the project over from 3D Realms and completed development.

It has been revealed that the game reached stores about two years after the layoffs. It shipped under a different developer from the one that first put its name in front of players.

Half-Life 2 was released on November 16, 2004, more than 13 months after Valve's original target of September 30, 2003. The game's source code was stolen and leaked in September 2003, the same month the planned launch was due.

Valve had set September 30, 2003, as the release date for the first-person shooter. That date passed without a finished game reaching players.

Source code is the underlying programming a studio writes to build a game. A leak of that material puts unfinished work in the hands of people outside the manufacturer before the developer chooses to release it. It can expose how a project is built and how far along it is.

On October 2, 2003, Valve's Gabe Newell publicly discussed the theft. His comments came two days after the original target date. By then, the scheduled launch had already been missed.

The record places the theft, the leak and the missed date close together on the calendar. Those dates do not show what pushed the release back. They show only that the events fell within weeks of one another in the fall of 2003. Any account that links them as cause and effect goes beyond what the timeline itself establishes.

Counted from the original target, players waited 413 days for the finished game. That stretch is measured from a fixed release date rather than from a first announcement. It tracks the slip of one specific promise.

The Half-Life 2 delay is defined by its sequence. A missed launch came first, followed within days by a public account from Gabe Newell about stolen code. More than a year later, the finished game arrived.

Recent findings suggest that final Fantasy XV was released on November 29, 2016, 10 years after Square $SQ Enix first revealed it. At its 2006 announcement, the game had a different name, Final Fantasy Versus XIII, and was planned for PlayStation 3.

The original title tied the project to Final Fantasy XIII rather than giving it a number of its own. It was presented as a companion to another game, not as the next main entry in the series.

In 2013, Square Enix renamed the game Final Fantasy XV. The new number took it out from under Final Fantasy XIII and placed it in the main numbered series.

That same year, Hajime Tabata replaced Tetsuya Nomura as director. The director who brought the game to release was not the one attached to it during its years as Versus XIII.

It has been revealed that the 2013 changes split the game's public history into two stretches of unequal length. The first ran from the 2006 announcement to the rename and lasted seven years. The second ran from the rename to the November 2016 release and lasted three years.

According to recent reports, most of the decade between announcement and launch passed under a name the finished game never carried. Players bought it as Final Fantasy XV.

Kingdom Hearts III was released on January 29, 2019, more than five years after Square $SQ Enix revealed it at E3 2013.

The reveal took place at E3, the Electronic Entertainment Expo.

In a recent development, five full calendar years passed between the reveal year and the release year. The game did not reach players at any point from 2014 through 2018.

The release came in January 2019.

Sources indicate that the Last Guardian was revealed at E3 2009 as a PlayStation 3 game and reached players on PlayStation 4 on December 6, 2016. About seven years separated its first public showing from its release.

Sony $SONY introduced the project at E3 2009. It was presented as the next game from Fumito Ueda and Team ICO.

Industry observers note that at that reveal, the named platform was PlayStation 3. The game never came out on that console.

By the time it shipped in December 2016, The Last Guardian was a PlayStation 4 title. The machine named in the original announcement and the machine it launched on came from different PlayStation generations.

According to recent reports, that made this delay a matter of hardware as well as calendar time. The game did not simply arrive late on the console it was declared for. It moved to Sony's next generation before anyone could buy it.

Cyberpunk 2077 missed its first release date of April 16, 2020, and was delayed three times before CD Projekt Red rolled out it on December 10, 2020. Eight days later, Sony $SONY removed the game from the PlayStation Store after complaints about its performance on older consoles.

Recent findings suggest that CD Projekt Red unveiled Cyberpunk 2077 in 2012. The game went on sale eight years after that announcement.

It has been revealed that april 16, 2020, was the first firm date attached to the project. It did not hold. The first delay moved the launch to September 17, 2020. That shift added 154 days, or about five months, to the schedule.

According to recent reports, A second delay pushed the release to November 19, 2020. The new date sat 63 days after the September target.

The third delay was the shortest of the three. It moved the launch from November 19 to December 10, 2020, a gap of 21 days.

Recent findings suggest that each postponement was shorter than the one before it. The schedule moved in shrinking steps rather than in one long jump. Each step also named a specific new day rather than a season or a year.

The original April date and the actual launch ended up 238 days apart, or nearly eight months. Each latest date replaced one that had already been unveiled. Two of the replacement dates, September 17 and November 19, also passed without a release.

In a recent development, set against the full timeline, that stretch was short. Most of the time between announcement and launch passed before any firm date existed. The dated delays covered less than a year of a game first announced in 2012.

Recent findings suggest that sony took the game off the PlayStation Store on December 18, 2020. The PlayStation Store is the digital marketplace where PlayStation owners buy and download games. The removal came 246 days after the original April target.

Industry observers note that every date in this sequence, from the first target to the store removal, fell within 2020. The last entry was not a fresh release date but a removal from Sony's digital store.

Sources indicate that grand Theft Auto VI is scheduled for November 19, 2026, after Take-Two revealed two delays. Rockstar Games and Take-Two had originally targeted 2025 for the game's release.

That original target named a year, not a day. The first delay changed both. Take-Two revealed a upcoming release date of May 26, 2026. The game left 2025 behind and gained a specific day on the calendar.

That date did not hold. Take-Two later revealed a second delay, this time to November 19, 2026. The new date sits nearly six months after the May date.

The two delays did different work. The first took the game out of its original target year. The second kept it in 2026 but moved it late into that year.

It has been revealed that every date in this story so far comes from an announcement. None of them describes a finished launch. November 19, 2026, is the most recent target Take-Two has confirmed. It remains a scheduled date rather than a completed release.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Alan Boyle on Nov 13, 2026 at 2:35 pmNovember 13, 2026 at 2:35 pm.

Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin space venture has decided not to seek further NASA funding for its Orbital Reef space station project in order to tighten its focus on lunar missions.

According to recent reports, for the past five years, Blue Origin has played a lead role in Orbital Reef, alongside partners including Sierra Space and Boeing. In late 2021, Blue Origin won a $130 million contract from NASA in the first phase of the space agency’s Commercial Low Earth Orbit Destinations program, or CLD.

Now NASA is seeking proposals for the next phase of the program, which will fund the development of orbital outposts to replace International Space Station in the 2030s. Proposals are due on Dec. 8, with contracts expected to be awarded next spring.

Blue Origin indicated that it will not submit a bid.

“Blue Origin’s mission is to build a road to space for the benefit of Earth so that millions of people can live and work in space. Establishing a sustained human presence on the moon is a critical step toward that future,” the tech giant noted in an emailed statement.

In a recent development, “As our role supporting NASA’s Artemis and Moon Base missions continues to grow, we’re focusing resources on capabilities that directly advance our lunar projects,” Blue Origin said. “By sharpening that focus, we can move faster on the technologies and infrastructure needed to make lunar permanence a reality.”.

Orbital Reef was once touted as a “mixed-use business park” in space — and was even slated to star in a sci-fi thriller titled “Helios.” But much like that delayed film project, the space station is now on the back burner.

Orbital Reef isn’t the only initiative Blue Origin has put on hold to prioritize moon missions. In January, the organization suspended its suborbital New Shepard program for at least two years for similar reasons.

Industry observers note that blue Origin is building landers for delivering cargo and crews to the lunar surface for NASA. An uncrewed Blue Moon Mark 1 lunar lander is scheduled for launch early next year, and a crew-capable Mark 2 version is scheduled for testing in low Earth orbit next year during NASA’s Artemis 3 mission.

It has been revealed that last week, NASA awarded Blue Origin a $94 million base contract, plus a $140 million option, to deliver a nuclear-powered rover to the lunar south pole. Blue Origin also won a spot in NASA’s broader lunar cargo delivery program. In addition, Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin subsidiary, will contribute to a lunar power-generating project known as miniCAST.

Blue Origin is pursuing several other moon development initiatives, including a program called Blue Alchemist that aims to use lunar materials to manufacture solar cells and electrical wire.

Several competitors are still working on commercial space stations. Voyager Technologies, Airbus and Northrop Grumman lead the Starlab consortium, which received CLD Phase 1 funding from NASA and is expected to put in a proposal for Phase 2.

According to recent reports, axiom Space and Vast are also developing outposts that could take the place of the ISS. Meanwhile, Marysville, Wash.-based Gravitics is building space station hardware for Axiom and an orbital carrier for the U.S. Space Force.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in 2010, Brandon J.
  • Recent findings suggest that “This is what I did,” Hurst says in a new interview with Entrepreneur.
  • Sources indicate that the opportunity offered him a chance to learn the business directly from an operator.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in 2010, Brandon J. Hurst had just graduated from college. He had three options on the table. First, he could stay at Alabama State University, where he had received his Bachelor’s degree, to get a Master’s degree in accounting. Second, he could apply to law school and then go work on Wall Street. Or third, he could take a $12-an-hour job in Chicago working at Chick-fil-A with no guaranteed career path in sight.

Recent findings suggest that “This is what I did,” Hurst says in a new interview with Entrepreneur. “Two weeks after graduation, I packed everything I owned and drove 14 hours straight to start a brand new life in Chicago to work inside of a Chick-fil-A restaurant.”.

Sources indicate that the opportunity offered him a chance to learn the business directly from an operator. He moved there to become a director of operations at the branch — an opportunity he couldn’t pass up.

“I knew whatever I would be doing, I had to be in some type of entrepreneurial capacity,” he indicates.

Chick-fil-A offers an unusually affordable way to enter the restaurant business: Its initial franchise fee is $10,000 and has stayed that way for the past 50 years, per The New York Post. Applicants must use their own money, not borrowed or gifted funds, to pay the franchise fee.

However, that payment does not buy ownership of a restaurant.

Industry observers note that instead, Chick-fil-A selects operators to run locations that the company finances. The company handles major startup expenses, including construction and equipment, and retains ownership of the restaurant’s assets. Operators manage the business rather than acquire an asset they can eventually sell.

Sources indicate that that differs from traditional franchising, where franchisees typically fund the startup investment and own a business operating under another firm’s brand. ADP puts most franchise startup costs between $100,000 and $300,000, with restaurants and hotels among the most expensive options.

According to recent reports, chick-fil-A’s franchise business is also highly competitive. The Post reported that about 100,000 people apply annually to be operators, and of those, 200 are selected, or about 0.2%.

Sources indicate that selected operators must work full-time in the business and divest other non-passive business interests. Chick-fil-A explicitly states the program is not a passive investment. Operators do not receive a traditional corporate salary. Instead, their income comes from a profit-sharing model.

In a recent development, they earn a percentage of the store’s net profits and typically take home anywhere from $200,000 to $400,000 a year. High-performing operators earn more than $500,000 annually.

So operators need comparatively little upfront capital, but they do not build equity in the restaurant. They cannot sell it or pass it down to their children when they retire.

In a recent development, in 2012, Hurst was selected for Chick-fil-A’s leadership development program. For the next three years, he helped operators launch restaurants around the country.

According to recent reports, the work gave him repeated opportunities to practice opening a business without immediately taking responsibility for his own. He supported 14 operators, 12 of whom were external candidates who had never owned or worked at a Chick-fil-A restaurant.

“You ever heard the saying, ‘If you want to master something, teach it’?” Hurst notes. “That’s exactly what I had the opportunity to do.”.

The experience let him repeatedly practice opening restaurants before taking responsibility for one himself.

Sources indicate that in April 2015, at age 26, Hurst opened his first Chick-fil-A restaurant in downtown Baltimore. He wanted to help Chick-fil-A figure out how to operate in dense urban neighborhoods, where restaurants couldn’t rely on the large drive-thrus familiar to suburban customers.

Hurst was in Baltimore for five years before passing the torch to other local operators and relocating to Brooklyn, Latest York. He opened his first Brooklyn restaurant across from Barclays Center in 2019, followed by a second in Clinton Hill in November 2024.

Today, he describes his restaurants as among Chick-fil-A’s highest-grossing locations. According to Restaurant Business, Chick-fil-A’s stand-alone restaurants averaged nearly $9.2 million in sales in 2025. Its busiest location brings in more than $20 million annually, while its top-performing mall restaurant recorded $14.4 million in sales in 2025.

Presented with these statistics, Hurst remarked his restaurants were “well north of those numbers,” without providing an exact figure.

He credits the neighborhoods, customers attending Barclays Center events and, above all, his employees, for his success.

Chick-fil-A stood out to Hurst because he wouldn’t have to create a concept or a brand-new menu.

“Although I have a strong entrepreneurial spirit, I don’t have a whole lot of patience for building something from the ground up,” he says. “I can cook, but I’m more of an operational strategy and leadership development person.”.

Chick-fil-A already provided a brand and systems that allowed Hurst to “hit the ground running” and focus on his strengths.

The financial barrier to entry was also notable. Hurst was able to open his first Chick-fil-A restaurant at age 26 because of the relatively low $10,000 upfront cost when compared to other franchises.

Hurst states future franchise operators should determine their capacity to shoulder risk, then ask what they are willing to sacrifice. “You may have the financial means, but are you ready to invest the time and resources it will take?” he asks.

Hurst says his growth depends on retaining employees.

To that end, he purchased a multi-family building in Brooklyn where team members can live at below-market rents. He also provides access to free mental health care, including up to 10 sessions with a therapist, and telehealth services for employees and their households. Eligible college students can receive reimbursement for textbooks.

It has been revealed that the numbers show that his investments are working. He claims his leaders have an average tenure of about four years. For regular team members, retention rates greater than 12 to 16 months are a win.

Recent findings suggest that hurst says that hiring is about finding people who want to serve others. One question he asks is: “Tell me about a time you wanted to give up and why you didn’t.”.

The answer helps him understand how someone handles adversity in a busy, high-pressure restaurant. Another question he asks is: “How do you define care for yourself?” The answer helps him understand what meaningful support might look like for that person.

But supporting employees also means allowing them to take responsibility. Hurst claims one of his ongoing challenges is building an organization that doesn’t depend too heavily on him.

“If every major decision, relationship or problem” has to come through the founder, he claims, “then I really haven’t built the capacity to scale.”.

Hurst hired an executive assistant about five years ago, who helped him organize his calendar and create space for other work, including his forthcoming book, Outthink Yourself, which comes out in January.

“I wrote the book for anyone who is navigating growth, whether you’re in your first job leading a team or building a business,” Hurst claims. “This book was a four-year process in the making.”.

Hurst organizes his approach to growth around three stages: See, become and build.

The first is understanding the opportunity, problem or risk in front of you. The second is identifying the skills and capabilities you need to pursue it. The third is building systems that make progress sustainable.

He traces that framework through his own career. Assessing the Chicago job required him to get comfortable with uncertainty. Training other operators helped him become a stronger leader. Running two restaurants required him to build teams that could sustain the business.

Sources indicate that his next ambitions include expanding his Chick-fil-A portfolio and working with entrepreneurs through speaking engagements and training workshops. He has also begun developing a second book focused more directly on putting his ideas into practice.

It has been revealed that “More locations, more books,” Hurst says. “I do have very high aspirations for myself.”.

Shiba Inu (SHIB) is set to get more exposure in the U.S.-regulated financial market after the North American Derivatives Exchange (Nadex) self-certified a new strike event contract tied to the meme cryptocurrency's price.

According to recent reports, on November 10, 2026, an official Nadex notice remarked the exchange certified a swap based on the price of SHIB at a specific time and date. The product, called the Shiba Inu Strike Event Contract, began trading on or after Nov. 13, 2026.

The filing is available through the official records of the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC). The regulator’s database highlights that the SHIB Strike Event Contract is certified as a swap, with November 10 listed as the certification date.

Recent findings suggest that the product allows traders to wager that a particular price of SHIB will be attained or surpassed at some point in the future. This opens another avenue for market players to take positions based on the price fluctuations of Shiba Inu without having to buy or hold the underlying token.

In a recent development, nadex (North American Derivatives Exchange) is a CFTC-regulated U.S. financial exchange acquired by Foris DAX Markets (part of Crypto.com), bringing the Shiba Inu product to a regulated platform.

Shiba Inu Japan community member Kuro reacted to the development, saying SHIB is now the underlying asset for a newly introduced financial product in the U.S.-regulated market.

Industry observers note that "Nadex, an exchange owned by Crypto.com, has officially filed a newly introduced trading product based on SHIB’s price, and it has also been listed in the official records of the U.S. CFTC. This product lets traders predict whether SHIB will exceed a certain price at a specified time, alongside assets such as BTC, ETH, and XRP," Kuro added, saying another opportunity for SHIB to be used in the U.S. financial market has just opened up.

At the time of writing, SHIB was down 3.33% over the last 24 hours to $0.00000414 amid broader crypto market weakness that coincided with strength in the U.S. dollar.

The dollar index reached its highest level since April 2025 on Friday, following hotter-than-expected inflation earlier this week that increased expectations of further Fed tightening, pushing Treasury yields and the dollar higher while pulling down both cryptocurrencies and gold.

Industry observers note that workplace management platform firm Envoy Inc. today launched Visitors Critical, a latest tier of its visitor management service for defense contractors, semiconductor fabs and other high-security sites.

The new tier is aimed at a problem Envoy states is common at those sites, where visitor security is still run across email, spreadsheets and separate systems and letting the wrong person in can be costly. Penalties, debarment or a lost facility clearance are all possible after a wrong entry at a compliance-driven site. The person who signed the authorization can also be held liable, according to the manufacturer, which noted that settlements under the International Traffic in Arms Regulations have reached $51 million.

“We’ve spent the last 13 years building Envoy to deliver the highest levels of security, safety and compliance in a way that feels natural to the people using it,” mentioned founder and Chief Executive Larry Gadea, who worked as an engineer at Google LLC and Twitter Inc. before starting the manufacturer in 2013.

According to recent reports, visitors Critical scans a visitor’s government-issued ID and matches their face to the photo on it. Names are also screened against denied-party and export-control lists through Visual Compliance and Descartes MK, both from The Descartes Systems Group Inc. Contractor qualifications are checked through ISN Software Corp. From there, visits are sent for approval based on the organization’s own written policies. The approver’s reasoning is then kept on record in case of an audit.

Among Envoy’s existing customers is Attalon Inc., the former aerospace and defense business of Coherent Corp. Every visitor to all 12 of Attalon’s sites has their ID scanned by Envoy before being screened against denied-party lists. Tim Carr, Attalon’s director of security and environment, health and safety, remarked that an auditor who inspects one site “has effectively inspected them all.”.

The launch comes as new Envoy research of 1,000 security leaders found that 62% of enterprise leaders are very confident they would pass a physical security audit without preparation. Some 63% of that group had a security incident in the past year. At sensitive workplaces, 44% of leaders could not say with confidence who was in their building the previous day.

Visitors Critical is available now. Hardware-based ID verification, which uses supported readers to authenticate the document itself and catch forged IDs, is being offered through an early access program.

It has been revealed that envoy claims more than 16,000 workplaces in 170 countries as customers, including 92 of the Fortune 500. The company released Response, a threat intelligence and incident management product, in August. It raised $111 million in a Series C round in January 2022 at a $1.4 billion valuation.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Industry observers note that as a big believer in a domesticated superintelligence, I can’t pass up the Cheeky Pint podcast where OpenAI CEO suggested it’s a terrible idea to keep processing your personal data on your personal computers because his tech giant’s data centers could process your data more efficiently. He walked the remark back after immediate backlash.It’s hard to recognize, yet your business likely lives in that world of centralization already. When using inference via API, you often rent access to a black box that shifts its behavior, pricing and reasoning effort without your knowledge or consent.

Ask yourself: how many times has your team asked for more budget due to inconsistent behavior from GPT or Claude? In Harvard Data Science Review, Stanford and UC Berkeley researchers Lingjiao Chen, Matei Zaharia and James Zou tested identical prompts on GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 across snapshots three months apart. GPT-4’s prime-number accuracy fell from 84.0% in March 2023 to 51.1% in June, while its chain-of-thought boost collapsed from 24.4% to -0.1%.

Everyday workflows suffered similar drops. On a happy-number task, GPT-4’s accuracy fell from 83.6% to 35.2%, while directly executable code plummeted from 52.0% to 10.0% because extra formatting broke pipelines. Instruction-following on answer extraction collapsed from 99.5% to 0.5% under the same model name and API.

Sources indicate that A 2024 Carnegie Mellon and HKUST study by Wanqin Ma, Chenyang Yang and Christian Kästner found that 58.8% of prompt and model combinations lost accuracy after an API patch, and 70.2% of those drops exceeded 5 percentage points. Across updates, 10.9% of individual predictions regressed and 63.8% of those failures occurred at maximum confidence, breaking working predictions 87.9% of the time even when overall accuracy rose.

Researchers Emanuele La Malfa and colleagues at Oxford and the Alan Turing Institute warned in a 2025 AAAI paper — first published in Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research — that language-model providers deprecate models on short schedules, collect prompts under commercial licenses and alter serving layers while keeping your pinned model ID unchanged. The end customer takes the hit and is forced to reinvest in adapting to another model that’s not smarter but cheaper to run.

Industry observers note that anthropic is presently defending against a consolidated consumer class action in California federal court (In re Claude Service Degradation Litigation, No. 3:26-cv-07699-RFL) alleging that the company wrongfully degraded its paid Claude Pro ($20/mo), Max 5x ($100/mo), and Max 20x ($200/mo) tiers between March 4 and May 6, 2026. In April 2026, the problem became so obvious that Anthropic had to publish an anti-crisis investigation into Claude Code complaints where it pointed to three changes they intentionally degraded without touching the model. They lowered default reasoning effort from high to medium, introduced a bug that discarded earlier reasoning after idle sessions, and added a brevity instruction that hurt coding output.

In September 2025, Anthropic acknowledged three infrastructure bugs that corrupted responses and misrouted traffic. One routing error grew from 0.8% of requests to 16% of Sonnet 4 traffic and hit roughly 30% of active Claude Code users. Customers paid full price for degraded service, and transparency arrived only after complaints.

The financial incentives behind this opacity are enormous. OpenAI closed a funding round at an $852 billion valuation and discussed a round above $1.2 trillion, while Anthropic prepared for a public listing above $2 trillion alongside roughly $895 billion in non-cancellable compute commitments. High switching costs and forced migrations serve those valuations because every broken workflow requires more API calls to test, more compute for quality assurance and more tokens to rewrite system prompts so your business is not sued by your customers one day for a change in your product you don’t even control.

In 1970, Nobel laureate George Akerlof demonstrated in The Quarterly Journal of Economics how quality uncertainty creates a “market for lemons.” A 2026 CHI study by Alexander Erlei and colleagues at Göttingen, Cagliari, TU Delft and Columbia proved that this trap hits AI buyers. Without disclosure in a high-lemon market, 92.2% of delegations went to low-quality AI systems, whereas partial accuracy disclosure in a low-lemon market cut lemon delegations to 5.5% and raised earnings by 36.4 coins.

Regulators will not fix this soon. While Serena Booth argued at ICML 2025 that consumer protection laws apply to AI, a 2026 FAccT study by Abeba Birhane, William Agnew and colleagues found 249 instances across 100 news articles where AI firms used 27 capture mechanisms to fight oversight. Meanwhile, a 2026 report by Miles Brundage and 47 co-authors noted that frontier AI gets less independent scrutiny than consumer goods, with baseline AAL-1 audits costing $300,000 to $600,000 and AAL-2 reviews exceeding $1 million.

Industry observers note that data centers are great for training large models because they concentrate highly interconnected hardware at scale. Once a model is trained, however, is there any specific reason you share trade secrets and intellectual property with a data center?Tier one superintelligence models run on a domestic intelligence unit that costs less than three months of tokens. by Todd Bishop on Nov 13, 2026 at 3:04 pmNovember 13, 2026 at 7:58 pm.

Updated with officials’ explanation of the cause and the reopening of U.S. airspace.

Industry observers note that the nationwide ground stop that halted U.S. commercial air travel Friday was not caused by the Microsoft 365 outage that began a day earlier, federal officials said at an evening news conference, blaming aging FAA telecom equipment that was overloaded with data.

In a recent development, homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin opened the news conference by raising the Microsoft outage himself. “I want to make sure everybody understands that there is no connection between this and Microsoft,” he said. “I know a lot of people are making that jump.”.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy likewise ruled out a role for SMART, the FAA’s new AI traffic-planning tool, saying it isn’t connected to the core systems controllers use to track flights.

“There was no possible way SMART would have impacted what happened today,” he said.

The FAA reopened U.S. airspace at 5:15 p.m. Pacific, more than four hours after the problems began, Duffy said. He said flights would resume slowly, depending on whether airlines had crews available, and some may not depart until Saturday morning.

Microsoft confirmed in a statement that it had no indication the FAA ground stop was related to its service disruption.

Asked whether a cyberattack or “rogue AI” could be ruled out, Mullin mentioned there was “nothing completely certain right now,” but “it appears that this was mechanically driven.” He said he could not rule out the possibility of a cyberattack but said there was “zero evidence” of one so far.

What happened: Duffy noted the FAA began seeing unstable radar and communications data at air traffic control facilities across the country at 12:36 p.m. Pacific. Aging switches and routers in the agency’s telecom network “got overloaded with data” and began producing inconsistent information, he said, adding that the FAA still relies on “1980s little copper lines.”.

Duffy said newer equipment held up.

Recent findings suggest that “Our new IP switches did not go down. It’s the old hardware that went down,” he said. The FAA restored service after deploying fixes to reduce the overloading on its switches, he said.

Mullin said the overload appeared to have been triggered by upcoming equipment the FAA was installing. As the agency put “patches into the system” and added “new equipment and new technology,” he said, it “was overwhelming the older system.” Neither official said exactly what that equipment was.

It has been revealed that the FAA is in the middle of replacing its legacy telecom network with a modern internet-protocol network. AT&T took over the lead role on that project in August with an initial $74.3 million award, as the FAA works toward a goal of finishing by the end of 2028.

Industry observers note that duffy and Mullin used the briefing to press Congress for money to finish rebuilding the air traffic control system. Mullin noted President Trump has declared the situation a national emergency.

The administration has asked Congress for an additional $30.1 billion for aviation infrastructure, AeroTime reported. Duffy said at the evening news conference that he wants $50 billion.

Earlier in the day, Mullin had stated officials were looking into a possible link to SMART, including through DHS’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). The FAA said Tuesday it was expanding the system to the airspace managed by all 22 of its en route air traffic control centers.

It has been revealed that the agency describes SMART as a cloud-based system that pulls in about 200 data streams, including weather, flight paths and controller staffing, to recommend flight schedules and routes. FAA specialists review its recommendations, and local facilities decide whether to act on them.

Recent findings suggest that SMART is part of a 12-year, $875 million FAA contract with Boston-based Air Space Intelligence, which denied any connection to the matter. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company noted.

The FAA halted departures nationwide shortly before 1 p.m. Pacific. More than 3,500 planes were in the air at the time, Duffy said. It’s the second nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11 attacks, after a January 2023 failure of the FAA’s Notice to Air Missions system.

FlightAware counted nearly 7,000 flights delayed or canceled as of Friday afternoon.

💡 Key Takeaways
