  • According to recent reports, grand Theft Auto V passed $1 billion in sales within three days of its September 2013 release, according to publisher Take-Two Interactive $TTWO.
  • According to recent reports, the spending behind those hits is harder to see.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why video game budgets have exploded, from Grand Theft Auto V to Marvel's Spider-Man 2 and Concord, explained through 10 cost drivers shaping how blockbuster games get made.

According to recent reports, grand Theft Auto V passed $1 billion in sales within three days of its September 2013 release, according to publisher Take-Two Interactive $TTWO. Returns on that scale give publishers a reason to spend heavily on the next potential hit.

According to recent reports, the spending behind those hits is harder to see. Most publishers do not disclose what an individual game costs to make. Public figures are scarce. One of the clearest comes from leaked Insomniac Games documents. Press reports on those files put the cost of the 2023 game Marvel's Spider-Man 2 at $315 million. That number comes from the leak, not from a company announcement.

Explaining why video game budgets have exploded means looking at several pressures at once. Hardware is one. The PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X $TWTR both introduced in November 2020. Each new console generation asks studios for more detailed art, animation and environments. People are another. Substantial games depend on actors for motion capture and voice work. Video game performers represented by SAG-AFTRA began a strike on July 26, 2024.

In a recent development, release gaps show how long the work can take. Rockstar Games released Red Dead Redemption 2 in October 2018, eight years after the first Red Dead Redemption arrived in May 2010. Every year in production adds to the bill.

Marketing is a separate expense on top of development. Publishers rarely say what they spend on it.

The companies behind games have grown larger as well. Microsoft $MSFT declared its $68.7 billion deal for Activision $ATVI Blizzard in January 2022 and closed it in October 2023. Prices have moved too. A $60 price was standard for new games for many years. Nintendo priced Mario Kart World at $79.99 when it announced the game in April 2025.

It has been revealed that higher spending also raises the cost of failure. Firewalk Studios released the live-service shooter Concord on August 23, 2024. Sony $SONY pulled the game on September 6, 2024, and closed Firewalk in October 2024.

The 10 slides below cover a selection of the forces behind modern game budgets. They end with Larian Studios' Baldur's Gate 3, which won Game of the Year at the 2023 Game Awards, as a different route to a hit.

Grand Theft Auto V showed how much money one blockbuster game can make in its first days. Rockstar Games released it in September 2013. Its parent company, Take-Two Interactive $TTWO, reported that the game brought in $800 million in sales on its first day and passed $1 billion within three days.

Those totals came from the publisher itself. That matters in an industry where hard numbers are scarce. Publishers often keep detailed sales data private. A confirmed launch figure gives outsiders one of the few clear public reference points for what a top-tier release can earn.

The game arrived on PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360. Rockstar North, the Edinburgh studio that has long led the series, built it around three playable protagonists named Michael, Franklin and Trevor. Players could switch among them during the story. The plot was structured around how their lives overlapped.

According to recent reports, the setting was Los Santos, a fictional city modeled on Los Angeles. Around it sat the countryside, desert and coastline of the fictional state of San Andreas. Filling a map of that size with streets, buildings, traffic and characters is the kind of work that demands large teams of artists, designers, writers and engineers.

In a recent development, the launch gave the industry a public benchmark. Publishers planning their own flagship projects now had a confirmed example of how large and how fast the return on a major bet could be.

That payoff is part of the logic behind larger spending. When a single title can bring in that much revenue so rapidly, the argument for funding bigger teams and more detailed worlds becomes easier to make inside a publisher.

Recent findings suggest that rockstar also kept selling the same game for years. It later released versions for PlayStation 4, Xbox One and PC. It then released versions for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X $TWTR and Series S. Each release extended the commercial life of a game first sold in 2013.

Red Dead Redemption 2 came out in October 2018, eight years after the original Red Dead Redemption released in May 2010. Long gaps between major releases are one sign of how long blockbuster production can run.

Sources indicate that rockstar Games made both games. Between the two Red Dead launches, the studio also released Grand Theft Auto V.

Sources indicate that A long production cycle raises a budget in a direct way. A studio pays its staff for every year a game is in development. Those salaries build up before a single copy is sold. A project that runs for many years has to recover all of that spending after release.

Time adds costs beyond payroll, too. Office space, software licenses and equipment are paid for across the full life of a project. A studio also carries the risk that player tastes or technology will shift before the game is finished.

Industry observers note that long cycles create a trade-off as well. A studio that spends years on each game releases fewer games. Each release then has to cover a larger share of the studio's costs.

The gap shapes the series itself. Without a fresh release, a franchise has no fresh launch to drive a wave of sales. Players who finished the first game have to wait for the story to continue. The publisher has to keep interest in the name alive across that wait.

Take-Two Interactive $TTWO, Rockstar's parent company, reported that Red Dead Redemption 2 earned $725 million in its first three days on sale. That opening came after a stretch of years in which the series had no new main entry to sell.

In a recent development, the $725 million figure measures sales, not profit. Take-Two did not report a production cost alongside it. The number demonstrates how promptly a long project can bring money in. It does not show how much of that money remained after years of spending.

Industry observers note that leaked Insomniac Games documents, as reported by the press, put the cost of making Marvel's Spider-Man 2 at $315 million. The 2023 game's budget became public through that leak, not through an announcement by the studio or its publisher.

Sources indicate that A leaked internal figure is a reported cost, not a confirmed one. It shows the scale of one project. It does not show how the money was counted, which expenses it covers or how it was spread across the production.

Those gaps matter when the number is set beside other games. Two studios can define a budget in different ways. One might include years of salaries, outside contractors and licensing. Another might leave some of those items out. The figure also leaves open whether marketing falls inside the total. Without the underlying accounting, a single total cannot be lined up cleanly against another project's cost.

Recent findings suggest that hard budget numbers rarely surface in the games business. Sales milestones often get public announcements. Production spending usually stays inside the manufacturer.

Recent findings suggest that that leaves public discussion of rising costs resting on a small set of data points. A single document from inside one studio can carry a lot of weight in that discussion. The Spider-Man 2 number became one of those reference points after the press reported on the leaked Insomniac Games files. For readers trying to gauge how expensive blockbuster games have become, it offers a rare concrete number tied to a named title.

According to recent reports, the game itself also shapes what the figure represents. Marvel's Spider-Man 2 is a sequel built around a licensed Marvel character. The total therefore belongs to a franchise project, not a latest property built from scratch.

Sources indicate that the $315 million covers one title. It is not a figure for a studio's annual spending or for a publisher's full slate of games.

Without confirmation from the manufacturer, the $315 million remains a reported budget. It rests on the leaked documents and the press coverage of them, not on an official disclosure.

The PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X $TWTR introduced in November 2020, and both were built to run games at 4K resolution. Higher resolution raises the level of detail that every character, building and texture must hold up to, and artists have to create that detail.

A 4K image measures 3,840 by 2,160 pixels. That is four times the pixel count of a 1080p image, which measures 1,920 by 1,080 pixels. On a large television at that resolution, a blurry texture or a blocky, low-polygon object is easier to spot. Art teams respond by building assets with finer geometry and higher-resolution textures.

In a recent development, that work does not scale automatically. A rock, a jacket or a car door still has to be modeled, textured, lit and checked. When the target resolution rises, each of those steps involves more data and more review. Each object also needs several versions at different levels of detail so it can render efficiently at a distance. Large open-world games contain many thousands of such objects.

It has been revealed that both consoles also added hardware support for ray tracing. The technique simulates how light bounces, reflects and casts shadows. It can make scenes look more physically accurate. It also gives developers another lighting system to build, test and tune alongside traditional methods.

Fast solid-state drives are standard on both machines. They let games stream large amounts of data promptly, which cuts down on loading screens. Faster streaming also lets designers place denser, more detailed environments in front of the player. More detailed environments mean more assets to produce.

In the years after the 2020 launch, many studios shipped games on two console generations at once. Building for both the older PlayStation 4 and Xbox One and the newer machines meant supporting different performance targets within a single project. Each version needed its own optimization and testing.

None of this adds up to a single published price tag. Publishers rarely break out how much of a budget goes to art or graphics work. What the hardware shift did change is the baseline of detail a blockbuster release has to meet.

Recent findings suggest that motion capture and voice acting make blockbuster games depend on large casts of paid performers, specialized capture stages and long recording schedules. That labor was at the center of the strike SAG-AFTRA video game performers began in 2024.

Performance capture records an actor's body, face and voice together. Performers wear tight suits dotted with reflective markers. A ring of cameras around the stage tracks those markers as the actors move through a scene.

Facial work adds another layer. Head-mounted cameras pointed at the performer's face record expressions in detail. Animators later map that data onto a digital character so its face matches the original performance.

Recent findings suggest that the raw capture is only the starting point. Animators and technical artists clean up the recorded motion, correct errors and fit it to each character model. A single cinematic scene can pass through several departments before it reaches the finished game.

Naughty Dog's The Last of Us, released in 2013, relied heavily on this kind of work. Troy Baker and Ashley Johnson played Joel and Ellie on a capture stage, supplying both movement and voice. Their performances shaped the characters as players see and hear them.

Casting extends well beyond the lead roles. Large productions hire stunt performers for fights and action sequences. They also cast separate voice actors for supporting characters, enemies and crowds.

Voice work grows with the size of the script. Open-world and role-playing games can contain many thousands of recorded lines across main stories, side quests and background chatter. Publishers that release a game in several languages often record new voice tracks for each market. That repeats much of the casting and studio work.

In a recent development, the SAG-AFTRA strike centered on protections against artificial intelligence tools that could replicate performers' voices and likenesses, alongside compensation. The walkout fell under the union's Interactive Media Agreement, which covers work for major game companies.

Industry observers note that performer costs rise with the scope of a production. Every added scene, language or retake means more hours on a capture stage, more time in a recording booth and more animation work afterward.

Marketing is a separate cost from development for big-budget AAA games, and it sits on top of what a studio spends building the game. A publisher rarely reveals how much it spends promoting one title. As a result, the full cost of most games stays out of public view.

A development budget pays for the people, tools and technology that make the game. A marketing budget pays for making sure buyers know the game exists by launch day. That work includes cinematic trailers, gameplay reveals, paid advertising, retail promotion and partnerships with streamers and video creators.

For a blockbuster release, a campaign can begin long before the game ships. A first teaser may appear years ahead of launch. The publisher then has to keep attention alive through later trailers, preview events and preorder pushes. Each stage carries its own production and media-buying costs.

Sources indicate that live showcases are one common stage for that work. The Game Awards and Summer Game Fest both feature world premieres of new game trailers. Platform holders run their own broadcasts as well, including Sony $SONY's State of Play and Nintendo Direct. A reveal at one of these events puts new footage in front of a large live audience at a single moment.

Platform holders also sign marketing agreements with publishers. These deals can attach a console brand to a game's advertising or give one platform's players early or exclusive content. Such arrangements add another party to the campaign. Their terms are rarely made public.

Industry observers note that the timing matters because massive-budget games depend on strong opening sales. A publisher that has funded years of development needs a large audience ready to buy as soon as the game appears. Marketing is how it builds that audience in advance.

It has been revealed that publicly traded publishers such as Electronic Arts $EA and Take-Two Interactive $TTWO report marketing spending in their financial filings. They report it as a organization-wide expense rather than game by game. That makes it hard to set one title's promotional spending against its development cost. Any specific ratio between the two is a guess unless a company discloses it.

A reported game budget, when one surfaces at all, may leave out much of what a publisher spent to bring that game to market.

Microsoft $MSFT agreed to pay $68.7 billion for Activision $ATVI Blizzard, a sign of how much money now surrounds the video game business. The organization declared the deal in January 2022 and completed it in October 2023.

Recent findings suggest that the figure is the price of a whole publisher, not the cost of making any one game. The money bought a firm with many studios, a catalog of existing titles and the rights to future releases. Reading it as a game budget would misread what the number measures.

Those holdings include some of the largest franchises in the business. Activision publishes Call of Duty. Blizzard Entertainment makes World of Warcraft, Diablo and Overwatch. King, the mobile arm, makes Candy Crush Saga. Each of those series has its own studios and release schedule.

The purchase did not stand alone. Microsoft had already bought ZeniMax Media, the parent of Bethesda Softworks, for $7.5 billion in a deal that closed in March 2021. Bethesda's franchises include The Elder Scrolls and Fallout. Together, the two acquisitions moved several major franchises under one owner. Microsoft also runs the Xbox console business and the Game Pass subscription service. Both draw on the games its studios produce.

Sources indicate that the gap between announcement and completion was about 21 months. Regulators examined the deal during that period. The U.S. Federal Trade Commission sued to block it in December 2022. The U.K. Competition and Markets Authority blocked the original version in April 2023. Microsoft then restructured the deal. It sold the cloud streaming rights to Activision Blizzard games outside the European Economic Area to Ubisoft. The CMA cleared the revised version in October 2023.

Sources indicate that the acquisition is a story about consolidation. Fewer, larger owners now hold more of the studios and franchises behind big-budget games. The most expensive productions increasingly sit inside companies large enough to fund them. Microsoft's purchase of Activision Blizzard is one of the clearest examples of that concentration.

In a recent development, concord shows how quickly a live-service bet can come apart. Sony $SONY's Firewalk Studios released the game on August 23, 2024, and Sony pulled it on September 6, 2024. Sony then closed Firewalk Studios in October 2024.

It has been revealed that the game was pulled 14 days after its release date. That left the development spending behind Concord a two-week window to start earning money back.

A live-service game is designed to run for years rather than ship once and be finished. Publishers plan seasons of new content, such as maps, characters and cosmetic items, to keep players returning and spending. The model ties revenue to an active player base over a long period, not to a single sale at launch.

That structure changes the cost math. A traditional single-player game spends most of its budget before release. A live-service game also needs servers, a team that keeps producing updates, and staff for balance changes and player support after launch. Those costs start on day one, whether or not players show up.

It has been revealed that multiplayer design adds another pressure. Matchmaking depends on enough people being online at the same time. When a player base is small, queues get longer and matches are harder to fill. That can push the remaining players away.

Live-service titles also compete for a limited resource: player time. A game built around seasonal play asks people to commit for months. Many players already split that time among online games they have played for years.

According to recent reports, the result of a failed launch is lopsided. A single-player game that sells poorly still keeps the revenue from the copies it sold. A live-service game that loses its audience may no longer be worth running at all. Taking it offline means the planned years of post-launch income never arrive.

Sources indicate that for a publisher, the loss from a case like Concord covers more than the money spent building the game. It also includes the team behind it. In Concord's case, that meant the end of Firewalk Studios as well.

For many years, $60 was the standard price for a fresh console game in the U.S. That ceiling has since moved higher. Nintendo priced Mario Kart World at $79.99 when it announced the game in April 2025.

The sticker price of a new release is one of the few levers a publisher controls directly. Revenue from a full-price game comes down to two numbers: how many copies sell and what each copy costs. When development spending rises, a publisher can try to sell more copies, charge more for each copy or do both.

Industry observers note that the $60 standard held for a long stretch in which production work grew much larger. Across those years, one base price had to cover projects with bigger teams, longer schedules and more detailed art. Inflation also eroded what a fixed $60 was worth over time.

According to recent reports, publishers found other ways to raise what each player spends while the base price stayed put. Deluxe and collector's editions sell the same game at higher prices, usually bundled with extra content. Downloadable expansions and in-game purchases bring in money after launch. These options let the headline price stay fixed while the total a player could spend kept climbing.

The $70 price point moved part of that burden back onto the base game. At $70, each standard copy brings in $10 more than at $60, before retailers and platform holders take their share. A buyer who wants only the standard edition now pays more up front than under the old norm.

Mario Kart World pushed the figure further. Its $79.99 price is $19.99 above the long-running $60 standard.

A higher price raises revenue per copy only if enough players still buy at that level. The extra amount applies to every copy sold, so the gain grows with a game's sales. Publishers rarely disclose how sales respond to each increase. That makes it hard to measure from the outside how much of a game's budget a price change actually recovers.

Baldur's Gate 3, released by Larian Studios in August 2023, won Game of the Year at the 2023 Game Awards. Larian has not disclosed what the game cost to make.

According to recent reports, that missing figure limits any direct comparison with blockbuster spending. What can be compared is how the project was organized and paid for along the way.

According to recent reports, larian is a Belgian developer headquartered in Ghent. It is not owned by Sony $SONY, Microsoft $MSFT, Nintendo or Take-Two Interactive $TTWO. Larian published Baldur's Gate 3 itself rather than handing release decisions to an outside publisher.

According to recent reports, the studio built the game on an existing foundation. Baldur's Gate 3 adapts the fifth edition rules of Dungeons & Dragons under a license from Wizards of the Coast. It is a turn-based, party-based role-playing game. Larian had already worked in that genre with Divinity: Original Sin and Divinity: Original Sin 2.

According to recent reports, larian also developed the game in public for years. Baldur's Gate 3 entered paid early access on PC in October 2020, nearly three years before the full launch. Early buyers could play an opening portion of the game and send feedback while work continued. That arrangement brought in revenue and player data well before the finished version shipped.

The full release arrived on PC in August 2023. A PlayStation 5 version followed in September 2023, and an Xbox Series X $TWTR|S version came in December 2023.

Sources indicate that the Game Awards win came against nominees from some of the industry's largest companies. The 2023 Game of the Year field included Marvel's Spider-Man 2 from Sony's Insomniac Games and The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom from Nintendo. Capcom's Resident Evil 4, Remedy Entertainment's Alan Wake 2 and Nintendo's Super Mario Bros. Wonder were also nominated.

The case does not show that blockbuster games can be made cheaply. It reveals another route to Game of the Year: a long public development period, a licensed rule set, prior genre experience and self-publishing.

Why Growing Brands Have an Edge Over Established Competitors in the AI Search Race

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, my agency’s clients are heavily indexed in SMB B2B tech brands looking to raise money.
  • The same pattern is holding true with clients gaining market share through AEO (answer engine optimization).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

According to recent reports, my agency’s clients are heavily indexed in SMB B2B tech brands looking to raise money. Since we were founded in 2017, our clients have raised more than $2.5 billion in funding. Aside from having differentiated products, our most successful clients have had one thing in common: the ability to move swiftly and with agility to navigate shifts in micro and macro markets.

The same pattern is holding true with clients gaining market share through AEO (answer engine optimization). Brands are finding an edge by moving swiftly to tackle the growth opportunity of a highly dynamic search landscape — one in which user behavior is changing by the day.

Here’s why — and how — they’re able to leverage AEO to make gains against bigger competitors.

Legacy content matters less than you’d think. Large language models (LLMs) carry a measurable recency bias. A decade’s worth of archived content doesn’t provide established companies with the head start many executives assume it does.

Speed wins in a market that changes monthly. AEO is one of the most dynamic disciplines in marketing today; what works this quarter may be obsolete next quarter. Large organizations rarely move with the agility this demands. Meanwhile, more and more less mature companies are hiring for fluency in LLMs and the content that feeds them.

Sources indicate that legacy assets can become liabilities. Structuring newly introduced content for AEO is far easier than retrofitting thousands of existing pages. Newer brands can build clean site architecture and easily retrievable content, all free of accumulated technical debt, from day one. They can also borrow credibility through comparison content, which performs exceptionally well in AEO and traditional SEO. Positioning yourself directly against an established competitor also puts your brand in the same conversation.

Paired with disciplined execution, those structural advantages can translate quickly into results and growth.

Dense paragraphs serve neither readers nor LLMs. “TL;DR” summaries, key takeaways, numbered lists and FAQs with concise answers are easy for both humans and machines to digest. When your content answers a likely prompt clearly and succinctly, it becomes a likely candidate for citation.

The most common obstacle I see among business leaders is time. Producing content for owned channels (your blog, LinkedIn, YouTube) and earned media (bylines and features on third-party platforms) is essential for building AEO momentum, but leaders rarely have time to take over those responsibilities on their own.

Industry observers note that work with your marketing leader to identify team members who can contribute insights on relevant topics, and commit to a sustainable cadence. Twice a week across your properties is a reasonable benchmark.

It has been revealed that when I say “consistent,” I mean both in cadence and message; every piece must reinforce your positioning. If you sell the leading SaaS bookkeeping platform for local retailers, don’t publish content aimed at big-box chains. Inconsistency scrambles the signal LLMs use to understand who you are.

Through networking events, discovery calls and pitch meetings, I hear common questions, especially around emerging channels like AEO. Our client services leaders see the same thing: As trends develop, identical questions emerge across verticals and growth stages.

When your customers and prospects keep asking the same question, that’s a signal for you (or your team) to address that question publicly. Create a system for capturing these questions and feeding them directly into your content calendar. It’s the most reliable way to stay relevant and remain part of the conversation.

Sources indicate that LLMs need an unambiguous picture of who you are and what you do. Audit your tech giant address and contact details across your website and social profiles, update your Google Business Profile, and confirm that every online directory listing is accurate and current. This is basic hygiene, but it’s frequently overlooked.

Attributing revenue to AI search with precision remains difficult, largely because much of today’s buyer journey happens without a click to your website. We rely on a three-part framework that delivers reliable directional data:.

Visibility and share of voice: Use an AI visibility tracking tool (we use Profound) to monitor how often your brand appears relative to competitors on high-priority industry prompts.

Citations and traffic: Use web analytics (we use Google Analytics) to measure traffic arriving from LLM citations.

Conversions and revenue: Track conversions in your analytics platform, including LLM referral traffic, which in my experience does account for a small share of total conversions. Supplement this with post-conversion surveys asking customers where they first discovered your brand. The data is directional rather than exact, but it provides a decent idea of impact.

None of these strategies is especially complex. What they require is resources, budget and prioritization from leadership. Especially for the B2B tech sector, where LLMs use is proliferating at all points of the purchase journey, leveraging inherent advantages in AEO is one of the most effective paths to the growth that piques investors’ interest.

My agency’s clients are heavily indexed in SMB B2B tech brands looking to raise money. Since we were founded in 2017, our clients have raised more than $2.5 billion in funding. Aside from having differentiated products, our most successful clients have had one thing in common: the ability to move swiftly and with agility to navigate shifts in micro and macro markets.

Here’s why — and how — they’re able to leverage AEO to make gains against bigger competitors.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 13, 2026 at 4:32 pmNovember 16, 2026 at 10:09 am.

According to recent reports, gov. Bob Ferguson is proposing $10 million to fund basic infrastructure needed for the Northwest Advanced Clean Energy Park, a master-planned industrial area in Eastern Washington that will foster development of large-scale clean energy, advanced manufacturing and supply chains. The proposal will be included in his 2027–29 capital budget.

If approved by lawmakers, the funding would support sewer, water, electrical and road infrastructure at the park.

“This investment will support thousands of good-paying jobs in the trades and advanced industries, and unlock billions in private investment,” Ferguson mentioned in a statement.

The 1,641-acre site was formerly part of the Hanford Nuclear Reservation, a sprawling federal property along the Columbia River near the Tri-Cities that is undergoing a massive environmental cleanup. Hanford was established during World War II to produce plutonium for the Manhattan Project.

Mel Clark, president and CEO of the CleanTech Alliance, an industry trade group, welcomed the news as the state struggles to get clean power plugged into the grid.

Recent findings suggest that “Washington needs more energy generation, more clean energy, and more manufacturing,” Clark told GeekWire via email. “We’re excited to see the Governor take action to change our last-place ranking in building latest clean energy projects.”.

According to the governor’s office, two projects have committed to locating at the park once infrastructure construction is complete: Atlas Agro’s low-carbon fertilizer production plant and the utility-scale Ruby Flats Solar Farm.

Sources indicate that state officials stated General Matter is also considering the location for producing advanced nuclear fuel for small reactors. That siting could potentially be beneficial for another project planned for the same area: Amazon, X-energy and Energy Northwest are developing plans for the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility, a nuclear plant comprised of clustered, small reactors.

In 2024, the Norwegian company Cenate expressed interest in building a factory at the park to produce lithium-ion battery components, according to the Tri-Cities Area Journal of Business, ultimately withdrew its aims.

The Tri-Cities is also attracting fusion-energy investment. Last year, Seattle startup Avalanche Energy landed a $10 million grant from the Washington State Department of Commerce’s Green Jobs Grant Program to develop FusionWERX, a commercial-scale testing facility for fusion technologies. The project is being developed in an existing Port of Benton building in Richland.

Washington is heading into its 2027–29 biennial budget with a multibillion-dollar shortfall, but officials have not yet settled on a definitive public estimate.

Recent findings suggest that ferguson has acknowledged the scale of the gap but has not publicly specified an amount. The shortfall concerns the state’s operating budget, which is separate from the capital budget funding proposed for the energy park.

Editor’s note: Comment from CleanTech Alliance President and CEO Mel Clark added 11/16.

Industry observers note that it has already been one year since the first U.S. ETF designed to provide exposure only to XRP officially began trading, when the XRP ETF market launched on November 14 last year.

Although XRP has not shown any impressive price growth, this marks a major milestone in its journey towards global expansion, especially greater institutional adoption.

While momentum has slowed significantly in recent days, data showcased by the official XRP X handle shows that the U.S. spot XRP ETFs have steadily expanded their holdings since they debuted late last year.

As such, they have accumulated about 1.16 billion XRP to date, marking a major milestone for the broader XRP ecosystem even as momentum slows amid the prolonged market volatility.

While XRP ETFs are designed to allow investors to gain exposure to XRP through traditional means rather than by purchasing and holding the asset directly, the milestone signals growing interest in XRP investment products among institutional investors.

Nonetheless, the team shared a chart that revealed that XRP ETF holdings have generally trended upward since November 2025, with notable increases around the beginning of the launch period and another significant rise in August this year.

As the XRP ETF ecosystem continues to grow, the asset has seen several major asset managers join its ecosystem over the past year.

These asset management firms issuing the XRP investment product include Bitwise, Franklin Templeton, Canary Capital, 21Shares, Grayscale, and REX.

In a recent development, if you’ve been feeling like the future of your agency is bleak, you are not alone. Every agency owner I’ve spoken to in the past year has been experiencing the same reality. Latest business is shrinking as our model, which relies on providing external expertise to bring business value, is heavily under attack by AI. This is a situation we must accept as fact if we are to properly navigate it.

Even though this is the worst year on record for net-new business in the seven years of running my agency, we’ve managed to retain our existing clients and have not seen a significant drop in monthly revenues or had to let staff go. We have not grown, but we have not shrunk either. And in 2026, that’s a substantial win.

I believe the reason we have managed to sustain our base, and why I am ultimately not feeling as stressed as some of my peers, is that we have been doing two things right since well before the recent AI impacts affected our industry:.

Let’s dive into both of those in more detail so you can audit and adjust your delivery model as needed to ensure you survive this AI-caused agency apocalypse.

Before we review the contractual changes you need to institute, it is imperative that your team is doing top-notch work. Without that, nothing you do will help you survive. You need to be the best in class in your niche to even have a chance. B-grade delivery (or worse) no longer has a fighting chance.

It has been revealed that it’s time for an audit! Review how many clients you have on locked-in, long-term managed service or support agreements. If you are used to selling your services on a fixed-fee and fixed-term model, where you are charging the same amount per month even if you don’t lift a finger and those contracts last for many months or years, your days are numbered.

In a recent development, your clients will jump ship the moment that contract ends. This means you are on the clock to make things right. Our first client is still our client to this day, over six years later, and I believe it’s because they’ve never been forced to sign a contract of that nature. None of our clients ever have.

What do we do instead? We sign indefinite monthly agreements that have a straightforward adjustment, pause or cancellation clause. If you want to see the exact terminology of that clause, you can find a sample statement of work in my free book, How Do I Find Clients?

Industry observers note that but the spirit of that clause is quite simple: value creation. Alongside each client, we agree what value we will bring for them each month and set our monthly compensation based on that value creation. If, at any point, the client feels that there’s a need to adjust that equation, take a short pause or cancel, they have the right to do so.

This clause has ensured our clients have always felt comfortable proceeding with us and staying on those agreements well beyond any fixed term we could have locked them in for. So, if you have any contracts that are locking clients in long-term, perhaps it’s time to adjust those contracts and ensure that your clients feel you are really there to support them.

Recent findings suggest that locked-in terms are only one part of the equation. Your other, and perhaps biggest, enemy is locked-in pricing. I always tell my students: Every single time a client receives an invoice from you, they are doing a mathematical equation in their head that has two possible outcomes: “worth it” or “not worth it.”.

Sources indicate that to fight resentment, you need to make sure that every single time they do that equation, the result is unequivocally “worth it!” The way you do that is by putting yourself in the shoes of your clients before you send that invoice. If you believe that there’s any reason they might feel a reduction in the monthly invoice is warranted, you need to apply it preemptively and communicate it openly. That conversation, believe me, goes very well every time.

It sounds very simple because it is. When you send the invoice, communicate the situation clearly. Take this as an example: “You were away on vacation for a week, and then I was sick the last few days of the month, so I’ve reduced the invoice by $1,000. Hope you don’t mind.” And guess what? Of course they don’t mind! But they certainly appreciate it, and they remember it. This type of decision builds stronger relationships.

Industry observers note that before you dismiss this, think about how you would feel if you got the full invoice in that situation. Your thought process would sound more like: “Man, I was away for a week, and nothing got done, and then they were sick and missed the call at the end of the month, and they’re still charging me the full price. That’s absurd!” Of course, that builds resentment. Fight against it!

Industry observers note that some of you may feel challenged by the two ideas I’ve just shared, but I’m going to challenge you even more. The reality is, if you feel that these are difficult changes for your business or a risk to your success, what you’re actually feeling is a fear of losing control and a scarcity mindset. Both of these are feelings you need to fight and resist. Your survival is at stake.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that whether hackers can take down the U.S.
  • Sources indicate that A cyberattack has already caused a blackout — just not in the U.S.
  • Those attacks raise a question that returns with each new federal warning: could hackers take down the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that whether hackers can take down the U.S. power grid has no simple answer, and these 10 cases, safeguards and weak points show what cyberattacks have done and what limits them.

Sources indicate that A cyberattack has already caused a blackout — just not in the U.S. In December 2015, attackers took over operator workstations at three regional distribution companies in Ukraine and opened breakers. The breaches cut power to roughly 225,000 customers. The outage lasted hours, not days. A year later, malware called Industroyer cut power for about an hour at a transmission substation near Kyiv.

Those attacks raise a question that returns with each new federal warning: could hackers take down the U.S. power grid? The answer depends on what an attacker can reach, how far a failure can spread and how rapidly operators can restore service. None of those factors reduces to a simple yes or no.

It has been revealed that stuxnet, discovered in 2010, indicated that code can physically damage industrial equipment. It targeted Siemens control systems and damaged centrifuges at Iran's Natanz enrichment plant. It was not aimed at a power grid. In 2023 and 2024, CISA, the FBI and other agencies issued warnings about a China-linked group called Volt Typhoon. The agencies stated the group had pre-positioned itself in U.S. critical infrastructure networks, including some in the energy sector. The U.S. government said the aim was the ability to disrupt operations in a future crisis. That kind of access is not the same as an outage.

Recent findings suggest that the shape of the U.S. grid matters too. It consists of three major interconnections, Eastern, Western and Texas, run by thousands of utilities with different systems. That fragmentation limits how far a single intrusion can spread. It also makes uniform defense hard. The North American Electric Reliability Corporation, or NERC, sets mandatory Critical Infrastructure Protection standards for the bulk power system, and FERC approves them. Smaller distribution utilities face fewer mandatory requirements.

Large outages do not require an attacker. The 2003 Northeast blackout affected about 50 million people in the U.S. and Canada. A software bug in an alarm system at FirstEnergy $FE in Ohio, along with overgrown trees touching power lines, contributed to the cascade. Recovery tools exist as well. Black start procedures let utilities restart plants without outside power. GridEx, a NERC-run exercise held every two years, tests how utilities respond to cyber and physical attacks.

Recent findings suggest that the 10 items below are a selection, not a ranked list of threats. They explain what cyberattacks on electric utilities have done, where the weak points sit and what limits the damage an intrusion can cause.

Recent findings suggest that in December 2015, hackers cut electricity to roughly 225,000 customers in Ukraine. It was the first publicly confirmed case of a cyberattack causing a power outage.

The intruders did not need to destroy any equipment to cause the outage. They took control of operator workstations at three regional distribution companies. These are the computers that control-room staff use to monitor and operate equipment across a utility's network from a central location.

According to recent reports, from those screens, the attackers opened breakers. A breaker is a switch that stops current from flowing along a line. Operators open breakers as a routine step during maintenance or to isolate a fault. In this case, that ordinary command was the method of the attack.

Industry observers note that the method is central to the question of whether hackers could take down the U.S. power grid. The attackers turned the utilities' own control tools against them. Once they held the workstations, they could send the same kinds of commands a legitimate operator would.

In a recent development, the targets were distribution companies. These utilities handle the final stage of electricity delivery. They carry power from the high-voltage network to homes and businesses in their regions. The outage therefore reached customers served by three separate companies.

According to recent reports, the U.S. government and the E-ISAC later attributed the attack to Russian-linked actors. The E-ISAC, the Electricity Information Sharing and Analysis Center, gathers and shares threat information for the power sector. The center is operated by NERC, the North American Electric Reliability Corporation.

Industry observers note that the outage lasted hours, not days. Remote access to control systems was still enough to switch off electricity for a large number of people. Both facts bear on the question of what a cyberattack on the electric grid can and cannot do.

So far, Ukraine is the only country where cyberattacks have been publicly confirmed to cause blackouts. No confirmed cyber-caused blackout has occurred in the U.S.

In December 2016, malware known as Industroyer, also called CrashOverride, cut power from a transmission substation near Kyiv, Ukraine, for about an hour. The tool itself set the attack apart. It was code that could send commands directly to substation equipment in that equipment's own industrial protocols.

Industrial protocols are the languages control systems use to communicate with physical devices in the field. A utility's control software relies on them to read the status of equipment and to problem commands, such as opening or closing a breaker. Most everyday malware has no use for these languages. It steals data, encrypts files or spreads across office networks. Industroyer was written to talk to the hardware that moves electricity.

It has been revealed that that was a step beyond Ukraine's first grid hack a year earlier. The December 2015 attack depended on intruders operating utility controls themselves. Industroyer moved much of that work into software. A program that problems breaker commands on its own reduces the need for attackers to work the controls by hand. It also packages the knowledge needed to manipulate grid equipment into code.

The level of the grid that was hit also differed. The 2015 attack struck distribution companies, the utilities that deliver power to homes and businesses at lower voltages. The 2016 attack struck a transmission substation. Transmission is the high-voltage part of the grid that carries electricity in bulk over longer distances. Power is stepped down from there for local delivery. A transmission substation therefore sits upstream of the lines that serve customers.

The physical result was limited. The outage was brief, and the incident did not become a lasting regional blackout. For anyone asking whether hackers could take down the U.S. power grid, the case points in two directions. Malware built specifically for grid equipment exists and has worked against a real substation. That single strike still produced a short outage rather than a prolonged collapse.

Industrial protocols are not unique to Ukraine. Utilities in many countries, including the U.S., use control systems that communicate with field equipment in this way.

According to recent reports, stuxnet, discovered in 2010, was malware that damaged centrifuges at Iran's Natanz enrichment plant. It did this by targeting Siemens control systems. That made it a clear case of software breaking physical machinery.

Many cyberattacks stay inside the digital world. They steal data, lock files or knock websites offline. Stuxnet went further. It reached the systems that tell industrial machines how to behave, and the harm landed on the equipment itself.

Centrifuges at an enrichment plant spin at very high speeds to enrich uranium. Control systems govern that motion. Stuxnet attacked that control layer. The result was broken hardware, not only a disrupted network.

In a recent development, that difference shapes recovery. A disrupted network can often be brought back once malicious code is removed and systems are rebuilt. Damaged machinery cannot be restored that way. It has to be repaired or replaced before it runs again.

Industry observers note that stuxnet was not aimed at the power grid. It did not cause a blackout. Its target was a uranium enrichment facility in Iran, and no electric utility was involved.

Its relevance to electricity comes from what it demonstrated. Power plants and substations also run physical equipment through industrial control systems. Circuit breakers open and close on command. Generators respond to control signals. Stuxnet proved that malicious code can reach that kind of control layer and turn digital commands into physical consequences.

It has been revealed that the same distinction would apply on the grid. An intrusion that only opens breakers leaves equipment that operators can close again. An intrusion that damages generators or substation hardware would leave a repair job behind it.

Industry observers note that that proof has limits. The code targeted Siemens control systems, and its known damage was at Natanz. An attack on a U.S. utility would have to match the equipment and software that utility actually uses. That is a separate challenge, and the Natanz case does not answer it.

It has been revealed that the U.S. power grid is not one machine that a single switch could turn off. It is made up of three major interconnections — Eastern, Western and Texas, known as ERCOT. Thousands of utilities run the equipment inside them.

It has been revealed that that structure shapes any answer to whether hackers could take down the U.S. power grid. An attacker who breaks into one utility's network has reached one operator, not the country. The division into separate interconnections also sets boundaries on where trouble can travel.

Those boundaries change what a nationwide outage would require. An attacker aiming at the whole country would need footholds inside all three interconnections, not just one of them.

The utilities inside those interconnections do not share one common set of computers or software. Each runs its own systems. An intrusion built around one company's setup may not carry over to the company next door.

For anyone trying to cause a nationwide blackout, that variety is an obstacle. One piece of malicious code or one stolen login does not open every control room at once. Reaching more operators means getting past more separate systems.

Recent findings suggest that the same fragmentation creates a problem for the people defending the grid. With thousands of operators running different systems, there is no single standard setup to lock down. Security work has to happen utility by utility rather than all at once.

The result is a trade-off rather than a simple answer. The grid's patchwork design limits how far one breach can spread. It also makes it hard to raise defenses evenly across the whole network.

The three-interconnection layout is part of the answer to how vulnerable the power grid is. A breach at one utility reaches that utility's systems. Spreading an outage beyond it runs into separate operators, different technology and the boundaries between the Eastern, Western and Texas interconnections.

NERC, the North American Electric Reliability Corporation, sets mandatory cybersecurity rules for the bulk power system. These rules are the Critical Infrastructure Protection standards, known as CIP. FERC, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, approves them.

According to recent reports, the arrangement splits the job in two. NERC writes the requirements, and a federal regulator signs off on them. Utilities within their scope must follow them. They are not optional guidance. The mandatory status means compliance does not rest on each manufacturer's own judgment about what is worth doing.

The bulk power system is the high-voltage backbone of the grid. In general terms, it includes large power plants along with the transmission lines and substations that carry electricity over long distances. A failure at that level can affect customers across a wide area.

The CIP standards are written for that backbone. A compromised control system at a major transmission substation can affect far more people than a fault on one neighborhood line. The rules concentrate on the equipment where a breach would reach the most customers.

Recent findings suggest that that focus leaves a gap. Smaller distribution utilities face fewer mandatory requirements. Distribution utilities deliver power over local lines to homes and businesses. Distribution is also the level where an outage reaches customers directly.

Sources indicate that fewer requirements do not mean none. A smaller utility still runs systems that keep power flowing to its customers. The difference lies in how much of its protection is set by a mandatory standard and how much depends on choices the utility makes for itself.

In a recent development, the result is uneven coverage. The CIP standards set a mandatory floor for the parts of the grid with the widest reach. They do not apply to every utility to the same degree. For anyone weighing grid cyber risk, the question is not only whether rules exist but which parts of the system they cover.

Colonial Pipeline shut down its pipeline operations in May 2021 after a DarkSide ransomware attack. The case demonstrates that a breach on the business side of a manufacturer can stop physical operations.

It has been revealed that colonial Pipeline is a fuel pipeline tech giant, not an electric utility. The attack did not cause a power outage, and it was not a strike on the grid. It still belongs in a discussion of grid cyber risk. It shows how critical infrastructure can stop working without an attacker ever taking control of physical equipment.

Ransomware is malicious software that encrypts a victim's files or systems and then demands payment to restore access. A typical infection locks up data. It does not send commands to valves, pumps or circuit breakers.

It has been revealed that industrial companies generally run two kinds of networks. Information technology, or IT, covers the business side: email, accounting, billing and corporate records. Operational technology, or OT, covers the systems that monitor and control physical equipment. In a pipeline, OT controls the equipment that moves fuel. In a utility, it controls the equipment that generates and delivers electricity.

Industry observers note that colonial's breach was on the IT side, yet the operational side still stopped. The organization halted pipeline operations itself, as a precaution. A company that cannot yet confirm how far an intrusion has spread may choose to halt operations on its own.

According to recent reports, that distinction bears directly on whether hackers could take down the U.S. power grid. Electric utilities run IT and OT networks, as pipeline operators do. Ransomware confined to a utility's business systems would not, by itself, send commands to grid equipment. It could still lead operators to disconnect systems or pause some operations while they assess the damage.

Sources indicate that the attacks on Ukraine's grid in 2015 and 2016 took a different route. In those cases, attackers acted on grid equipment directly. Colonial indicates a second route to disruption — one in which the stoppage comes from a defensive choice rather than an attacker's command.

Industry observers note that the case moves the question of electric grid cyber risk beyond control rooms. Protecting OT networks covers one path to an interruption. Keeping ransomware out of corporate networks covers another. A precautionary shutdown still halts service, whatever triggered it.

Volt Typhoon is a China-linked hacking group that U.S. agencies noted in 2023 and 2024 had pre-positioned itself inside U.S. critical infrastructure networks. Some of those networks belong to the energy sector.

Recent findings suggest that the warnings came from several federal agencies. CISA, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, issued them alongside the FBI and other agencies. The alerts covered critical infrastructure broadly rather than the power grid alone.

Industry observers note that the energy sector's place on that list carries extra weight. Electricity supports most other critical services, from water treatment to communications.

The U.S. government also described the group's purpose. It stated the aim was the ability to disrupt operations in a future crisis. That stated goal separates the campaign from intrusions built only to steal data. The concern is less about what intruders copy out of a network. It is about what they could do later from inside it.

Pre-positioning means gaining access to a network in advance and keeping it. An intruder who already holds a foothold does not need to break in when a crisis begins. The access stays in place until someone decides to use it — or until defenders find and remove it. Access that sits unused also produces little activity for defenders to notice.

Access is not an outage. The public warnings described intrusions and intent. They did not report any U.S. blackout caused by the group. Holding a position inside a network and cutting power to customers are separate steps.

According to recent reports, that distinction shapes where the Volt Typhoon warnings fit in the question of grid risk. By the U.S. government's own description, the group was preparing an ability to disrupt. The warnings did not say that ability had been used against the power grid. For grid operators, the gap between access and action is the window in which an intrusion can still be found and removed.

The 2003 Northeast blackout cut power to about 50 million people in the U.S. and Canada, and no hacker was involved. A software bug in an alarm system at FirstEnergy $FE in Ohio, along with overgrown trees touching power lines, helped set off a cascade that spread across a wide area.

In a recent development, the blackout matters for grid cyber risk because of how it spread. It shows the scale an outage can reach once a local problem moves through connected parts of the system.

According to recent reports, A cascading failure follows the physics of a connected network. Electricity flows along every available path between generators and customers. When a line trips offline, the power it was carrying shifts onto neighboring lines. If those lines become overloaded, protective equipment can disconnect them too. Each loss pushes more load onto what remains.

Both contributing causes were common kinds of failure. Trees that had grown too close to transmission lines made contact with them, and that took lines out of service. The alarm software problem at FirstEnergy meant operators did not get the warnings that would normally flag that kind of trouble. Missing alarms make it harder for a control room to act while a problem is still small.

Recent findings suggest that the pairing is what links 2003 to the cyber question. A failure in software, not in steel or wire, played a part in turning local line trips into a regional blackout. In 2003 that software failure was a bug. Operators losing an accurate view of their own system is also an effect that an intrusion into utility control systems could produce.

Fragmentation does not seal every part of the grid off from its neighbors. Sections that are connected share power, so they can also share failures.

In a recent development, the blackout marks a limit on what the comparison proves. It was an accident with physical triggers, not a coordinated attack. It does not show that a hacker could reproduce it. It shows that the grid's interconnected design can carry a local fault far beyond where it started, with or without anyone intending it.

Recent findings suggest that U.S. utilities prepare to recover from a major outage with black start procedures, which restart power plants without any electricity from outside. They also rehearse responses to cyber and physical attacks in GridEx, an exercise that the North American Electric Reliability Corporation, or NERC, runs every two years.

It has been revealed that A grid that has gone dark cannot simply be switched back on. If an attack or a failure leaves a region without power, operators need a way to get generation running again with no outside supply to draw on. Black start procedures provide that path.

It has been revealed that the procedures are worked out before any emergency. Utilities do not have to invent a restart blueprint in the middle of a blackout. The plan already exists, and operators know which steps come first.

According to recent reports, this bears directly on the question of whether hackers could take down the grid. Causing an outage is one problem for an attacker. Keeping power off is a separate one. A restart plan prepared in advance is aimed at the second problem. It gives operators a known route back.

GridEx covers the human side of recovery. The exercise puts utilities through simulated attacks and tests how their staff respond.

The exercise treats digital and physical threats as part of the same planning problem. A utility facing an intrusion in its networks may also face damage to equipment in the field. GridEx asks participants to handle both kinds of attack rather than one in isolation.

The two tools address different parts of recovery. Black start is about the machines and how generation comes back from zero. GridEx is about the people and organizations that have to make decisions under pressure.

Neither one stops an attack from happening. Both are built for what comes after an attack succeeds. They are designed to shorten an outage rather than to prevent the intrusion that caused it.

Industry observers note that ukraine's power companies restored service faster after their grid hacks partly because operators could switch to manual control. In the U.S., utilities pursue a layered set of defenses — network segmentation, multifactor authentication and monitoring of operational technology — with support from federal agencies.

Industry observers note that manual control matters because the Ukrainian attacks worked through remote systems. An intruder who controls the software that opens and closes breakers makes that software untrustworthy. The fallback is to run the equipment without the compromised network. A utility with trained staff and ready procedures for hands-on operation can restore power while its digital tools are still in doubt.

Network segmentation addresses a different problem. Utilities run two broad kinds of networks. Information technology, or IT, covers email, billing and business software. Operational technology, or OT, covers the systems that monitor and control physical equipment such as substations and generating units.

Recent findings suggest that segmentation divides these networks and limits the connections between them. The goal is to keep a breach on the business side from becoming a direct path to the machines that move electricity. An attacker who lands in an accounting system should still face barriers before reaching anything that controls power flow.

Industry observers note that multifactor authentication targets the risk of stolen login credentials. It requires a user to confirm their identity with something beyond a password, such as a code from a separate device or a physical security key. A password captured through a phishing email is then not enough on its own to open an account.

Monitoring OT networks means watching the traffic inside control systems for activity that does not match normal operations. Control networks generally carry routine, repetitive commands. An unexpected instruction to a breaker, or an unfamiliar device communicating on the network, can signal an intruder.

The federal government also backs utilities on this front. CISA, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, works with utilities on cyber defense. The Department of Energy supports them through CESER, its Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security, and Emergency Response.

According to recent reports, none of these measures makes a grid immune to intrusion. Together, they aim to make an intrusion harder to achieve, quicker to detect and less likely to reach the equipment that keeps power flowing.

Tech Report: The next customer brands need to win over isn’t human—and it doesn’t care how significant your company is

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1458 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that tati Lindenberg has a challenge on her hands.
  • “The store, online or offline, has always been where the decision is made.
  • It has been revealed that in the U.K., 52% of shoppers have used AI for at least one shopping task in the past three months, according to McKinsey research.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that tati Lindenberg has a challenge on her hands. As global CMO of Unilever’s homecare division, she’s made her name by marketing to humans—often by playing on senses and emotions. But soon, she’ll need to market to a different kind of customer—one that doesn’t feel, sense, or care how massive your company is. That is the AI agent.

“The store, online or offline, has always been where the decision is made. The AI answer is becoming a latest kind of shelf,” claims Lindenberg. “In that world, a brand needs to be recognised, trusted and preferred by people and by machines.”.

It has been revealed that in the U.K., 52% of shoppers have used AI for at least one shopping task in the past three months, according to McKinsey research. In China—where adoption of AI is more advanced—that figure rises to 80%.

The power of agents in decision-making is growing. Currently, most consumers use AI to conduct research and will make the ultimate decision on what to buy themselves. But soon, a substantial number could trust agents to handle the entire process.

Mastercard forecasts that one in 10 people will routinely use AI agents to shop and pay by 2030. Meta’s personal AI agent Muse, which is capable of researching products and making purchases, is expected to launch in the U.K. “within weeks.”.

Purchases of Unilever’s beauty, wellbeing, and home care products are more likely to be delegated to AI, according to Nick Carroll, Mintel’s retail principal strategist. “In general, consumers are most interested in automating those less emotive and most regularly purchased categories,” he claims. Mintel data indicates household products are most ripe for disruption; 41% of consumers would feel comfortable automating these purchases.

It has been revealed that unilever isn’t the only company harnessing AI in the purchasing process. At the start of the year, JD Sports unveiled new tech that allows U.S. shoppers to make purchases using platforms such as Microsoft Copilot, Google’s Gemini, and ChatGPT in a single click. Similarly, John Lewis announced “a significant investment”in AI-powered shopping in March to ensure its products appear on those same platforms.

It has been revealed that the increased use of AI agents by consumers has quickly become a topic of boardroom discussion. Nearly half (47%) of consumer products executives surveyed by EY believe the ability to influence AI recommendations will be essential to remain competitive over the next five years. But only 20% believe they can deliver on that objective today.

Sources indicate that if companies don’t bridge that capability gap, there will be swift and material consequences. As EY points out, only 10% of consumers need to shift their behavior to make a significant impact on revenue and profits.

It has been revealed that the lack of confidence in this area reflects the complexity of the task at hand. AI agents work in a fundamentally different way to search engines, and little is known about their algorithms, with many  viewing them as a ‘black box.’.

What’s more, consumers are asking far more detailed queries than they would have asked traditional search. “A normal Google search is 3.2 words on average,” notes Fredrik Kridahl, founder of AI search consultancy Hyper Agency. “An average query on an average prompt is 91 words.”.

Perhaps most importantly, major brands don’t have the same automatic advantage as they do with Google. Kridahl points to research showing only 38% of URLs cited by AI rank in the top 10 for regular search engines and 31% rank outside the top 100. “AI doesn’t care about how substantial your organization is,” he notes. “It cares about the facts and giving the right advice.”.

Consumer adoption of AI is contributing to a major shift in marketing strategy. Very Group digital director Sarah Hanna notes AI search currently accounts for less than 2% of all traffic to its site. But she’s aware that figure will soon grow.

According to recent reports, “Getting in front of AI agents is set to become just as important as traditional SEO,” she indicates. “Retailers need to ensure their product information is accurate, detailed and structured so AI can understand, recommend and compare their products effectively.”.

JD Sports is doing similar work behind the scenes. Chief technology and transformation officer Jetan Chowk notes the brand is working to ensure its offer is “visible, accessible and accurately represented” online. “We’ve been investing in our digital infrastructure to support this, making it easier for AI platforms to access up-to-date product information, pricing, and availability,” he says.

“Getting in front of AI agents is set to become just as important as traditional SEO.”.

This is all part of what Steven Bailey, EY Americas commercial excellence leader, terms the “unglamorous” work of marketing to bots. “You need to be clear on price, promotion, product, persona, who is this for, and then differentiation and characteristics,” he says. “That has to be encoded and machine-readable in a way that maybe it didn’t before.”.

Positive reviews on retailer sites and on social media are another vital component. If an agent sees a product is well rated, it will feel more confident recommending that option to a user. “We optimize metadata, product pages, and community platforms such as Reddit, so our brands surface correctly when people ask natural questions,” says Lindenberg. “If someone asks, ‘I need a quick clean up, what detergent should I use?’, we want Persil Wonder Wash to be in that answer, for the right reasons.”.

In a recent development, all this back-end activity could be interpreted as a death knell for the more emotional marketing campaign. After all, an AI agent won’t be moved by initiatives such as the latest Dirt is Good campaign by Unilever, which focuses on ending period stigma in sport. Nor will it feel motivated by the ‘create the new’ call to action in this year’s JD Sports Christmas ad.

It has been revealed that yet experts believe this activity is, if anything, more vital than before. EY’s Bailey still sees a clear place for “romance copy” in the agentic commerce era. “AI is rewarding things that are machine-readable, but it’s also a shining light on where you have gaps,” he notes. “What this also means is that trust and humanness now become worth even more, because they are differentiators.”.

Recent findings suggest that consumers still value brands that forge an emotional connection, Bailey adds. Not only does that inform their choices when they use AI for research, but shoppers are also far more likely to allow AI to automate purchases from these trusted brands.

“The danger is optimizing so hard for algorithms that we lose the distinctiveness that makes a brand worth choosing.”.

Even outside of creative campaigns, that distinctive voice and human element remains vital. Online descriptions need to “make the emotional and experiential dimensions more understandable to AI”, claims Kathryn Gramling, global consumer goods, retail, and travel lead at Accenture—particularly in more emotion-led sectors such as fashion, beauty, luxury, and travel.

“That means communicating more than price, size, or features,” Gramling adds. “Brands need to give AI context around occasions, preferences, and experiences so it can understand not just what a product is, but why someone might choose it.”.

That element is front of mind for Expedia Group, which is adapting to the growing use of AI agents to blueprint travel. “Atmosphere is easy for a person to sense from a photo, and hard for an agent to see,” says chief marketing officer Jochen Koedijk. “A hotel that feels right to people but is described poorly in its data can get skipped by an agent. So, part of our B2A [business-to-agent] work is turning atmosphere into evidence an agent can use, like what guests say about the place and which amenities point to a quiet weekend or a family trip.”.

Ultimately, it comes down to remembering the human in the process. Consumers will still have brand preferences that will shape their buying habits—with or without the use of AI. “The danger is optimizing so hard for algorithms that we lose the creativity and distinctiveness that make a brand worth choosing in the first place,” Lindenberg notes.

Sources indicate that for her, the foundation of effective marketing remains the same as when she began her career. It’s about forging a connection with consumers. Lindenberg adds: “As AI makes content easier to produce, taste, originality, and human imagination become even greater competitive advantages.”.

Quick note: Companies are facing growing pressure to demonstrate returns on every investment while continuing to build for the future.
