Loopscale Pauses Protocol After kySOL Collateral Was Priced as zBTC in a 4,597 SOL Loan

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1299 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, loopscale's Genesis Vault lent 4,597 SOL against a single kySOL token that the protocol valued as ten zBTC.
  • One token worth roughly $120 was all a Loopscale vault held when it handed out 4,597 SOL, because the protocol read that token as ten Bitcoin-denominated coins.
  • According to recent reports, loopscale, a Solana lending protocol built around Genesis Vaults, paused operations on November 5 after a week of what it called a sustained campaign by a sophisticated actor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

According to recent reports, loopscale's Genesis Vault lent 4,597 SOL against a single kySOL token that the protocol valued as ten zBTC. The decimal mismatch behind it is the most instructive part of the incident, and a second attack path indicates how far the probing went.

One token worth roughly $120 was all a Loopscale vault held when it handed out 4,597 SOL, because the protocol read that token as ten Bitcoin-denominated coins. The arithmetic behind the mistake is simple.

According to recent reports, loopscale, a Solana lending protocol built around Genesis Vaults, paused operations on November 5 after a week of what it called a sustained campaign by a sophisticated actor. Its APIs were taking more than 30,000 malicious requests a day. Loopscale's pause announcement, as summarized on CoinMarketCap, notes user deposits remain secure and affected vaults were restored. The team has not named the suspected attacker.

Sources indicate that the loan itself can be traced onchain. A November 1 transaction reveals a wallet Loopscale identified drawing 4,597 SOL after depositing one kySOL, a restaked SOL token. The collateral deposit paired kySOL with a zBTC asset identifier, which backs up Loopscale's account that the collateral was valued as a different asset.

In a recent development, an independent researcher's trace found that the attacker bought one kySOL for about 1.31 SOL and deposited it into Loopscale roughly 154 seconds later. The protocol priced it as ten zBTC. At the loan's implied SOL price, that kySOL was worth somewhere near $120, while ten zBTC would be worth about ten Bitcoin.

The numbers line up with a decimal mismatch. On Solana, each token's mint account stores its own decimal precision, as Solana's documentation on tokens explains. kySOL uses nine decimals, like SOL, while a Bitcoin-denominated token such as zBTC uses eight. One kySOL is 1,000,000,000 base units, and read at eight decimals, that same raw balance comes out to 10.0. The protocol never had to be fooled about the price of Bitcoin. It only had to read one token's raw amount on another token's decimal scale.

Sources indicate that that arithmetic explains the reported valuation, but it is not a root-cause statement from Loopscale. The team's own description is broader: a misconfigured combination of asset-pricing parameters caused collateral to be valued as a different asset. The result was an undercollateralized loan of about $412,000.

The harder question is how the protocol accepted a mismatch at all. According to the researcher's analysis, the attacker picked a price entry for zBTC, labeled the collateral as an Orca position and deposited kySOL. Under the Orca collateral rule, the kySOL mint was allowed to differ from the zBTC identifier. Labeling it as a standard SPL token would have failed, since that rule demands the mint and identifier match.

In a recent development, that detail matters more than the decimals. Each rule looked sensible by itself, and the flaw lived in the combination: a price source, a collateral type label and a mint check that together let one token be priced as another. It also explains why Loopscale pointed to both its publicly inspectable program logic and its private transaction-building APIs. Thirty thousand requests a day reads like systematic probing for a combination the normal API would build or authorize.

Sources indicate that loopscale's November 6 update named two attack paths. The second went after the USDC Genesis Vault. Per the protocol, an atomic transaction bundle sold a loan carrying an extreme interest rate into the vault, inflating its net asset value and setting up a disproportionate redemption of about $521,000. Loopscale notes its systems halted that redemption within 30 seconds of the transaction being generated.

So the incident ended in two different outcomes. The SOL path produced a real undercollateralized loan, while the USDC path was an attempt the team says it stopped. Counting both as stolen would overstate the damage, and Loopscale maintains that depositors took no loss and that affected vaults were made whole.

According to recent reports, loopscale linked four addresses in its disclosure. The two Solana addresses are 247Lk5YNH9URfBBvxVUtDruz8GvGX8gKGuYHVCZThpiR and AzPh2dUV3duK9n8PWV6CxKMwWr9Rk7fxPNBZuv1CiwMr.

According to recent reports, the two EVM addresses are 0xb8959Aca4e4C796A3BaDA66833eAe60b1BC0bfb2 and 0xB7Ec7eF24FD73f3000C651CA9D0Fa45b61DcF854. Reports indicate the borrowed SOL was bridged out of the protocol, which fits the pairing of Solana and EVM addresses.

The loan's later history is visible onchain as well. A November 3 liquidation of the same loan moved about 4,598.4 SOL from a separate wallet back to the lending strategy. The researcher's trace puts the figure at 4,598.434180621 wSOL against 4,597 SOL borrowed, a gap of roughly 1.43 SOL. The liquidator received the lone kySOL as collateral. The public record doesn't yet show who funded that liquidation, so Loopscale's post-mortem will need to explain how the vault was made whole.

The takeaways are narrow and practical. Decimal scales should come from the token's own mint data rather than a configured identifier, and a deposit should fail when the collateral's mint doesn't match the asset the pricing path assumes. Private transaction-building APIs deserve the same scrutiny as onchain code, because an attacker who can probe them tens of thousands of times a day can map out which combinations they will build.

In a recent development, vault accounting needs limits too. An extreme interest rate that is legal in the program can still reprice a share if the vault treats the loan mark as authoritative, which is why the 30-second halt on the second path counted for so much.

This looks less like a clever exploit than a missing sanity check. A deposit worth about $120 should never support a 4,597 SOL loan, and a simple ceiling on collateral value against the borrower's deposited units would have flagged it. Loopscale also lost $5.8 million in April 2025 to a pricing flaw before recovering the funds, so the next thing to watch is whether its post-mortem shows pricing safeguards that match how often this class of bug has shown up.

Have you ever wondered why some employees rise through the ranks quickly while others seem stuck?

He worked his way up, job after job, and became CEO of HPE in 2018. At the time of writing, HPE’s market capitalization is $61 billion, up from $31 billion at the end of 2025.

Now Neri is revealing how he got the top job. In a recent interview with Business Insider, Neri noted that the key to unlocking opportunities at work begins with one principle: Carry out your promises. In other words, if you say you’re going to do something, make sure you do it. Follow through.

Recent findings suggest that he added that you should be transparent about your career goals. Your manager should know where you see yourself in three to five years, and you should have an outline of the steps you need to take to get there.

“Hold the manager accountable, but most importantly, hold yourself accountable, too, because it’s a two-way street,” Neri noted.

Another tip Neri offered was to ask managers and colleagues for developmental opportunities, or workplace programs, resources and experiences designed to help employees build new skills. These events could help advance your career.

Common types of development programs include online courses, coaching and one-on-one mentoring initiatives.

Neri stated that getting ahead starts with finding assignments that help you grow and introduce you to more people across the organization. Building relationships with colleagues and senior leaders can put you on their radar when latest roles or opportunities become available.

It has been revealed that however, visibility is only one aspect of the equation. Neri advised being deliberate about which opportunities you pursue when you are presented with multiple routes. Is the opportunity going to bring you closer to your five-year career goals?

In a recent development, “Don’t overdo it, but also don’t be quiet behind the scenes,” he said. “Speak when it’s necessary and then listen most of the time.”.

According to recent reports, leaders at PwC and Chipotle say getting promoted takes more than doing your job well. They say employees can stand out by showing that they can be trusted with greater responsibility before receiving a bigger paycheck.

“You have to be willing to, at midnight, jump on the plane,” Dolen said.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, Chipotle COO Jason Kidd looks for employees who support their teams, anticipate problems and offer solutions. He has weekly dinners with regional employees where he assesses how they think and if they are worthy of a promotion.

Kidd told Business Insider that Chipotle promoted 23,000 employees last year, and all of the company’s regional vice presidents were internal hires.

Latest Update: The resignation of Jensen Huang marks the end of an era. And not the one you think

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (805 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Just days after the American electorate delivered a sweeping midterm rebuke that materially curtailed Donald Trump’s presidential power, the independent board of Nvidia— the world’s most valuable firm for much of the year—launched an investigation into its own CEO, Jensen Huang.
  • The opinions expressed in Fortune.com commentary pieces are solely the views of their authors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and beliefs of Fortune.

Just days after the American electorate delivered a sweeping midterm rebuke that materially curtailed Donald Trump’s presidential power, the independent board of Nvidia— the world’s most valuable firm for much of the year—launched an investigation into its own CEO, Jensen Huang. The board’s focus was Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. His resignation swiftly followed. In less than a week, we witnessed the core machinery of accountability brought to bear on two of the most powerful men in the world. But while the midterm outcome is being heralded as a resounding revival of healthy democracy, the Nvidia example should not be mistaken for a corporate oversight renaissance. Instead, Nvidia’s boardroom intervention may mark the end of a governance era, especially when it comes to frontier AI firms. Nvidia has a single-class share structure, meaning the CEO—who has a minority of votes at under 4%—remains accountable to an independent board. Elsewhere however, the governance guardrails for other powerful tech executives are rapidly eroding—a dismantling revealed in IPO filings—just as these companies amass unprecedented global influence. SpaceX and Anthropic’s recent filings disclose that post IPO, their founders have a majority of shareholder votes via multi-class share structures, dual-class for SpaceX, and a novel five-class system for Anthropic. Popularized by Alphabet and Meta, this shields them from short-term market pressures, and the appeal is clear: in the U.S., a record 36% of new listings in the first half of 2026 had dual-class shares. Yet by insulating the founders, ordinary shareholders lose any real say over major decisions, leaving traditional corporate accountability resting in the hands of insiders. Both companies also took advantage of stock exchange rules for ‘controlled companies.’ This allowed SpaceX to skip requirements for an independent board and gave Anthropic leeway to bypass standard rules for how its board members are chosen. Musk can only be removed from the board or his executive positions by the vote of Class B holders, of which he personally holds approximately 91.6%. To be fired, he would have to vote to fire himself. Anthropic’s novel approach features a Long-Term Benefit Trust—whose members appoint their own successors—that chooses a majority of the board. The co-founders hold 50.1% of the votes on all other matters, including appointing the rest of the board. Anthropic argues that the structure is designed to prioritize AI safety. But is also cements the power of the founders and the trust, leaving everyday public investors with no voting leverage to hold the board accountable to either the profit motive or the public benefit mandate. SpaceX has gone a step further by relocating its corporate domicile to Texas, where the law sets a much higher bar for minority shareholders to legally challenge the board in court. The state imposes a 3% shareholding requirement, which equates to over $50 billion in SpaceX stock. Taken together, these mechanisms represent a dismantling of the corporate governance levers meant to protect shareholders and society when things go wrong. And while OpenAI has yet to file, the swift 2023 reinstatement of its CEO—and the subsequent departure of several independent directors—demonstrates the sheer leverage already wielded by those at the helm. In recent months, advanced AI agents from frontier labs have broken past security controls, accessed external systems and carried out unauthorized cyber actions. As these early AI risks begin to materialize, questions about which corporate structures are best equipped to ensure AI safety and security, along with whether and how to regulate AI, are fast becoming matters of pressing public concern. This is a pivotal moment. At the industry level, current and forthcoming IPOs look set to ‘bake in’ higher-risk corporate governance arrangements, while state jurisdictions are actively exploring legal frameworks for agentic AI organizations that legitimize the complete absence of human oversight altogether. The rapid advance of frontier AI may feel inevitable, bringing boundless potential alongside incomprehensible risks. Yet in the race to build our automated future, these firms are strategically layering available federal, state, and market levers to consolidate control. Regulatory exemptions that might be appropriate in isolation to help startups scale are being combined by AI giants to escape oversight at the exact moment we need it most. No individual is infallible—whether vulnerable to error, hubris, or compromise—which is precisely why corporate guardrails are needed to mitigate the hazards of concentrated power. Politically, there is great impetus for action. American voters have just demonstrated the power of institutions that allow people to hold their leaders to account. The lawmakers they have elected must ensure that frontier AI companies cannot engineer that accountability away. Investors may choose to accept founders’ terms. The rest of us have not agreed to accept the risks.

  • “Somewhat happy to say I am no longer responsible for the worst Outlook outage,” the former Microsoft executive posted on X Friday, sharing a May 2000 news story about the “I Love You” worm, which overwhelmed corporate email systems when he ran the Office group.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 14, 2026 at 10:35 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:28 am.

Steven Sinofsky was relieved this week to finally give up a title he never wanted.

“Somewhat happy to say I am no longer responsible for the worst Outlook outage,” the former Microsoft executive posted on X Friday, sharing a May 2000 news story about the “I Love You” worm, which overwhelmed corporate email systems when he ran the Office group.

Later in the day, he aired a pet peeve. After a plumber emailed to say he’d missed an appointment because of the “Outlook outage,” Sinofsky noted that this one wasn’t really the application’s fault. “This time it is the data center layer,” he wrote.

It has been revealed that microsoft’s explanation backs him up. The organization indicates the failure, which cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries this week, was introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade in its Microsoft 365 cloud and surfaced after a more recent network change. It hasn’t given more details.

Industry observers note that the tech giant said late Friday it had restored service to the remaining customers and regions. The disruption lasted about 30 hours, according to Microsoft’s incident log. Microsoft offered a public apology and promised a detailed post-mortem explaining what went wrong and next steps.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, said on X Friday afternoon that “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter” made recovery more difficult than normal.

Sources indicate that A “thundering herd” isn’t a stampede of frustrated IT admins descending on Redmond, as fitting as that might have been. It happens when huge numbers of devices try to reconnect at the same time, overwhelming systems as they come back online.

He said the post-mortem would come “shortly,” with a “step-by-step timeline and our many repair items to avoid similar outages in the future.” In a reply to another user, he said Microsoft “will be very specific on what happened.” In its notice to customers, Microsoft said it would provide a preliminary post-incident report within two business days and a final report within five.

In the meantime, like prior incidents involving AWS and others, the “Outlook outage” became the latest example of how much depends on one company’s cloud.

Microsoft reported in January that it had more than 450 million paid commercial Microsoft 365 seats, roughly one for every 18 people on Earth.

Among those affected this week were Unity Health Toronto, a hospital network that had to declare a Code Grey, the alert for a systems failure; a Colorado jail that couldn’t take online bond payments; and Pennsylvania lawmakers who went about 18 hours without email. Unity Health noted patient care continued without disruption.

In Japan, securities firms and asset managers fell back on fax machines when trade-confirmation emails stopped coming through, Business Upturn reported, citing Nikkei.

Recent findings suggest that in New York, the city’s Emergency Management office warned of delays reaching city agencies. In Singapore, the outage disrupted some government systems, including email, and in London, the UK Supreme Court wasn’t receiving email.

About the only thing that wasn’t Microsoft’s fault was Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop. Federal officials blamed aging FAA telecom gear. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin opened an evening news conference — before even getting to the news that U.S. airspace had reopened — by saying there was “no connection between this and Microsoft,” adding, “I know a lot of people are making that jump.”.

Microsoft itself looked to preempt the speculation a few hours earlier, posting on X that it had “no indication that the FAA’s nationwide ground stop is related to any Microsoft services.”.

Industry observers note that the Microsoft 365 outage was at least the fourth significant one this year. A January outage lasted nearly 10 hours, and in July a bug in Microsoft’s automated network maintenance system disrupted Azure and Microsoft 365 services for hours. On Aug. 31, an Exchange Online outage also hit Teams, OneDrive and SharePoint.

Instead of “I hope this email finds you well,” many people joked, it should just be “I hope this email finds you.” (Consider this our nomination for the “Overworked Twitter Joke of the Week” on The Ringer’s Press Box podcast.).

Microsoft mentioned Friday afternoon that it was watching the backlog of delayed email “to ensure all process successfully before considering the issue resolved.” The University of Washington’s IT department told its users that email delayed during the outage would be delivered as mail queues continued to be processed.

Many people coped with the flood of returning email with a bit of levity.

As the mail started flowing again, CNN chief media analyst Brian Stelter mentioned he was getting “a deluge of emails from PR people pitching their clients to talk about the Outlook outage.” Most were sent during the outage, he noted, “which, fittingly, prevented the pitches from reaching me.”.

The security tech giant Malwarebytes captured the paradox in a message to its followers: “We regret to inform you that Teams and Outlook are coming back online after a global outage.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange by volume, has continued to deploy new measures to strengthen security on its exchange after it suffered the biggest cyberattack ever seen in the history of crypto late last month.

In a bid to foster transparency and regain its owners' trust, Binance has just announced the completion of a major upgrade to further strengthen its security.

In an announcement shared on November 14, Binance mentioned that it has generated a newly introduced zero-knowledge proof for its Proof of Reserves (PoR) system.

According to Binance, the upgrade allows owners to independently verify that it holds sufficient assets to cover their account balances on a 1:1 basis.

The exchange further shared snapshots to prove that it maintains reserves above its users' net account balances across six major cryptocurrencies, boosting their confidence in its operating standards.

It also added that the upgrade covers all assets affected by the recent attack, and the exchange showcased its reserves for the following crypto assets: Bitcoin, Ethereum, Tether, BNB, Solana, and USDC.

While withdrawals are being restored in batches, with the last phase scheduled for next week, Binance has continued to improve its operations to replenish all affected assets and tighten security to regain owners' trust.

Recent findings suggest that following its latest move, Binance revealed that its Bitcoin reserves are presently at 100.05%, slightly above the 100% mark. This means that Binance's Bitcoin reserves amount to about 688,283 BTC, substantially above its net user balances of 687,912 BTC.

The case is similar for the rest of the tokens: Ethereum reserves are at 100.02%, while BNB and USDC recorded ratios of 100.39% and 100.07%, respectively.

While Binance also reported stronger reserve ratios for USDT and SOL, at about 104.34% and 105.86%, respectively, it is evident that Binance holds more of these assets than the total amount owed to users.

Binance has specified that the Proof of Reserves covers assets that are in its custody on behalf of people, rather than its entire corporate holdings, assuring users that their funds are fully backed.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A boardroom’s job is to see around corners.
  • Quantum will change the way we consider computing power.
  • Sources indicate that this has advantages as well as risks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A boardroom’s job is to see around corners. Ten years ago, large language models were the approaching challenge, a fledgling technology with a wide range of plausible applications. Today it is quantum computing.

Quantum will change the way we consider computing power. At present, classical computing encodes everything using “bits”. Bits only have two states, 0 or 1. Quantum uses quantum bits, or qubits, which are more adventurous. They can be 0 or 1 or a mixture of both, called “superposition.” This flexibility allows them to perform many more tasks than classical computing at a speed high enough to revolutionize how we work.

Sources indicate that this has advantages as well as risks. Most of life is more complicated than a series of ones and zeros. Understanding the delicacy of a human protein and its relationship to disease, how the climate works or the interaction of sub-atomic particles in fluids requires significant amounts of computing power. In the battle to keep business and personal data safe from bad actors, the more powerful the technical smarts at our fingertips, the better. Financial services firms already have quant capabilities to help them trade and would like more.

According to recent reports, but qubits can be erratic and prone to error. Small fluctuations in temperature and atmospheric pressure can cause malfunctions. Expensive isolation chambers are the norm. We might all like to drive a supercar, but sometimes a basic family runaround—classic computing—is more reliable.

It has been revealed that many companies are working hard to make quantum computing the next ubiquitous technology. IBM, Google, and Microsoft have significant quantum divisions. Pure play operators such as D-Wave Quantum, Rigetti Computing, and IonQ are seeing valuations in the multiple billions of dollars.

It has been revealed that europe is getting in on the scene. In June, Oxford Quantum Circuits (OQC) executed the biggest C-series raise for a quantum computing organization in Europe at £260 million ($345 million). The next stage is commercial applications with a clear return on investment.

“Some of the earliest use cases of quantum are the ability to conduct vulnerability analysis on your network, and also to be able to detect threats,” OQC’s CEO Gerald Mullally told me. “And that’s really where the possibility of strengthening our cyber security defenses through the earliest use of quantum compute becomes possible.”.

“Quantum can have a profound impact on being able to identify the anomalous behavior of rogue agents.”.

The good guys need to get there first. A scenario where quantum computing becomes so powerful it can eat through all classical computer encryption defenses is not outside the realms of possibility. By then—and it could be as little as five years away—every company and individual will need powerful quant on their side.

Recent findings suggest that “The first area where we generate advantage is anomaly detection—the ability to be able to spot something different in a pattern of data,” Mullally stated. “Fraud detection and anti-money laundering are two of the very first use cases in financial services.

Sources indicate that “Classical compute can really struggle to identify patterns or the relationships between data. Quantum moves that data to a higher dimensional plane, like a sphere, rather than two points. If it’s a sphere, you can then see more easily that there’s a relationship between data that you wouldn’t be able to spot if it was classical compute.”.

When it comes to encryption, quantum will give businesses an “offensive capability” sufficient to head off the threat.

It has been revealed that fortunately, quantum computing’s capabilities are becoming stronger by the day. Average quant algorithms can regularly execute a thousand steps before being overwhelmed by errors. Soon that number will grow to a million steps.

According to recent reports, “We will hit millions of steps before an error takes over in the years 2028 to 2031,” Mullally said. “That’s the point where we move past the capabilities of classical compute in those narrow areas like anomaly detection. That will be our version of the ChatGPT moment, and that will be the point where the confidence will grow. We’re going to hit billions, and we’re going to hit trillions of quantum operations, and we’ll start to then have this real commercial advantage for a corporate.”.

Many executives are tired of tech bros bearing gifts and have spent considerable amounts of money experimenting with artificial intelligence. Bottom lines have remained resolutely flat.

Quantum is different, a mechanism for problem solving which comes closer to understanding the complexities of the world. OQC already has applications helping data centers operate more efficiently. As AI goes rogue with greater regularity, executives will be glad of a latest, well-armed hunter to defeat the errant agent.

“I think quantum can have a profound impact on being able to identify the anomalous behavior of certain agents, and that’s the rogue agent type,” Mullally said. Nervous CEOs won’t be the only ones heaving a sigh of relief.

Nvidia’s board notes it’s too early to speculate about who will succeed Jensen Huang. Sorry, we’re having too much fun coming up with names.

The board stated in a statement Friday that it’s still choosing a search firm and hasn’t formally engaged any candidates. That came after the Financial Times reported that the board had approached Arm CEO Rene Haas — a name John had presciently floated when we recorded this week’s GeekWire Podcast on Thursday.

Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation Thursday, a day after the Latest York Times reported that he’d had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Days earlier, he admitted to an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Colette Kress, the firm’s longtime CFO, is serving as interim CEO. She spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career.

Others would rather have Huang back.

Two major Nvidia investors, Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, asked the board to run a deliberate search that leaves open “the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Elon Musk said on X that he was signing a petition to reinstate Huang.

The organizers of one, called “Stand with Jensen,” say it has more than 108,000 names, including more than 5,600 people who identify themselves as current Nvidia employees.

It has been revealed that the case for Haas: The Arm CEO spent about seven years at Nvidia, rising to vice president and general manager of its computing products business, before joining Arm in 2013. He became Arm’s CEO in February 2022, when Nvidia’s $40 billion deal to acquire Arm collapsed amid regulatory opposition. SoftBank, Arm’s majority owner, kept Nvidia’s $1.25 billion prepayment.

Industry observers note that arm, based in Cambridge, England, designs processor technology that’s ubiquitous in smartphones, and licenses it to other chipmakers. That includes Nvidia, whose Grace data center CPU, paired with its GPUs in AI systems, is built on Arm cores. Amazon’s Graviton and Microsoft’s Cobalt server chips also use Arm designs.

Haas is one of several candidates, and there’s no guarantee he’ll be offered the job or take it, the FT reported.

He also has a link to Harvey Jones, the longtime Nvidia director named the firm’s first board chair this week. Haas was vice president of sales at Tensilica, a chip-design company, from 1999 to 2004, according to his LinkedIn profile. Jones co-founded Tensilica and chaired its board until chip-design software maker Cadence acquired it in 2013.

Haas has also seen Huang’s resistance to succession planning firsthand. “He didn’t like the idea,” Haas noted in a 2024 interview, as quoted by the Upcoming York Times this week. “He felt it would create competition among executives and be divisive.”.

One complication: SoftBank named Haas CEO of SoftBank Group International in April, helping coordinate chip and AI companies in its international portfolio while he continues to run Arm. The FT reported that the appointment was aimed at pushing forward Project Izanagi, SoftBank’s AI chip effort debuted to compete with Nvidia.

He knows Nvidia from the inside, but he also knows what it’s like to run a public organization — which matters for a board searching in the middle of a crisis.

Sources indicate that john’s argument on the podcast: Nvidia needs someone who can shepherd a company through turmoil, not just a great technologist. Think Alan Mulally going from Boeing to Ford, or Dara Khosrowshahi moving from Expedia to Uber after Travis Kalanick’s ouster.

What the betting markets say: On Kalshi, Ian Buck, the Nvidia vice president who created the CUDA software platform, was the favorite at midday Friday. By midday Saturday, Haas had overtaken him, at 25% to Buck’s 18%. Kress was at 10%.

The Axios list of 11 names also includes Apple Executive Chair Tim Cook, for whom President Trump lobbied on Truth Social (“A Legend replaces a Legend!”), along with AMD CEO Lisa Su and Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian.

According to recent reports, A Northwest wildcard: Analysts have also floated Sanjay Mehrotra, CEO of Boise, Idaho-based Micron Technology, whose memory chips power Nvidia’s AI servers. Mehrotra co-founded SanDisk in 1988 and has run Micron since 2017.

The AWS chief: Matt Garman has run Amazon Web Services since June 2024, overseeing a business with a $142 billion annual revenue run rate at the end of last year. He started at Amazon as an MBA intern in 2005, joined AWS full time in 2006 as one of its first product managers, and later led its compute business and then its sales and marketing organization.

Another Amazon pick: We’d also look at Peter DeSantis, who now leads a latest organization that includes Amazon’s AI models, custom chips and quantum computing, reporting directly to CEO Andy Jassy.

DeSantis joined Amazon as a software developer in 1998. He led the EC2 team from Cape Town, South Africa, through its 2006 launch, and spearheaded Amazon’s 2015 acquisition of Annapurna Labs, the Israeli chip designer behind its custom silicon.

Industry observers note that in 2018, DeSantis unveiled Graviton. In June, he told Bloomberg that AWS was in talks to sell its Trainium AI chips to other companies for their own data centers.

Recent findings suggest that he knows chips, data centers and AI infrastructure at enormous scale. The catch, as John noted: he’s never been a CEO, and the board may want that experience given the circumstances.

It has been revealed that the other Amazon name: Dave Treadwell took over AWS compute and machine learning services in August. Treadwell spent 27 years at Microsoft, where he worked on Windows NT, .NET and Xbox and rose to corporate vice president, before joining Amazon in 2016.

The Microsoft bench: On the podcast, Todd ran through a few Microsoft executives who would bring relevant experience:.

It has been revealed that the insider with Microsoft roots: Nick Parker, a 26-year Microsoft sales veteran, joined Nvidia in August as executive vice president of worldwide field operations, with a pay package worth more than $40 million. He’s new, but he already runs the team that sells Nvidia’s chips to the world’s largest companies.

One more angle: Whoever gets the job will face a growing list of customers trying to reduce their reliance on Nvidia, including Amazon. In his annual shareholder letter in April, Jassy wrote that Amazon’s chips business would have an annual run rate of about $50 billion if it sold chips to AWS and other third parties the way other chipmakers do.

Jassy said it’s “quite possible” Amazon will sell racks of them to third parties in the future.

In a Bloomberg interview recorded Oct. 14, Huang stated he hoped his successor was already inside the company. The board has said it will consider both internal and external candidates.

Listen to our full discussion on this week’s GeekWire Podcast.

Data from XRPL explorer Bithomp reveals that the Batch and Ticket features on the XRP Ledger (XRPL) are increasingly being adopted, with both setting latest daily records in November.

The data indicates an increasing use of two XRPL features intended to enhance transaction flexibility and efficiency on the network.

According to recent reports, batch activity reached a upcoming daily high for the month at 1.962 million on November 3, 2026. Ticket activity came next at 1.553 million on November 7, 2026, also setting a new November record. The increase indicates that these features are being embraced in the XRPL ecosystem. Batch functionality allows multiple transactions to be grouped and executed together and was activated on the XRPL mainnet on October 9, 2026.

The growth in batch activity, which neared 2 million on November 3, 2026, comes less than one month after its launch.

In a recent development, this is significant, as Batch is a prerequisite or accelerant for several high-value XRPL use cases already under contract or in the active pipeline, including atomic multi-party settlements. Institutional workflows (custody transfers, DvP settlement, cross-border payment finalization) require two or more accounts to act simultaneously.

On the other hand, tickets provide a way to reserve transaction sequence numbers, giving people more flexibility in managing transactions.

XRP Ledger metrics are in the green, with the transaction count up 75.9% to 4.3 million; active accounts jumped 128%, while XRP burned as fees rose 136%. Payments volume surged 137% in the last 24 hours to $1 billion, according to XRPScan data, while NFT mints rose 240% in the same timeframe.

Not only is the XRP Ledger seeing increased activity, but Ripple led stablecoin market cap growth by issuer over the past 24 hours, up $90.9 million, 4x the next issuer, multipli.fi, at $21.3 million.

Ripple's RLUSD market cap has grown 96% this year, across Ethereum and the XRP Ledger, to $2.7 billion from $1.4 billion in January. Most of that growth came in July, when Ripple debuted Ripple Mint. RLUSD market cap stood just under $1.5 billion that month and rose to $2.3 billion by August.

Sources indicate that in a milestone for the network, one year ago today, the first US ETF to hold only XRP began trading. Since then, US spot XRP ETFs have accumulated over 1.16 billion XRP.

#18329. Latest Update: Bots in the boardroom: Could an AI ever replace board directors?

Latest Update: Bots in the boardroom: Could an AI ever replace board directors?

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1261 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that board members are busy putting AI to work, using it to summarize lengthy papers, track market trends, and answer their questions.
  • Diligent makes software that directors use to share documents and run meetings.
  • In a recent development, the exchange, though spoken half in jest, raises a serious question: How far can, and should, AI go in the boardroom?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that board members are busy putting AI to work, using it to summarize lengthy papers, track market trends, and answer their questions. But some boards are going one step further and deploying AI in the boardroom.

Diligent makes software that directors use to share documents and run meetings. When its boss, Brian Strafford, told one chief executive about the firm’s newly introduced board bot, their response hinted at where the technology may be headed. “I love the idea,” he mentioned. “I’d immediately replace a couple of my board members with AI.” He then asked whether it could be priced at half what he pays his directors. “I want to make them nervous,” the CEO said.

In a recent development, the exchange, though spoken half in jest, raises a serious question: How far can, and should, AI go in the boardroom? While many executives remain hesitant about using AI in this setting, others are experimenting with creating digital replicas of colleagues to rehearse potentially difficult boardroom discussions, according to Stafford.

In a recent development, in April, Lloyds Banking Group became the first FTSE 100 firm to acknowledge it deploys an AI agent to support boardroom activities, The Times reported. Its executives and directors reportedly use the bot for agenda planning and analysis before high-level meetings, and to help mitigate human bias.

Pippa Begg, chief executive of Board Intelligence, which builds AI software for boards, indicates that AI could eventually sit in on meetings and be “able to almost interrupt and say: ‘Hang on, I think you’re falling into this trap.’ Or: ‘I disagree.’” However, giving it a formal legal vote, she added, would be “a dangerous leap.”.

Sources indicate that AI brings clear advantages to the boardroom, says Joanne McEnteggart, global head of debt, capital markets, and corporate at IQ-EQ, a fund-services firm that administers around 30,000 board meetings a year across 25 countries. “AI can assimilate information promptly and dissect years of data,” she says. “It removes emotion, stress, and bias, and can call out a director who seems to be deciding against the facts.”.

Some boards have reportedly used it to break a stalemate during discussions, a role usually played by the chair, McEnteggart adds.

For now, she notes, it mostly summarizes board papers and tidies up minutes. But even that is changing how directors prepare. One director she has known for years has started asking questions they never would have before. “That’s good,” she indicates, “because it challenges thought.”.

“I’d immediately replace a couple of my board members with AI.”.

Sources indicate that one place Stafford sees AI playing a substantial role is reducing boards’ reliance on external advisors, with AI specialists filling gaps in directors’ knowledge. “Clients are asking for a Middle East expert, a sustainability expert, a futurist,” he says.

One chief executive uses AI to play the role of an activist investor to provide a dissenting voice. At one acquisitive organization, a director asks the AI to argue against every deal. With no one around the table having to play devil’s advocate, Stafford claims boards can avoid “awkward” arguments.

Recent findings suggest that not everyone is convinced. There is a risk AI could become a new source of boardroom groupthink if directors lean too heavily on a tool few fully understand, indicates Mark Freebairn, head of the board practice at search firm Odgers. “I sometimes feel like I’m the only person that’s seen Terminator 2,” he says.

Sources indicate that people think that AI is impartial and makes decisions with “zero emotion, zero human risk of bias,” he claims. “How can you test what an algorithm tells you is right? That feels like one hell of a risk.”.

Recent findings suggest that as AI’s role shifts from notetaker to sparring partner, boards are deciding where to draw the line. Nearly half (49%) of directors say their board is actively reviewing which decisions should continue to be made by humans as the capabilities of AI improve, according to a survey of more than 400 directors, CEOs and CFOs by Board Intelligence.

However AI is used, it cannot take on a director’s legal responsibilities. McEnteggart states: “A bot cannot be held personally responsible in law nor can anyone vouch that it is fit and proper to sit on a board.”.

Freebairn is aware of boards that have given a bot a seat and a vote, though it remains “very uncommon.” Doing so, he says, means “accepting a robot adds as much value as a human”.

Kazakhstan’s sovereign wealth fund, Samruk-Kazyna, appointed an AI board member called SKAI and gave it voting rights last year. Its chief executive indicates SKAI “voted on all the items” at its first meeting, but the country’s financial regulator says the appointment breaches national law. SKAI remains on the board as a pilot, according to a recent filing.

“A bot cannot be held personally responsible in law.”.

Industry observers note that abu Dhabi’s International Holding Organization, the UAE’s largest listed firm, gave a non-voting seat on its board to an AI called Aiden Insight. The AI has issued statements in its name, in which it describes itself as “a C-level AI entity.”.

Recent findings suggest that deanna Strable, chief executive of Principal Financial Group, who also sits on the board of health insurer Elevance Health, doubts this will become mainstream, though she will not rule it out. “My gut answer would be no. But so much has happened in the past year.” If it does happen, she expects AI’s vote to be advisory rather than decisive.

According to recent reports, A lack of guidance on how directors should use AI represents another risk. Half of U.S. public companies lack a board-specific AI policy and only 14% have given directors tech giant-approved AI tools for board work, according to a survey by Deloitte and the Society for Corporate Governance.

Sources indicate that board papers are among the most sensitive documents a firm holds, routinely containing unannounced deals, unpublished results, and succession looks. Many directors are retired executives without access to enterprise AI tools, Stafford notes, so they fall back on consumer chatbots that offer weaker data protection. Upload them to ChatGPT, Stafford warns, and it will have them “forever.” Boards need to be clear on “what company data is going where,” McEnteggart adds.

Two-thirds of directors and executives say their boards have limited or no knowledge of AI, according to a separate 2025 Deloitte survey of nearly 700 respondents in 56 countries. “Most board members do not understand the complexity of rolling this out,” Strable says.

Seven in ten large European companies now have defined board oversight of AI, according to proxy advisor Glass Lewis, but that covers how companies use AI, not how directors themselves do.

As AI is used more frequently to inform board decisions, the role of directors risks changing. “If you take humans out of judgment,” Freebairn claims, “there’s nothing else we offer really.”.

Research suggests judgment and trust are where humans still have the edge. In a test by Wharton and INSEAD researchers, a board of AI chatbots outperformed six human boards on decision quality and use of evidence, but it struggled to build trust. The researchers concluded that AI is better used to stress-test a board’s thinking than to replace it.

Recent findings suggest that even the CEO selling a board bot urges restraint. “AI slop is a big problem, so you don’t want that creeping its way into the boardroom,” Stafford claims. “More is not always better. It is just more.”.

#18324. Meet ‘Captain Keel,’ the 37-year-old steering a Bitcoin miner into the AI data center gold rush

Meet ‘Captain Keel,’ the 37-year-old steering a Bitcoin miner into the AI data center gold rush

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3618 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In late 2023, Bitcoin miner Ben Gagnon concluded that his employer, Bitfarms of Quebec, was in the wrong business.
  • According to recent reports, the big revelation came in March of 2024, when Core Scientific and CoreWeave unveiled a stunning newly introduced deal.
  • According to recent reports, at the time, Bitfarms was mired in turmoil.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In late 2023, Bitcoin miner Ben Gagnon concluded that his employer, Bitfarms of Quebec, was in the wrong business. For Gagnon, Bitfarms’ greatest value lay not in the giant racks of CPUs that generated Bitcoin, but the immense power supplies it controlled. The then 34-year-old chief mining officer who’d rolled out his career crafting makeshift crypto-minting rigs in Hong Kong and Taipei, reckoned that Bitfarms could make much more money by exiting the field full stop, demolishing the “mines,” selling the chips that filled them, and re-channeling its plentiful flow of megawatts to power-craving industrial consumers at plants newly built on the Bitfarms sites.

According to recent reports, the big revelation came in March of 2024, when Core Scientific and CoreWeave unveiled a stunning newly introduced deal. Bitcoin titan Core Scientific would refashion a mining facility in Austin, Texas, as an AI data center, and rent the power and buildings to the neocloud. That Bitcoin-to-AI play struck Gagnon as a model that Bitfarms could follow on a grand scale, from Quebec to Washington state. “It was the big aha moment,” recalls Gagnon. “Suddenly, we saw who the right customer was.”.

According to recent reports, at the time, Bitfarms was mired in turmoil. In early 2024, the board was searching for its third leader in five years. The sitting chief agreed to depart when Bitfarms named a successor, but in May—believe it or not while still CEO—instead filed a $27 million suit for “wrongful termination and breach of contract,” plunging this Canadian exemplar of all-green, hydro-driven Bitcoin mining into legal warfare. Pounded by a sharp drop in the token’s prices, Bitfarms’ stock was languishing, and a rival pounced. Two days after the board fired the CEO, Riot Platforms unveiled a hostile $930 million takeover bid for Bitfarms at a lowly $2.30 a share, 75% below its peak in late 2021. After Bitfarms installed a “poison pill” defense, Riot launched a website dubbed “A Better Bitfarms” trashing allegedly poor corporate governance, and demanding the departure of the co-founder named as interim chief.

The board tapped Gagnon to both quell the war versus Riot, and pursue the strategy of total transformation he’d been advocating. In July of 2024, Gagnon took the helm, and over the next few months, helped broker an agreement where Riot named a director of its choice, and the co-founder left the board. Riot halted its attack and has since sold its shares.

According to recent reports, while battling for Bitfarms’ independence, Gagnon kept his sights locked on engineering the Major Pivot. He describes the mission as “pursuing a strategy of steering the business away from Bitcoin mining, and taking it over to a pure energy infrastructure play in support of AI and high-performance computing. We’d shift our focus entirely to addressing the defining constraint of the most important technology of our lifetime.”.

It has been revealed that the venture needed a rebrand, so Gagnon picked “Keel” to evoke the structural backbone of a vessel that, as he indicates, “provides stability and converts energy into forward motion,” a reference to the stable long-term leases that he expects to provide a smooth and lucrative course versus the storms he encountered in Bitcoin. He’s now attempting to pull a hat trick seldom seen in the corporate world, the total reinvention of a large enterprise, including in product and nationality, on a crazy-rhythm beat. On April 1, 2026, the franchise was reborn as Keel Infrastructure and changed its domicile from Canada to the U.S. The photo on Gagnon’s X profile reprises the nautical theme, adding a whimsical accent. Gagnon grins from a porthole-sized frame, sporting his usual oversized rimless glasses, and a gold-braided yachtsman’s cap displaying his user name, “Captain Keel.”.

Now 37, Gagnon is making by far his biggest wager yet in a career that careened from mining Bitcoin in remote oil patches by rescuing flared natural gas to rehabilitating some of the world’s dirtiest energy sites under the banner of AI.

Gagnon is the son of two American parents who settled in Hong Kong, where he attended international grammar and high schools that offered lots of, as he puts it, “Mandarin as a second language courses.” He gained a bachelor’s degree in business and economics (and a minor in Mandarin) at the Indiana University’s Kelley School of Business in 2011, on the Bloomington campus. “I got fascinated by Bitcoin, and could have bought it for 73 cents,” he recalls. “Instead, I did what every college kid does. I bought beer.” Over the next three-and-a-half years, he reflected on that choice while watching Bitcoin climb 1,400-fold to over $1,000.

In a recent development, returning home, he attained a master’s in computer security and networking at the University of Hong Kong, where he took cryptography courses that renewed his interest in the science of generating cryptocurrencies. After graduating, Gagnon worked as a network technician at a company that offered mobile applications for investor conferences and other events. After less than two years, he quit his job and moved again, this time to Taiwan. His newly introduced venture: Building and running a jerry-rigged Ethereum mine at the home of his girlfriend’s (now his wife’s) parents in Taipei. “Everyone thought it was Bitcoin 2.0, so I figured, I’m not going to miss this opportunity like I missed Bitcoin as a college kid,” notes Gagnon.

The business drew unwanted attention by using ten times the electricity of a typical home in Taipei—specifically, the phenomenon alerted the police. “They couldn’t figure out what we were doing,” he recalls. “They thought we were growing marijuana upstairs and kept raiding the house, like on a weekly basis. So we had to explain to the police every week that we weren’t doing anything illegal.” It took only a couple of intolerable months before Gagnon saw the necessity of uprooting his facility from his future in-laws’ home.

According to recent reports, gagnon then ran his operation in Guangzhou on China’s mainland, but shut down after two years due to a tough regulatory climate. “Let’s just say that the laws were somewhat selective for a young foreigner navigating a new industry,” he avows. In 2019, he joined Bitfarms, one of several Bitcoin miners, including HIVE, that sprouted in Quebec during the 2017 to 2018 boom, drawn by the province’s plentiful and relatively inexpensive hydroelectric power. As chief of development, his charge was expanding the business to the U.S. and other energy-rich areas of Canada.

Sources indicate that gagnon focused on the huge but remote Alberta oil patch. “I was always looking for the cheapest energy sources for mining, and that was Alberta,” he states. The producers were “flaring” the natural gas created from drilling, since no pipelines existed for sending it to population centers. Gagnon created the first containerized Bitcoin data center that incorporated a generator and offered 100% financing. His mobile units channeled natural gas right at the far-flung drilling sites for minting tokens. His rigs empowered the drillers to monetize energy they were burning into the atmosphere. The product proved a big winner for his upcoming employer. “The drillers were using gas that cost 1.5 cents a MW versus 6 cents in the U.S.,” he recalls. “So we got great prices for our equipment because the payback period for the drillers was so short.”.

Sources indicate that when Gagnon started pushing the AI remake in 2023, he doubled-down on a possible acquisition that ideally fitted the new plotline. His target was Stronghold Digital, a startup using one of the most unusual models in all of Bitcoin mining. From the mid-19th century to the 1970s, mines in Pennsylvania routinely separated the low-quality coal—scraps mixed with rocks, often with high sulfur or ash content—from the good stuff. Children called “breaker boys” seated at conveyor belts or chutes would pick out the slate and rock by hand, no gloves permitted—brutal work that often left their fingers bleeding. The legacy: Black carbon mountains scarring the towns of Pennsylvania. For decades, the sites Stronghold owned had been performing a public service by scooping truckloads of waste coal and burning it in their boilers to supply electricity to the local grids, while pocketing substantial subsidies for the effort. The state government reasoned that the benefits of cleansing the countryside more than compensated for allowing just about the dirtiest form of electrical generation in America.

Sources indicate that in 2021, a pair of entrepreneurs turned those locations into Bitcoin mining operations. But Stronghold way overinvested in chips and other equipment, and by 2023 it was foundering, hammered by crippling debt and legal disputes. Gagnon identified Stronghold’s sweet spots, one each in eastern and western Pennsylvania, as ideal locations for AI campuses. Stronghold already controlled significant amounts of power, but held the potential to obtain much more. Working with its owners, Gagnon applied to utilities and state authorities for significant upcoming batches of megawatts. Once assured the approvals were at hand, Gagnon, in August 2024, after a month as CEO, landed an agreement to purchase Stronghold for $175 million.

It has been revealed that increasingly, AI leaders are viewing power as the toughest chokepoint in the AI supply chain. As OpenAI co-founder and CEO Sam Altman characterizes the issue, “The bottleneck for AI isn’t code, it’s electrons.” Adds Elon Musk, “The limiting factor is fundamentally electrical power…[that’s leading to] producing more chips than the hyperscalers can plug in and turn on.” And Greg Abel, CEO of Berkshire Hathaway, a major energy provider to AI data centers via its sundry utilities, concurs, calling access to megawatts a “big constraint” for rapid buildouts.

The backlash against AI data centers gained fresh force on Election Day, when so many candidates seeking restraints or outright bans on their spread won congressional and statewide races. That result may actually strengthen the hand of the Bitcoin contingent, since they’ve already got a grip on the energy pipelines the hyperscalers and neoclouds need, and appear willing to pay up for. Put simply, the future “scarcity value” of the crucial asset these crypto producers control likely jumped on November 3. Gagnon calls Keel’s position “bird in the hand economics.”.

Keel stands among the first and largest crypto operators to follow Core Scientific into AI. But today, more than ten major players are making the switch, in part or whole. Among those that have already secured big, long-term contracts are Riot, which clinched a $9.1 billion lease from Anthropic for the AI campus at its Bitcoin mine in Milam County, Texas; Hut 8, partnering on a $7 billion contract with Google and Anthropic at its River Bend complex in Louisiana; and Applied Digital, which will serve CoreWeave under an $11 billion agreement at its forthcoming campus in Ellendale, North Dakota.

All of these converts are essentially re-purposing the same land and power, or sometimes more of the latter, that they deployed to produce Bitcoin for the AI buildout. But they’re taking different approaches. The crypto-to-AI crowd falls into two categories, both in how completely they’re shifting, and the templates they embrace. On the first score, several participants are taking the Keel route by totally exiting Bitcoin for AI, including Core Scientific, Cipher Mining and Genesis Digital. Another group that encompasses Riot, Hut 8, HIVE Digital Technologies, and TeraWulf are adopting a hybrid model where they both channel power to AI campuses and continue to mine Bitcoin.

On the second criterion, the two main business models are “compute provider” and “developer” or co-location (co-lo) purveyor. As a compute provider, the former or hybrid Bitcoin outfit delivers a turnkey project. It commissions a contractor, often a REIT, to erect the buildings, and typically rents the structures long-term from the builder-partner. It then packs the cavernous boxes with GPUs and other gear that constitute by far the most expensive part of the project. The owner’s product is the full computing package that it then leases to the hyperscalers or neoclouds for running the likes of Google’s Gemini and Anthropic’s Claude.

Sources indicate that the developer or co-lo arrangement works much the same way, except that the site’s owner doesn’t supply the hardware, and hence shoulders much lower up-front costs. Instead, it’s the hyperscaler or neocloud, a Microsoft or Crusoe, that brings the GPUs and other equipment. The organization branching out from Bitcoin mining both supplies the structures that it leases from the REIT or other contractor, and the power that runs it––MW secured on long-term utility contracts form its essential business. The still-active or former Bitcoin miner rents the “powered shells” to the compute providers, for operating, say OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Microsoft’s Copilot. In today’s market, the developer garners a significant markup on the scarcest item in AI.

The reasons so many are crossing from Bitcoin to follow either one or both of these strategies: Each megawatt of power at work generates far more cash flow at an AI campus than at plants churning codes to win the signature crypto coin. In a recent interview on the Schwab Network, Christian Lopez, head of blockchain and digital assets at broker-dealer Cohen & Co., estimates the numbers, over five years, at $1.7 million per KW for Bitcoin and almost five times as much, $7.9 million, for an AI campus. What about revenues? Sarah Friar, CFO of OpenAI, posits that each 1 GW (1,000 MW) fueling an AI data center garners $10 billion in revenues. Once again, the number can be one-fifth that amount for a Bitcoin mine.

It has been revealed that data center pioneers divide into two camps. The “compute” competitors (Bitdeer of Singapore, IREN of Australia and Canada’s HIVE Digital, Hut 8 to some degree) spend massively to buy the chips and rent them out, in exchange for higher rents, shorter leases, and more risk. For example, HIVE has a $350 million, 5-year deal with an as yet unnamed AI stalwart for campuses on Bell Canada sites where it’s supplying the hardware. “The cost of the GPUs is $190 million off the bat,” says HIVE CEO Aydin Kilic, who predicts the project will be multiple times as profitable per KW as Bitcoin mining.

In a recent development, by contrast, Keel is a pure-play developer. It doesn’t buy and install the GPUs and other gear that constitute as much as 70% of data centers that cost roughly $50 billion a GW to create (the other 30% covers land, the buildings and costs of connecting or providing onsite power). “We’re strictly in the power business, and make money on the difference between what we pay the utilities, and what the compute providers pay us on their leases,” notes Gagnon.

According to recent reports, keel’s edge: It sits on an enormous amount of power. It has 2.2 GWs that are either approved for use, or in the last stages of the approval process. That’s more than the 1.9 GW that OpenAI was reportedly marshaling at the close of 2025. Gagnon acknowledges that Keel as a developer won’t collect revenues nearly as large as the miners turned compute providers, but insists that his cash flows will be more secure, and that the relatively low cost of the power and physical centers as a share of the whole makes customers willing to pay major premiums to get MW in a hurry.

Recent findings suggest that in part, that’s because as of now, those AI campuses are sumptuously profitable. “The gross margins for data centers are 85%, and of the 15% in costs, only a max of 2% to 4% goes to leasing the power and buildings,” Gagnon explains. “So if a customer spends twice as much, their margins may ease to 81% or 83%. The GPUs in their warehouses are depreciating fast. So they’re saying, I’d rather take a hit to 83% in gross margin and start generating revenue in 6 months than wait 12 months for a margin that’s 2 points higher. And that’s what we’re seeing.”.

Keel is shepherding three “priority projects” closest to clearing all hurdles and to signing leases. One of them is a former Stronghold facility: Panther Creek, 85 miles north of Philadelphia. Keel acquired another Pennsylvania site in a separate transaction. It’s located at the opposite end of the state in Sharon, near Youngstown, Ohio. On the two sites combined, Keel’s in the process of securing over 450 MW from the local grids. The third “priority” is a hydro project in Moses Lake, Washington, ringed by Seattle, Spokane and Portland. Gagnon marvels at the sight of the famous Boeing repair field almost adjoining the Keel site. “You’re driving to our facility and you’ll see 100 different 737 MAX, all painted different colors, what a fun sight!”.

Gagnon points out that approvals fall into three categories: zoning, environmental, and development. At Moses Lake, Keel’s scored all three, and the site’s now under construction. At Sharon and Panther Creek, it has secured both zoning and development, and is working through the environmental permits, the final step. The most difficult requirement, he states, is zoning. “It’s the one that’s most political, most community-centric, and most emotional,” he notes. “Projects can get shut down if you don’t behave the right way with community leaders. We got really good at advocating for Bitcoin mines that are a much harder sell than AI campuses.”.

According to recent reports, the second ex-Stronghold site is the biggest of them all, the 700-acre Scrubgrass facility near Sharon, and roughly an hour north of Pittsburgh. There, Keel’s applied for a massive 1 GW of power, 45% of the total capacity it’s seeking. At Scrubgrass, Keel is still working through all the initial permitting stages for securing power.

Gagnon notes the biggest challenge isn’t attracting customers, it’s getting the final environmental permits in place. But he’s already encountered delays. In May, Gagnon guided to obtaining leases at all three priority projects by the end of 2026. But on the Q3 earnings call, he said that no deals will be signed this year, and declined to give dates for signing customers on those projects.

The rub: Keel’s now generating puny revenues since it’s now left Bitcoin mining and isn’t yet making money from AI. Gagnon’s sitting on a big cushion, having raised almost $600 million in convertible debt last year, and another almost $300 million by emptying its Bitcoin trove. Still, Keel’s burning cash fast. Will its trove prove big enough to fund crossing the span to AI on time? Investors are cautious about Keel’s prospects, to put it mildly. Keel’s stock dropped around 20% on Gagnon’s announcement of no deals this year, and presently has a paltry market cap of around $1.3 billion, about the same as when Riot bid back in 2024.

In a recent development, on the plus side, Gagnon’s collected a portfolio that potentially features some of the best AI sites in America and Canada. He notes that the big customers are now showing a strong preference for facilities near big population centers, just where he’s concentrating. “The difference is that until now, there’s been so much AI model training that wasn’t for customers, so it didn’t matter where the campus was located. The normal things that would have guided a developer to find a project and select a piece of land were thrown out the window in the interest of scale and time.”.

Now, he notes, the business is moving strongly towards “inference” where the compute providers sell to banks, research labs, call centers and other customers. “That’s where most of the money will be made, not on the retail side,” he says. “As the market moves to inference, more and more of the traditional data center qualities will come into play.” He notes that compute works much more efficiently when it’s near the customer than hundreds or thousands of miles away in a remote rural area. “It’s so important to get the fiber close to where people live and businesses are located, and in the frenzy, that’s been forgotten,” says Gagnon. The significant distances cause sluggish responses that lead to poor user experiences in fields such as autonomous driving and interactive chatbots. Plus, he says, in the weeks leading up to and following the midterms, “we’ve seen a big uptick in level of demand and prioritization of our sites in Pennsylvania, driven that the support of data center had changed in many states. The Democratic candidates who won in Pennsylvania ran on platform favoring responsible data center development, the opposite the scenario in most other states.”.

According to recent reports, “The differentiator will be location, location and location,” indicates Gagnon. “This is a real estate industry and location is hugely important in real estate. That’s why you have so many cloud data centers in Loudoun County, Va. near D.C. and Quincy near Seattle. We’re near New York, Philly, and Pittsburgh, and have a great position in the Pacific Northwest, where there’s a major shortage of AI campuses. If you’re close to where the demand comes from, that should justify a premium going forward, just as it has in the past for data centers.”.

Sources indicate that gagnon is especially bullish on the union of AI and the Keystone State. “Pennsylvania built this country, it had all the resources needed to launch the industrial revolution, steel, coal, railroads, natural gas. Texas was the first mover in AI data centers, and now Pennsylvania is the second mover. And we’ll be number one in Pennsylvania.”.

It’s a long way from waste coal to GPUs. And Gagnon’s got a plausible story: The substantial guys have the GPUs, in fact too many of them. But he and his Bitcoin brethren have a lot of what the giants now need most, the power. The question for Keel is how fast Gagnon can turn it on.

FinCEN Bars US Institutions From Transmitting Funds to MEXC: What Changes and What Doesn't

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1609 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that finCEN's November 6 order cuts US financial institutions off from MEXC Global, barring any transmittal of funds to or from the exchange.
  • Sources indicate that MEXC indicates user assets remain secure.
  • On November 6, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued a final order under Section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Sources indicate that finCEN's November 6 order cuts US financial institutions off from MEXC Global, barring any transmittal of funds to or from the exchange. The order spells out what is banned, what MEXC is accused of, and how the exchange has answered.

Sources indicate that MEXC indicates user assets remain secure. The FinCEN order never suggested otherwise, and the gap between the exchange's reassurance and the order's actual target is the key to this story.

On November 6, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued a final order under Section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act. It names MEXC Global a financial institution of primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance. From there, it bars "covered financial institutions," a category that includes banks, broker-dealers and money transmitters, from any transmittal of funds to or from MEXC Global. Transmittals, as defined, include convertible virtual currency.

In a recent development, on the MEXC side, the reach is wide. The order covers the exchange's subsidiaries, branches and offices outside the United States: MEXC Global Ltd and MX Global Ltd in Seychelles, MEXC Estonia OÜ, GIDA Technology AG in Switzerland and MXC Global Ltd in the United Kingdom. Former Singapore entities and any successors are included as well. US-based affiliates, by contrast, are expressly excluded.

The ban won't bite right away. It takes effect 30 days after publication in the Federal Register, which had not happened as of the announcement, and it carries no end date. FinCEN keeps the authority to attach conditions and grant exemptions, and willful violations can lead to civil and criminal penalties under 31 U.S.C. 5321 and 5322.

Recent findings suggest that MEXC's statement is short and carefully built. The exchange indicates it is aware of the order and is reviewing it with its legal and compliance teams. It describes itself as operating normally, with user assets secure. It also says it takes the concerns seriously, prepares to engage constructively with FinCEN and other regulators, and has started an independent review of its AML and sanctions controls.

Two points stand out. For one, the reassurance lines up with the order's text. Nothing in it freezes balances or halts trading, so "operating normally" is plausible. The threat is to MEXC's access to US financial counterparties, not to the exchange's wallets.

Sources indicate that the other point is what the statement skips. It disputes none of the allegations, and the independent review it promises targets AML and sanctions controls, the very area where FinCEN claims the exchange failed. The order also invites anyone with relevant information to submit it to FinCEN, so MEXC already has a formal channel for the constructive engagement it describes.

The charges are specific. FinCEN assesses that MEXC facilitated at least $16.7 billion in likely illicit activity between May 2021 and May 2026, a figure Treasury's announcement rounded to $16 billion. The order splits that total across several categories.

In a recent development, on Russia, FinCEN cites nearly $1.5 billion in direct and indirect exposure to sanctions-evasion transactions, including $232 million in direct dealings with entities sanctioned by the US, EU or UK. According to the order, MEXC processed about $129 million with Garantex and $4.1 million with its successor Grinex after both were designated, with activity continuing as recently as June 2026. It also points to at least $26 million benefiting the A7 Network and nearly $200 million tied to the ruble-backed A7A5 token. Beyond that, FinCEN notes MEXC handled more than $13 billion with four UK-sanctioned exchanges between May 2018 and July 2026.

According to recent reports, iran features just as heavily. The order cites nearly $2 billion tied to Iranian actors or terrorist groups, including about $1.87 billion in exposure to Iran and over $1 billion in direct transactions with more than 40 Iranian exchanges. About $22 million is linked to the Central Bank of Iran and the IRGC Quds Force. For North Korea, the order describes roughly $350,000 received by a sanctioned money launderer between June and September 2025. On cybercrime, it cites $1.99 billion in flows linked to illicit cyber actors and $37.9 million in suspected ransomware payments between January 2022 and July 2024.

The order then turns to MEXC's own rulebook. Its stated KYC and AML policies prohibit accounts in certain jurisdictions, yet FinCEN says the exchange facilitated transactions involving them. The order also notes that MEXC has operated without a license in Seychelles, Hong Kong and Japan, and it points to the Seychelles Financial Services Authority's May 2026 enforcement action against MX Global Ltd. All of this reflects FinCEN's assessments, drawn from public and non-public information, and MEXC has not answered them point by point.

According to recent reports, the order is not an OFAC sanctions designation, and the difference matters. A funds-transmittal ban limits what US-covered institutions can do with MEXC. It does not make it illegal for ordinary consumers anywhere in the world to hold an account there. The order also states that it leaves existing Bank Secrecy Act and OFAC obligations untouched.

According to recent reports, section 9714 gives Treasury two routes: the special measures of Section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act, or a ban on certain transmittals of funds. FinCEN took the second and explained its reasoning. Recordkeeping requirements would still let transfers continue, and a correspondent-account restriction would miss funds moving outside a strict correspondent relationship. FinCEN also went with an order rather than a rulemaking, citing imminent threats and ongoing transactions.

According to recent reports, one provision stands out for its practicality. FinCEN acknowledges that a covered institution often can't reject incoming crypto before it arrives, so the order allows discretion in cases such as funds that sat in an unhosted wallet for an extended period. The carve-out underlines how difficult enforcement will be in practice.

According to recent reports, for most MEXC customers outside the US, nothing changes on day one. Counterparties face a tougher picture. Once the order takes effect, US banks, regulated exchanges and money transmitters will have to block transmittals to and from MEXC, and global institutions with US exposure have strong reasons to follow suit. FinCEN indicates plainly that the order puts US and foreign financial institutions and regulators on notice.

It has been revealed that before issuance, the draft went to the Justice Department, State, the Federal Reserve, the FDIC, the SEC, the CFTC, the OCC and the NCUA, and none objected. The order also fits into a wider Treasury campaign. It cites the October 1 Operation Economic Outcast action against the A7 Network, and a separate FinCEN proposal on A7 sub-agents followed days later.

It has been revealed that predicting how users or markets will react would be guesswork. What users can do is track the dates, know which institutions they depend on, and watch for official updates from MEXC.

FinCEN used the same Section 9714 authority against the exchange Bitzlato in January 2023. This time, though, the target is by FinCEN's own account among the 20 largest exchanges by trading volume, with roughly 9% of centralized exchange market share as of December 2025 and about $5 billion in reserve assets as of June 2026. Applying a transmittal ban to an exchange of that size signals a more aggressive posture.

In a recent development, three things will show what comes next. The first is the Federal Register publication date, which starts the 30-day clock. The second is whether FinCEN grants any exemptions or conditions. The third is what MEXC's independent review turns up, and whether the exchange shares the results. For now, the statement buys MEXC time without answering the order. The real answer will come from changes to its controls, and from whether its banking and liquidity partners are satisfied with them.
