📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Deutsche Bank flagged roughly $582 million of Jeffrey Epstein-linked transactions as suspicious, more than twice what Senate investigators identified, according to the Financial Times.

Industry observers note that the bank submitted 21 suspicious activity reports to U.S. authorities in 2019 that spanned 3,200 transactions connected to Epstein and his businesses, according to the Financial Times. Among the flagged transactions were payments to women, transfers routed through shell companies, donations to charity that may have been misused, and money received from billionaires such as Leon Black and Glenn Dubin.

Industry observers note that the figure comes from about 15 million leaked bank files that range from internal email traffic and compliance reports to financial documentation. A journalist consortium numbering over 200 reviewed the files and released its findings Tuesday, according to Forbes.

In a recent development, an August Senate Finance Committee investigation led by Sen. Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, found wire transfers tied to Epstein that it deemed suspicious and that totaled $250 million, according to Forbes. Deutsche Bank's internal review also took in checks and transactions that passed through other banks, which explains part of the gap.

Epstein signed on as a Deutsche Bank client in 2013, five years after being convicted of soliciting a minor for sex, according to the Financial Times. The bank told him in December 2018 that it was ending the relationship, the Financial Times stated in its account. Deutsche Bank shut the last two accounts he held three days after he was arrested in July 2019, according to Financial Mail. An internal probe found no fewer than 112 "high-risk transactions," according to Financial Mail.

Deutsche Bank mentioned in a statement that the reporting refers to purported internal documents that whistleblowers allegedly disclosed. “The matters which are in focus of the media reports date back many years and in some cases as much as two decades,” the bank said, according to Bloomberg. It said it had examined the concerns when they arose and collaborated closely with regulators. The bank said it invested €7 billion ($7.8 billion) in its control environment between 2019 and 2025.

It has been revealed that the bank said testing with a security firm found no indication that its current IT environment was compromised or that account information, login credentials or payment data were accessed. It said it has informed the relevant authorities, including the data protection authority.

Industry observers note that lawmakers led by Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, and Rep. Robert Garcia, a California Democrat, in October introduced a bill that would require federal financial regulators to release records on Epstein and investigate banks and executives tied to him. The Wyden investigation concluded there was “significant evidence that JPMorgan $JPM Chase, Deutsche Bank, and Bank of America $BAC violated federal anti-money laundering laws by failing to screen and report Epstein’s suspicious financial transactions in a timely manner.”.

Industry observers note that deutsche Bank has spent upward of $200 million on penalties and legal settlements connected to its Epstein dealings, without admitting wrongdoing, according to Bloomberg. Suspicious payments do not, on their own, establish that each transaction amounted to a crime, according to CNBC.

Deutsche Bank stock slid by upwards of 6% during the opening hours of trading Tuesday.

It has been revealed that when you buy gas at the pump, you’re covering more than the cost of crude oil. You’re also paying for every step in the process, including refineries, wholesalers, taxes, and the markup your local gas station adds.

When oil prices jump, gas prices usually climb right along with them. But when oil falls, gas prices often slip much more slowly—a pattern sometimes called “rockets and feathers.”.

If an emergency hits, the U.S. keeps a backup supply of crude oil called the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. It’s mainly there to protect energy security during crises, such as sanctions, catastrophic storm damage, even war. It can also help cushion the blow when supply shocks send prices soaring.

It’s not meant to solve long-term problems. Instead, it provides quick relief for consumers and helps keep vital parts of the economy moving, like essential industries, emergency services, and public transit.

According to recent reports, oil and natural gas are two of the world’s primary energy sources. A big change in oil prices can affect natural gas by extension. For example, if oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, which which increases demand for natural gas.

When looking at how oil performs, two main benchmarks stand out:.

Sources indicate that of the two, Brent gives a better picture of global oil performance because it prices a large share of the world’s traded crude. It’s also the go-to for tracking oil’s historical trends. In fact, even the U.S. Energy Information Administration now relies on Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook.

If you look at the Brent benchmark over several decades, oil has been far from stable. It has experienced sharp rises tied to wars and supply cuts, along with steep drops linked to global recessions and oversupply (called a “glut”). For example:.

To sum up, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. Again, it’s heavily influenced by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, shifting energy policies, and much more.

In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic.

The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing.

In a recent development, in short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply.

#18320. Breaking: Etzioni on AI: Startup speed is not a strategy

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1149 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Geekwire ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Etzioni on AI: Startup speed is not a strategy

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1149 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Oren Etzioni on Nov 15, 2026 at 8:13 amNovember 15, 2026 at 8:14 am.
  • The world of AI startups has fetishized “speed” and whipped itself into a frenzy.
  • A startup is a marathon, and a team that attempts to sprint the whole way will burn out before the finish line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 15, 2026 at 8:13 amNovember 15, 2026 at 8:14 am.

The world of AI startups has fetishized “speed” and whipped itself into a frenzy. Sure, the feature that took a quarter to build back in 2023 takes a mere AI-fueled weekend in 2026, but many AI startups are running on FOMO, caffeine and tokens without a clear strategy.

A startup is a marathon, and a team that attempts to sprint the whole way will burn out before the finish line.

Recent findings suggest that sam Altman’s Startup Playbook puts the speed creed in one line: “I have never, not once, seen a slow-moving founder be really successful.” I was singing from the same hymnbook earlier this year. In my column on ten commandments for AI startups I wrote that “velocity is the new moat.” Then everyone got fast, and I stopped singing.

Here are the five arguments usually made for that creed.

The window is closing. Each model release opens a gap that the frontier labs close within a release cycle or so. But if the labs will close it anyway, speed merely buys you a nicer funeral. The argument supports picking a different direction, not running faster in this one.

It has been revealed that competitors are everywhere. AI makes building cheap, so clones show up in weeks. True, and that’s the reason velocity isn’t a moat. When building is cheap, defensibility matters more than being first. Peter Thiel’s last-mover argument from Zero to One is stronger today than when he wrote it. In his words: “It’s much better to be the last mover—that is, to make the last great development in a specific market and enjoy years or even decades of monopoly profits.”.

It has been revealed that the data flywheel. Early users generate data that improves the product, so get there first. Except that each new model generation resets the flywheel, and data that taught a fine-tuned model something in 2024 is worth little once a frontier model does the task out of the box.

The data that matters is data the labs can’t easily get: clinical records, industrial sensor readings, proprietary transactions. Access to proprietary data often comes through trust and partnerships, which take time, and moving too fast can cost you the trust required to obtain that precious data.

It has been revealed that momentum attracts capital and talent. That’s true. However, capital raised on growth hype may be planting the seeds of its own demise. A high valuation can box you into the growth story that justified it. Startups that raise at a saner pace retain the option to change direction.

Learning speed. Fast iteration finds product-market fit sooner. This one holds, but there are two kinds of speed.

Fast iteration means cheap experiments: a prototype, a pilot, a feature shipped to 20 owners and pulled if it flops. Fast scaling means hiring ahead of revenue, signing multi-year contracts, buying compute and raising at a valuation you then have to grow into.

Iteration should be as fast as you can make it, because each cycle is cheap to undo. Scaling should come more slowly, because each step is a major commitment that’s hard to unwind, and scaling too early is one of the most expensive mistakes a startup can make: a 2011 study of more than 3,200 high-growth technology startups blamed premature scaling for about 74% of internet startup failures.

It has been revealed that jeff Bezos drew a similar distinction in his 2015 letter to Amazon shareholders. A few decisions are one-way doors, irreversible once you walk through, and deserve deliberation. Most decisions are two-way doors, and those should be made fast by a small group. A startup’s experiments are two-way doors. Its big commitments, a large raise, a long contract, a hiring spree, are not.

According to recent reports, at AI House, Sri Chandrasekar, one of our managing directors, puts it this way: “We don’t hand founders a thesis. We expect them to find the right problem, and that takes judgment, not speed. Building is nearly free now, so run every experiment fast and manually, and only build the machine once something works.”.

It has been revealed that finding the right problem takes iteration, acumen and judgment. Speed helps with the first and does little for the other two. A hamster on a wheel at 200 mph has plenty of speed and no chance of progress. Even Altman’s playbook states Y Combinator looks for “businesses that get more powerful with scale and that are difficult to copy.”.

According to recent reports, prof. Herbert Simon, the Nobel laureate who helped invent AI at Carnegie Mellon, advised his graduate students to pick crucial problems for which they had a secret weapon, because they would win only “by having access to some knowledge or research methods the others do not have.”.

Swap students for founders and research methods for data and relationships, and the advice holds. A startup’s secret weapon is an asset you hold that a competitor can’t acquire by moving faster: a dataset nobody else can assemble, a relationship that took years to nurture.

Farecast, the airfare prediction organization I founded in 2003, developed a secret weapon by gathering a massive amount of labeled data. By 2007 we were mining more than 175 billion airfares, and every prediction we made was later scored against what the fare actually did, so the labeled set grew every day, and it grew only by waiting for fares to play out.

A startup that signs a data agreement with a hospital network has the same kind of weapon. So does a payments company whose fraud labels come from its own transaction stream. In each case the data is the asset a faster rival can’t copy.

Laurence Peter, of Peter Principle fame, mentioned it decades ago: “If you don’t know where you are going, you will probably end up somewhere else.”.

So pick a direction where frontier labs won’t go and clearly articulate why. Run experiments fast but make commitments slowly. Jim Collins, the Good to Great author, called it firing bullets before cannonballs: cheap shots to find the range, then the one massive shot once you have it.

Chase the data and the relationships the labs can’t buy and accept that trust is the slow road to both. Raise at a pace that leaves you the option to pivot when the next model lands. And name your secret weapon in one sentence.

Recent findings suggest that to repurpose an old joke: two bulls stand on a hill above a herd. The young one notes, let’s charge down there. The old one retorts: charge and they scatter. Walk, and they’ll be waiting when we arrive.

In AI right now, everyone is charging. The founders who end up with the prize will be the ones who are more judicious.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sixteen Robert Pattinson films show a career split between franchises and director-driven risks, from Twilight to The Batman Part II.
  • Credit: Georges Biard / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0).
  • In a recent development, robert Pattinson did not build his career by climbing from small parts to big ones.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sixteen Robert Pattinson films show a career split between franchises and director-driven risks, from Twilight to The Batman Part II.

Credit: Georges Biard / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0).

In a recent development, robert Pattinson did not build his career by climbing from small parts to big ones. He made big-studio films such as The Batman, Dune and Tenet in the same years as bleak, odd films such as The Lighthouse, Good Time and High Life. An actor who leaves teen-idol fame for art-house work risks losing his place in the franchise business, but Pattinson kept his. Amazon $AMZN MGM Studios has named him to replace Daniel Craig as 007, according to Parade, which puts him at the center of the James Bond franchise. His move away from his Twilight image led him back to the biggest kind of franchise role, not away from it. "He hasn't been defined by Edward Cullen," film critic Luke Goodsell told ABC News. The strange films were not a retreat from big-studio work. Pattinson made them alongside it, and viewers should see his films as two careers running at once.

Pattinson takes on Bond during the busiest stretch of his career. Dune: Part Three, The Odyssey, Primetime and The Drama all come out in 2026, according to ABC News. The Bond job adds a major franchise film to that crowded calendar without a fixed place on it, because the next Bond film has no title and no revealed release date, according to CNBC. That leaves the order of his coming projects uncertain. Viewers no longer need to ask whether Pattinson can move between blockbusters and director-driven films. The open question is which kind of work his next few years will favor, and nothing announced so far answers it.

Wikipedia surveyed Pattinson's notable films across blockbusters, independent work and upcoming projects. Its entries include his brooding lighthouse keeper in The Lighthouse, his role in Christopher Nolan's film about reversing time, Tenet, Bong Joon Ho's satire Mickey 17 and The Take, a New York heist film with Denzel Washington. The franchise hits, the art-house gambles and the films still to come appear side by side, in the same mix in which Pattinson made them. Viewers who look at them together can see which choices kept him in the franchise business, which directors came back to work with him again, and which risks critics valued more than their scores suggest. The films he has yet to release show what his two-track career now has to balance.

Pattinson's unusual, director-driven choices all came after one defining part: Edward Cullen, the brooding vampire at the center of a teen romance. His fame built over a series of films rather than from a single hit. His role as Cullen in the Twilight films, released from 2008 to 2012, made him a worldwide star, according to Wikipedia. ABC News reports that he finished five films in the saga before he turned to independent work. His stardom and the role grew together over the same stretch until the public had trouble telling them apart. That closeness was the risk in his success. An actor who plays one part through a long series can become that part in the minds of the people watching.

The fame came with a forecast that his career would end when the series did. Pattinson and his Twilight co-star Kristen Stewart were "assumed, I think, to be doomed after that, and both of them went out and said, 'OK, we're going to revive our careers in different ways'," film critic Luke Goodsell told ABC News. Failure was the expected outcome for both actors, and each took a separate path away from it. His move away from franchises was not a fall from stardom. He made that move at a time when many people had already written him off.

He came out of the saga famous and widely expected to fade.

Pattinson's turn as Batman placed him in a gloomy crime story rather than a bright superhero spectacle. He plays Bruce Wayne in Matt Reeves' dark 2022 noir reboot of the character, according to Wikipedia. The tone matters for an actor known for bleak, odd films. In The Batman, his two tracks meet: the film carries the name of one of the best-known franchises, and its dark noir style matches the brooding work he made away from franchises.

In a recent development, batman is no longer the only defining franchise role on his calendar. Pattinson is due back as Bruce Wayne, and USA Today reports that his newest casting makes him the eighth James Bond in the film series. He is now committed to two of cinema's best-known characters at the same time, so his Batman run is one half of a pair rather than the peak of his career. He spoke about the latest job in the grandest terms. "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson remarked.

Recent findings suggest that pattinson took on Bond before the Batman sequel existed as anything more than a planned release. The Batman Part II is set to reach theaters in 2028. His Bond casting became public on Nov. 16, 2026, according to USA Today. The two franchises now overlap in his future. Nobody can yet say whether the sequel will anchor his franchise career or get squeezed by the newer role.

For now, the 2022 film is the only finished chapter of his Batman.

Pattinson's first substantial break came inside a franchise that was already running at full scale, not in a new project built around him. He played Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, his early breakthrough in 2005, according to Wikipedia. Parade reports that the film was the fourth installment in the Harry Potter series. Pattinson joined a story whose world and audience were already in place, and he did not have to launch anything himself. His part still carried real weight in that story. Cedric is selected as a Triwizard Tournament champion, which puts Pattinson's character in the competition at the center of this installment rather than in the background. His first prominent credit was a franchise credit, and his career began on the blockbuster side well before he took on strange, director-driven films.

Pattinson made his Potter film under a producer who is also part of his Bond future. David Heyman, the producer behind Goblet of Fire, oversaw every one of the eight Harry Potter films, Parade reports, and he is among the producers of the coming Bond film. Pattinson's first franchise and his newest one share a key producer. He will work again with a man who has already guided one long series from its first film to its last. Pattinson acted in Heyman's 2005 film and will work with him again on the Bond film declared in November 2026. The connection spans every film Pattinson made in between.

The Potter credit is less a youthful footnote than the first film Pattinson made with a producer who is now behind his Bond film.

It has been revealed that in Tenet, Pattinson works on one of Christopher Nolan's biggest productions as the hero's partner rather than the hero. He plays Neil in Nolan's 2020 science-fiction film about reversing time, according to Wikipedia, and The Associated Press reports that John David Washington leads the cast as The Protagonist. Pattinson is billed as a co-star, second in line on a spectacle that Nolan built around his own ideas about time. That matters for an actor whose career runs on two tracks, because it highlights he did not wait for lead roles before taking on blockbuster work. He reached a Nolan event film through a supporting part, and he took it without needing his name at the top of the poster.

It has been revealed that the second billing still placed Pattinson among the largest productions of his career. The film had a $200 million budget in 2020, according to The Associated Press, and it belongs with his major franchises and blockbusters rather than with his small, strange films for art-house directors. The filmmakers' record shows why a supporting role was worth taking. By 2020, audiences had spent nearly $4.8 billion over 20 years on films directed by Nolan and produced by Emma Thomas. For Pattinson, joining their cast in a secondary part still meant working at the top of the commercial film business, alongside people with a long record of hits.

Tenet showed that Pattinson could share the screen at the largest scale without having to carry the film himself.

Recent findings suggest that christopher Nolan has cast Pattinson twice, which makes The Odyssey a sign of a director's trust more than a star vehicle. Nolan had already worked with him on Tenet, where Pattinson played Neil. For The Odyssey, a separate film, Nolan cast him as Antinous, according to the Arizona Daily Star. That second casting is the reason the film stands among his notable credits. A director who had already worked with him wanted him back for an unrelated project, and repeat casting is the plainest sign that a working relationship held up.

In a recent development, pattinson does not lead the film. Matt Damon plays Odysseus, the title character, according to the Arizona Daily Star, so the center of the story belongs to someone else and Pattinson's Antinous is a supporting part. He still stands out in the role. Bruce R. Miller, a reviewer for Lee Enterprises, singled him out as "the sharp, sly Robert Pattinson." The choice resembles his art-house work on a smaller scale, because he took a distinct supporting character over the largest share of the screen.

According to recent reports, miller's verdict on the film itself is strongly favorable. He gave The Odyssey 3½ stars and judged it worth its running time of about three hours, according to the Arizona Daily Star. In his view, the film covers a great deal of ground while keeping its focus, landing each moment promptly and then moving on. For a film of that length, his review suggests the hours do not drag.

For anyone following Pattinson, The Odyssey is worth seeing as proof that Nolan wanted him back, not as a measure of what he can carry alone.

In a recent development, dune: Part Three puts Pattinson beside the director who will make the next James Bond film, and that pairing matters more than the trilogy the film completes. On its face, the film belongs to the franchise side of his career at full scale. Pattinson joined Denis Villeneuve's 2026 film, which closes the director's science-fiction trilogy, according to Wikipedia. CNBC reports that Villeneuve will also direct the next Bond film, the one Pattinson will lead as 007. Dune is the first of Pattinson's two Villeneuve projects and the one audiences will see first, while the Bond film still has no title and no revealed release date.

It has been revealed that audiences will watch the film already knowing that its director and its star have a Bond film ahead of them. The Bond casting was announced Nov. 16, 2026, according to CNBC. Dune: Part Three is due in theaters Dec. 18, according to ABC News, so the Bond news reached the public first. Villeneuve openly welcomed the actor into the larger franchise. "He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely newly introduced," Villeneuve said. His praise carries more weight than a studio statement would, because he has already directed Pattinson on a film. The last chapter of a science-fiction saga is also the first substantial-screen result of a partnership whose next assignment is 007.

The Lighthouse is the clearest case of Pattinson betting on a film made to provoke viewers and winning their approval anyway. He won acclaim for his 2019 horror turn opposite Willem Dafoe, and the film is rated 7.3 out of 10, according to Wikipedia. Its early reception surprised the man who made it. Before the film's release in 2019, director Robert Eggers mentioned he was shocked it had not divided audiences more, given how many bold and exaggerated choices went into its story and its filmmaking, according to CBC News. The extremity extended to the film's form. It is a psychological horror film shot in black and white, and Dafoe said at the time that the film had stayed with the people who saw it. The festival audiences Eggers described were receptive rather than split, even with those choices on screen. For an actor still shedding a heartthrob image, this was no safe detour.

Industry observers note that the praise for Pattinson here belongs partly to the place where the film was made and to the actor he played against. The cast filmed at Cape Forchu in Yarmouth County, Nova Scotia, according to CBC News, so the isolation on screen is a real stretch of coastline rather than a studio set. In a psychological horror film, the actors took their tone from that coast. "The location really told us how things had to be played, what kind of story we were telling. It informed everything," Dafoe said in 2019. Pattinson worked in that same setting, which Dafoe credited with shaping how the cast played the story.

His boldest gambles have worked partly because of whom he chose to work with and where, not on nerve alone.

According to recent reports, A few years after the vampire saga, Pattinson took a part with none of a heartthrob's shine. In Good Time, he played a desperate robber for the Safdie brothers in 2017, and the film carries a 7.3/10 rating, according to Wikipedia. The Chicago Sun-Times reports that the brothers' earlier features were Daddy Longlegs and Heaven Knows What. Both sides of the camera took a real risk, because a star with worldwide fame trusted his post-Twilight career to filmmakers with only a short list of features behind them. The gamble held up. A rating of 7.3 marks a film that people respected rather than one they adored.

In a recent development, not every critic offered that respect when the film opened. Richard Roeper, a Chicago Sun-Times reviewer, gave Good Time 2.5 stars in 2017, according to the Chicago Sun-Times. His verdict was mixed rather than dismissive, and he found both strengths and faults in what the Safdies and their star had attempted.

According to recent reports, roeper's score is one critic's view from the year of release, and the film's 7.3 rating sits well above that welcome. Good Time has kept its place among Pattinson's notable work despite the cool reception from a major critic. Playing a man whom audiences might not like was the risk he chose to take, and he took it while he was still working to move past Twilight.

Here he demonstrated he was willing to be disliked on screen, which asks something different of an actor than being liked in a franchise.

Pattinson took a part in The Lost City of Z that keeps him beside the story rather than at its center. He played Corporal Henry Costin, a British explorer, in James Gray's 2016 adventure, a film rated 6.6/10, according to Wikipedia. That rating points to a reception that was favorable but far from enthusiastic. In a 2017 feature, Smithsonian magazine reports that Costin serves as aide-de-camp to the expedition's leader, Percival Fawcett, and that Charlie Hunnam plays Fawcett. Gray, the film's writer and director, set out to tell a straightforward story about Fawcett. The film follows the leader, and Pattinson's corporal works at his side.

The supporting part came with a demanding shoot. The production spent eight weeks filming in Colombia, according to a Smithsonian magazine feature published in 2017, so the cast worked on location rather than on a soundstage. Gray made clear before the film's release that the production had faced real danger. "We escaped catastrophe on a few occasions," he told Smithsonian magazine. For viewers, that means the expedition on screen was filmed far from a studio, under conditions its director describes as dangerous at times.

In a recent development, the Lost City of Z belongs among Pattinson's notable films as a supporting role in a director's own project, made years before his biggest franchise parts. It gave him no franchise and no starring role. Viewers who come for Gray's account of Fawcett will find Pattinson as the explorer's aide, working in the background of someone else's story.

Cosmopolis is the strongest case that Pattinson's art-house choices cost him. His 2012 film with David Cronenberg carries a 5.1/10 rating, according to Wikipedia, a score barely above the middle of the scale. He plays a billionaire asset manager on a trip across Manhattan, CBC News reports, and nothing about the part resembles the teen romance that made him famous. Viewers still have to decide whether the film's craft earned that score or whether people reacted to how hard it is to watch.

Cronenberg built the film around talk. He adapted Don DeLillo's 2003 novel and took its dialogue from the book, according to CBC News, and long conversations take up most of the screen time that a thriller would give to action. He saw that choice as the film's main strength. "It's the dialogue first of all which carries everything...It's incredibly funny, incredibly profound, incredibly adept and very philosophical. I mean, you don't get that very often," Cronenberg told CBC News. Viewers who want plot are likely to find long philosophical exchanges hard going, and a film made this way tends to split its audience. Seen in that light, the low rating looks more like a divided response to a demanding film than proof that Cronenberg and Pattinson made a bad one.

Sources indicate that pattinson also took this risk in public. Cronenberg's film was first shown to anyone at the Cannes Film Festival, according to CBC News, so the gamble was on view from its first screening. Pattinson has remarked he was deeply frightened when filming began. That makes Cosmopolis the hardest case against the idea that the strange films did him no harm, because a film with such a modest rating is also one that unsettled him from the first day on set. Still, the rating shows how people received the gamble. It does not show that taking the gamble was a mistake.

Of all the risks Pattinson has taken, High Life makes the least effort to please, and that is why it belongs here. Wikipedia reports that he starred in Claire Denis' 2018 art-house space drama, a film rated 5.7/10. Stephanie Zacharek, a film critic at TIME, called it "brilliant if not exactly likable" in 2019. The middling score and her praise describe the same quality, because Denis made a film that is difficult on purpose. For a viewer, the 5.7 is a warning about how hard the film is to sit through, not a sign of weak craft. It does not make High Life a lesser entry in his art-house work.

Sources indicate that the difficulty is built into the setup, which gives Pattinson almost no one to play against. In the opening scene, his character, Monte, repairs the ship and talks to an infant over a monitor, TIME reports, so he begins the film alone with a baby who cannot answer him. With no adult scene partner, the starring role rests on what he can show without words. In 2019, Zacharek found tenderness, suspicion and ruthlessness in his expressions alone. Plot and spectacle carry little of the weight in this film, and his face carries most of it. His franchise roles never asked that of him, since those parts surround him with action, dialogue and large casts.

For fans who came to Pattinson through The Batman, High Life is a test of whether they follow the actor or the franchise.

Bong Joon Ho uses science fiction in Mickey 17 to tell a satire about a worker whose life is treated as cheap. His 2025 film casts Pattinson as that disposable worker, according to Wikipedia. The Korea Times reports that the film is science fiction. That genre runs through much of Pattinson's major-studio work, including Dune and Tenet. In this film, a director with his own ambitions sets the terms instead of a studio series. Pattinson does not have to choose between the two sides of his career here. He works in the genre of his blockbusters for a filmmaker known for satire.

The character's disposability is both the film's joke and the hardest part of Pattinson's job. Mickey is an "expendable" worker, and in this story being expendable means being duplicated, so Pattinson has to play more than one version of the same man. Bong praised the way Pattinson handled the two versions, according to The Korea Times. That praise carries weight because the director who designed the challenge is the one judging the result. The part asks Pattinson to keep two versions of one character distinct on screen, and it tests his range more than his star presence.

Viewers who know him from Dune or Tenet will find the same genre in Mickey 17, put to a satirist's purpose and built around a role that asks more of the actor than of the star.

Industry observers note that pattinson's coming years are crowded with epics and franchises, yet he still made room for the kind of small, odd film that built his reputation for risk. In The Drama, a 2026 black comedy directed by Kristoffer Borgli, he stars opposite Zendaya, according to Wikipedia. ABC News reports that the independent studio A24 made the film and that Borgli earlier cast Nicolas Cage in Dream Scenario. That puts one of the biggest young stars around in a director's project rather than a spectacle, with a filmmaker who has built a film around an offbeat star before. It is the trade Pattinson keeps making: he goes where a demanding director wants a stranger version of him.

Industry observers note that at the center of The Drama is a couple, not a world to save, and Luke Goodsell, a reviewer for ABC Arts, judges Pattinson's work in it the strongest of his career. Pattinson plays Charlie, a museum head curator, an ordinary professional in an intimate story. That makes it a rare character-driven part among the franchise films and director-led epics he has lined up next. Goodsell keeps the film's plot twist out of his review, so audiences can still come to the film without knowing it. The small films may show more of his acting than the big ones do.

Borgli is Norwegian, ABC News reports, and the film looks at America from the outside. Some viewers may find its handling of race and the U.S. clumsy, though Goodsell argues the clumsiness is deliberate, a portrait of a European misreading the country. The likely response is a split rather than a consensus, with some viewers seeing satire and others seeing carelessness.

That is the bargain of the second track. Pattinson accepts that a film like this may be judged a misstep in public, and that willingness has kept his franchise career from fixing him as one type.

Primetime is a Pattinson film that audiences know by its director's name, not by his character's. Pattinson appears in Lance Oppenheim's 2026 thriller, according to Wikipedia. That filmmaker, that genre and that year make up the whole public picture of the project for now. Before anyone knows whom he plays, they already know whose film it is and what kind of story it tells. This is the director-first side of his career in its plainest form. On the smaller, stranger half of his work, Pattinson has repeatedly signed on for a filmmaker's project, and the part has mattered less than the person making the film. Here that choice shows clearly, because the film's identity starts with Oppenheim, with no character or plot to point to.

Industry observers note that nothing about his character is on record yet. The film's entry lists no character name, co-stars, plot or release status for his part, so viewers have no way to weigh the role itself. Anyone curious about Primetime has only the pairing of actor and director to go on. Pattinson has asked for that kind of faith throughout his art-house work, and he asks for it here in its simplest version. Viewers who have followed him into odd, demanding films for years will recognize the request. They back the director now and find out about the role later.

It has been revealed that the Take has not reached audiences yet, so the reason to watch for it is the people attached. Pattinson stars opposite Denzel Washington in the heist film, which Meirelles is directing in New York City for release in 2027, according to Wikipedia. He signed on for a director and a co-star before there was anything on screen to point to, and many of his other choices followed the same logic. The film is due after his already crowded 2026. For now, The Take is best read as a sign of the kind of work he intends to keep doing rather than as a finished entry in his career.

It has been revealed that the Take fits neither of his two tracks neatly. It is not one of his giant franchise parts, and nothing known about it so far marks it as one of his bleak, strange gambles. It is a heist thriller, a mainstream genre meant to entertain, made under a director's name rather than a franchise's banner. That makes it a quieter test of how Pattinson divides his time. The question is whether a director-led genre film with no franchise behind it still has room on a schedule he now has to share with the Bond job.

Pattinson's next few years will show which side of his career The Take ends up on, and how much room he keeps for a film with no franchise behind it once he is 007.

Sources indicate that of all the films still ahead of Pattinson, his return as Batman is the one with both a year and a shoot behind it. The sequel is scheduled for 2028 and brings him back as the caped crusader, according to Wikipedia. CNBC reports that Pattinson is already in production on it, so this is a film being made, not a project waiting to begin. For now, Batman is the most secure part of the blockbuster side of his career and the significant-studio role fans can most confidently expect to see him in next. The sequel also keeps him with the same filmmaker, because Matt Reeves, who directed the first film, is directing this one as well. Pattinson has a habit of working with directors who come back for him, and Reeves is one more of them.

According to recent reports, batman is no longer the only major franchise role in Pattinson's future. The Bond casting gives him a second famous character to carry alongside Bruce Wayne, and he speaks about the upcoming part with open reverence. "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson said, as reported by USA Today. The sequel remains scheduled for 2028, but his time now has to stretch across two franchise productions. How he will divide it between them has not been made public.

The Batman Part II will be one of the first tests of whether Pattinson can keep both franchise roles going without one pushing the other aside.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Good morning. Mars Inc., maker of M&M’s, Snickers and Pedigree, plans to invest an estimated $1.4 billion in U.S. manufacturing and operations in 2027, its largest single-year investment.

Industry observers note that “It is fundamentally a growth investment,” Mars Inc. CFO Claus Aagaard told me. “In the near term, we are putting capital behind high-demand, high-growth brands and businesses where additional capacity can unlock growth.”.

Longer term, Mars is modernizing its network with automation, high-speed lines and standardized systems “so we can scale efficiently and build a stronger, more resilient supply chain,” Aagaard explained.

Sources indicate that following its combination with Kellanova, Mars is now a more than $65 billion family-owned business, based on combined 2025 net sales, according to the company. In the Q&A below, Aagaard discusses the rationale for the investment in manufacturing, how Mars will measure its return and what it means for the communities where it operates.

Why is 2027 the right time for Mars’s largest single-year investment?

In a recent development, we have invested more than $9 billion in U.S. manufacturing and operations over the last decade, and while this $1.4 billion commitment is the largest we’ve invested in a single year, it is part of our long-term approach. Demand across our business is high, and American manufacturing is very strong.

Advances in smart factory automation, energy-efficiency technology and digital tools mean that retrofitting or building facilities today can deliver a higher return than it did a decade ago. Right now, we’re seeing a compelling opportunity to not only invest in meeting growing demand, but to unlock capabilities and ensure operational excellence for generations to come.

How is the $1.4 billion divided, and how do you measure the return?

The $1.4 billion investment in 2027 and the $9 billion that has been committed over the past decade, supports manufacturing and operations across our snacking, food and pet businesses, with capital allocated where we see clear opportunities to expand capacity, modernize facilities and strengthen resilience.

For example, we’ll spend more than $34 million to open four upcoming Mars Veterinary Health hospitals in 2027, expand access to emergency and specialty veterinary care, bring innovative medical capabilities to growing communities, and support the development of highly skilled veterinary professionals.

We have invested $60 million in Salt Lake City to add two Trü Frü production lines to our recently opened Nature’s Bakery facility, unlocking capacity for 17 million frozen products annually. And, we have spent $49 million in Columbus, Ohio, to bring Temptations Lickable Treats manufacturing to the U.S., with a target of 400 million pouches annually.We measure return across several dimensions, including our ability to meet consumer demand, improve efficiency and productivity, strengthen supply chain resilience, support profitable growth, and expand access to high-quality veterinary care.

Why does keeping 94% of U.S. products made domestically matter to Mars?

Industry observers note that mars has operated in the U.S. for 115 years—it’s our largest market, and we’re globally headquartered here. The U.S. is critical for Mars. Making 94% of the products we sell in the U.S. domestically gives us an key foundation for long-term growth. A strong local manufacturing footprint puts production closer to consumers, creates greater supply-chain resilience, and allows us to expand capacity as demand grows. It also means that when we invest in growth, those investments can translate directly into facilities, capabilities, and jobs in the communities where we operate.

What does this investment mean for the communities where Mars operates?

In a recent development, we have operated in many U.S. communities for generations, so these investments are about more than adding capacity. They modernize and strengthen facilities, support skilled jobs, and create additional economic activity locally.

This month, our facility in Waco, Texas is celebrating 50 years of operations. Mars has steadily expanded and modernized the Waco site, which produces Snickers, Starburst, and Skittles, to meet growing consumer demand while advancing environmental sustainability. Mars has invested $165 million in the facility since 2024, with recent capital projects heavily focused on enhancing energy efficiency and operational excellence.

Today, the site is powered by nearly 900 dedicated associates, but the milestone speaks to the dedication of generations of associates and longstanding partnerships we share with the Central Texas community.

What would success look like for this investment a few years from now?

Industry observers note that success means we have converted this capital into durable growth and a stronger operating network. We should be able to serve more consumers and pet owners, scale high-growth brands, operate more efficiently, and have greater resilience across our supply chain.

Amazon loses 40 Leo satellites in ULA Vulcan launch failure — a new setback for its Starlink rival

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (772 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 15, 2026 at 1:41 pmNovember 15, 2026 at 2:16 pm.
  • A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket malfunctioned about 10 minutes after liftoff Sunday and failed to reach orbit, losing 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the Seattle tech giant’s planned challenger to SpaceX’s Starlink internet service.
  • It was ULA’s first total mission failure since the Boeing–Lockheed Martin joint venture was formed in 2006, Spaceflight Now reported.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 15, 2026 at 1:41 pmNovember 15, 2026 at 2:16 pm.

A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket malfunctioned about 10 minutes after liftoff Sunday and failed to reach orbit, losing 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the Seattle tech giant’s planned challenger to SpaceX’s Starlink internet service.

It was ULA’s first total mission failure since the Boeing–Lockheed Martin joint venture was formed in 2006, Spaceflight Now reported. The flight was Vulcan’s first in nine months, and the first of 38 Vulcan launches that Amazon has purchased.

ULA said it doesn’t yet have specific data on what went wrong, and that it will work with Amazon and others to find the cause and return to flight as quickly as possible.

Amazon Leo remarked in a post on X that “there is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01.” It added, “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.”.

Sources indicate that the rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station at 12:40 p.m. ET (9:40 a.m. PT), after two days of delays and a countdown hold with 20 seconds left on the clock to resolve a technical issue. It isn’t known whether that issue played any role.

The rocket’s six solid rocket boosters, made by Northrop Grumman and the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appeared to perform normally and burned out less than two minutes after liftoff, according to Space.com and Spaceflight Now.

The first stage, powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin, fired from liftoff before separating from the Centaur upper stage, which carries the payload the rest of the way to orbit.

The anomaly came about 10 minutes into the flight, during the Centaur’s burn, according to Spaceflight Now. The Centaur is powered by two RL10 engines made by L3Harris.

Industry observers note that spaceflight Now also reported that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned, and that a telemetry-driven animation demonstrated the Centaur making unusual orientation adjustments early in its burn. ULA hasn’t identified the cause.

It has been revealed that impact on Amazon Leo: Before Sunday, Amazon had launched 396 satellites for its Redmond-based satellite internet network, formerly known as Project Kuiper, on 14 missions since April 2025. Its last successful launch was in July, when ULA flew the last of eight Leo missions on its Atlas 5, the older rocket that Vulcan is replacing.

The larger Vulcan carried 40 satellites on Sunday, compared with 29 on the last Atlas 5 launch, and is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

Melissa Wuerl, Amazon Leo’s director of launch systems, called it the program’s “primary workhorse over the next several years” in a preview of the mission. Amazon had mentioned the second Vulcan mission could fly within weeks of the first. That flight now has to wait for ULA’s investigation.

Amazon also has 24 introduces reserved on Blue Origin’s New Glenn, which has been grounded since a May ground-test explosion, and has booked others on Arianespace’s Ariane 6 and SpaceX’s Falcon 9.

In June, the Federal Communications Commission gave Amazon permission to keep deploying satellites even if it missed its July 30 deadline to put 1,616 into service. Satellites that weren’t operational by then temporarily lose priority in key spectrum bands.

Industry observers note that amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy and operate all 3,232 first-generation satellites. Amazon has said it prepares an initial rollout of commercial internet service this year.

Recent findings suggest that vulcan’s track record: Sunday’s mission was the fifth for Vulcan, which debuted in January 2024, and the first with six solid boosters. Boosters suffered nozzle failures on the second flight in October 2024 and on a national security mission in February. Both reached orbit, but the Space Force paused Vulcan national security debuts after February.

ULA flew Sunday’s mission with an improved nozzle design. The rocket’s BE-4 engines had also been retrofitted to fix the oxygen valve problem behind the Latest Glenn explosion in May, ULA CEO Mark Peller stated before the flight, CBS News reported.

According to recent reports, ULA is also under latest leadership. Longtime CEO Tory Bruno left last December for Blue Origin, and Peller, who led Vulcan’s development, was named CEO in August.

Industry observers note that amazon’s next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for Nov. 23 at the earliest.

Latest Update: Americans worry capitalism won’t work for them in the AI era. Here are 3 ways for companies to show that it can

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1169 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that according to Just Capital’s 2026 Americans’ Views on Business survey, three in four Americans believe the nation’s best days of innovation are happening now or are still to come.
  • Bridging this divide is the defining leadership challenge of our time.
  • Americans haven’t given up on business as a driver of solutions—78% say large companies have a role to play in solving important societal problems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that according to Just Capital’s 2026 Americans’ Views on Business survey, three in four Americans believe the nation’s best days of innovation are happening now or are still to come. Yet only half say our current form of capitalism gives people like them a fair shot at getting ahead financially. The percentage of people who believe they will be financially worse off this time next year is at its highest since 1960. In other words, Americans believe that—in the age of AI and related innovation—our economic system is working for someone else, not them.

Bridging this divide is the defining leadership challenge of our time. And as the recent midterm elections highlighted, when people feel strongly enough about something they are apt to seek change.

Americans haven’t given up on business as a driver of solutions—78% say large companies have a role to play in solving important societal problems. The key is to show Americans they have a place in the AI-powered economy. Our assessment of the 500 largest American employers highlights that so far approximately 180 companies have publicly reported AI-related actions affecting their own employees or the broader workforce since December 2025. 161 of those companies announced actions that specifically aim to support their workers and the American workforce at large.

Sources indicate that these companies are primarily in industries with large frontline workforces like Personal Care, Drug, & Grocery; and Telecommunications. Companies in industries with close ties to the AI buildout such as Energy; Construction & Materials; and Utilities were less likely to have declared an action in our analysis. Of the twenty industries we examined, six had a higher percentage of companies taking action than the Technology industry, which sits at the center of the AI transition. However, the Tech companies that did announce an action took roughly twice as many as peers in other industries.

The first movers can offer lessons for leaders in every industry: redefine roles rather than eliminate them, open pathways into skilled trades, and equip the next generation of innovators.

According to recent reports, many experts now predict AI will reshape jobs rather than lead to a wholesale disruption of the workforce. Our data reflects the same trend. In the Fall 2026 edition of Just Capital’s quarterly survey of the American public, investors, and corporate leaders, 52% of corporate leaders say they have redefined or transitioned existing roles over the past 12 months compared to 15% who say they have conducted layoffs. Several companies show how this could work in practice.

Recent findings suggest that at General Dynamics Information Technology (GDIT), 12,000 employees have moved into new roles inside the company since 2023, and more than 9,000 have earned certifications in AI, cyber and other technologies. Kimberly-Clark takes a similar approach to training. Its “IT Digital University” covers 17 skill areas, and employees are assessed before and after, with completers averaging 60% skill growth. ServiceNow put AI agents to work on its own operations, and they now resolve 90% of IT service desk tickets. Instead of laying off the service desk team, the company assessed everyone’s skills, provided role-based training and held one-on-one career conversations before moving anyone. As a result, 85% of the service desk moved into new roles in security, AI operations and executive briefing, and the other 15% now supervise the AI agents.

While the dominant narrative has focused on the negative impacts AI may have on the American workforce or on communities across the country, the real story may be a revolution of reskilling and internal mobility.

According to recent reports, our polling shows 47% of Americans aged 18 to 25 worry AI will make it harder to land an entry-level job in their field, yet only 20% of recent grads are considering a trade or licensed profession despite the U.S. facing a historic skilled trades labor shortage.

In a recent development, several companies are tackling the issue head on. Caterpillar is investing $100 million over five years in manufacturing and industry technician jobs in Illinois and Indiana, building a pipeline in the communities where it operates. Lowe’s has gone further by convening the nation’s largest skilled trades coalition, with NVIDIA, AT&T, Bank of America, Carrier, General Motors, DEWALT and Duke Energy, and a goal of training 1 million people. Beyond the founding corporate partners, Lowe’s also brought on over 75 educators, businesses, workforce organizations, industry vendors and stakeholders, including the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), The National Center for Construction Education and Research (NCCER), SkillsUSA and Carhartt.

The message here is that workforce readiness is not a problem to be owned by any one tech giant, and the firms with the most to gain from solving it are well placed to lead.

24% of Americans in the Americans’ Views on Business survey say that individual entrepreneurs and innovators are the primary driver of American innovation, more than large companies R&D investments (23%), venture capital and private investment (14%), government funding (13%), and universities and academic research (13%).

Several companies stand out for cultivating entrepreneurial capacity. Boeing put $250,000 behind Technovation, pairing its engineers as mentors with 25,000 girls building AI-powered solutions worldwide. DoorDash offers a one-day Local Business Workshop that gives small business owners training, tools, local connections and advertising credits. Duke Energy sponsored the third annual high school AI design contest at the University of Florida, where student teams used AI tools to design a smart power grid for their own communities.

Recent findings suggest that investments like these, aimed at people early in their careers or businesses, can widen who gets to participate in what comes next. Investing early in entrepreneurs is also an investment in the customers, suppliers and talent pools companies will depend on later.

Just Capital’s monthly National AI Monitor asks 1,000 Americans how they are experiencing AI as workers, customers, community members, investors and stewards of the environment. Americans are net positive about AI today (+37 overall, +44 at work). But their outlook for the next few years falls to +13, with job loss among the main concerns for the future.

The examples of corporate action outlined here illustrate the path forward for leadership to address these concerns in a fresh era. By redefining roles, creating internal mobility, and fostering the skills of the future, including a focus on entrepreneurship, these companies are showing how to broaden access to opportunity rather than narrow it.

What’s needed next is to measure the success of these initiatives, scale those that work, and continue to explore other pathways. Leaders willing to make meaningful investments in and test new solutions for the American workforce will be repaid in the form of greater trust, goodwill, growth, and social license to operate; all crucial determinants of success in the AI-powered economy. They will also strengthen Americans’ faith in capitalism in the process.

Recent findings suggest that consider a hyperscaler investing billions in GPUs and AI infrastructure. Those purchases become capital assets rather than immediate operating expenses. Companies subsequently recognize depreciation across their estimated useful lives.

Now, can future AI revenue justify today’s investment?

Why Microsoft is aiming to make Copilot the ‘OS for work’

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Mary Jo Foley on Nov 16, 2026 at 5:44 amNovember 16, 2026 at 5:44 am.

  • These days, Microsoft executives have likened Copilot to an operating system, or as CEO Satya Nadella called it, “a new OS for work.” This doesn’t mean Microsoft is replacing Windows with Copilot (even though there was a Microsoft incubation project, codenamed “Project Aion,” that focused on the idea of a “Copilot OS”).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Mary Jo Foley on Nov 16, 2026 at 5:44 amNovember 16, 2026 at 5:44 am.

According to recent reports, it’s been quite a while since Microsoft was “the Windows company,” meaning it derived the bulk of its revenues from Windows. However, Windows — along with Office — has helped Microsoft build a moat that has largely shielded it from forces that have battered some of its competitors as AI has risen to prominence.

These days, Microsoft executives have likened Copilot to an operating system, or as CEO Satya Nadella called it, “a new OS for work.” This doesn’t mean Microsoft is replacing Windows with Copilot (even though there was a Microsoft incubation project, codenamed “Project Aion,” that focused on the idea of a “Copilot OS”).

Plus, as the head of Windows discovered the hard way, many Windows users are dead set against Windows morphing into an “agentic OS.”.

Instead, the Copilot as “a fresh OS for work” descriptor is a metaphor, but one with considerable history and significance.

According to recent reports, microsoft is betting that the race to bring AI into the workplace will be won by whoever controls the layer underneath the models — the data, permissions, security and management tools that businesses already run on Microsoft software. That’s the job Windows has done for decades, and it’s the part of the AI business where Microsoft starts out ahead.

Many of the components behind the OS metaphor are likely to be on display at the company’s annual Ignite conference in San Francisco this week. According to the session list for the weeklong event for customers and partners, Microsoft will highlight how Copilot acts as a platform for building, hosting and managing AI solutions.

The high-level pitch: Copilot can do it all. It can be the foundational layer for your agents, applications, and business processes.

Recent findings suggest that operating systems like Windows provide people with a way to interact with their applications and resources via a common interface across software and data. They orchestrate under the covers what’s happening when users perform specific tasks.

Taking the metaphor to the extreme, if Copilot can be seen as the upcoming Windows, agents are the new apps; skills are the Win32 programming interfaces; and the Graph and IQ layers are like File Explorer.

The Newly introduced OS Metaphor: Why Now? For the past year-plus, Microsoft has been working to get customers to think about Copilot as not so much a chatbot, but more a full-stack platform. Its recently introduced Copilot “super app” is meant to be the unifying interface across this platform.

Sources indicate that at the moment, the fresh Copilot app provides customers with Code, Cowork and Autopilot access. But beneath that top layer, Microsoft is adding other integrations to its core Microsoft Office experiences, Microsoft IQ intelligence backends, its CRM and ERP Dynamics capabilities, and agents and applications from other vendors and customers, as well.

Microsoft’s inclusion of its core Office capabilities in the fresh Copilot comes none too soon, as Anthropic last week introduced new Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards, and previewed one for meetings, that compete more directly with Microsoft’s Office apps.

The “Copilot as New OS” metaphor also works when you consider that Microsoft is looking to the new Copilot app to raise the level of abstraction, or hide the underlying complexities, of how agentic computing works.

Industry observers note that if you believe the AI story lines, we’re moving to a world where many customers expect to be able to ask a system to turn a bunch of slides into a business blueprint and then share that plan with a group of coworkers. In this scenario, owners don’t have to think about which apps and data sources they need to pull together to achieve this; they will count on their AI system to figure it out and just do it on their behalf.

Sources indicate that “We increasingly think of all our apps together as a latest operating system for work that transcends traditional software categories to understand user intent and act on it,” noted Nadella in his letter to shareholders, published as part of Microsoft’s annual report on Oct. 21.

Recent findings suggest that the end goal? “As our apps move toward agent-first capabilities that can be called and orchestrated in the flow of work, the system becomes more valuable and more deeply embedded,” Nadella said.

The Slow and Unsexy Enterprise Race: In the enterprise space, being first and fastest doesn’t always win the race. While AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic vie to be the AI model kingmakers, Microsoft is content to focus on the less sexy but more difficult-to-deliver elements like context, permissions, skills, orchestration, governance and security, all hallmarks of operating systems like Windows.

Microsoft will try to pull all these OS-like pieces together at this week’s Ignite and show customers that it’s got what it takes with Copilot to make AI promises more than just demoware.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The role of the Federal Reserve in the AI boom has, so far, been undefined: Will the central bank be reactive, sitting on the sidelines until data impacting its mandate demands action? Or will it seek to get ahead of economic shifts driven by transformative technology? The Fed’s upcoming chairman, Kevin Warsh, doesn’t seem content to watch from the sidelines.Speaking yesterday in San Francisco at the Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference, hosted by the Federal Reserve Board and the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, Warsh noted the Fed is conducting contingency planning.

In a recent development, “The Board’s staff has begun to evaluate various contingencies, applying stylized, model-based frameworks to generate scenarios,” Warsh said. “These are illustrative scenarios, not forecasts. Moreover, many other outcomes—probably including one that will prove most accurate—could be drawn.”.

Of course, the Fed’s expertise and analysis of AI are nothing new: it already publishes datasets monitoring everything from AI adoption rates by firm size to the impact of AI-related investment on the economy.

Industry observers note that but Warsh hinted at work that establishes what outcomes may look like, rather than observing current trends. He continued: “As policymakers, we have to be mindful that great opportunities rarely come risk-free. And the risks in this case, if overlooked, can be highly disruptive and economically costly. SI [Super intelligence] empowers all, including bad actors, so we are thinking especially of critical infrastructures and their potential vulnerabilities.”.

Before his return to the central bank (Warsh was the Fed’s youngest governor in history, previously serving between 2006 and 2011), hawkish analysts had been somewhat alarmed by how bullish the incoming chairman had been about AI.

Industry observers note that but since his nomination by President Trump this spring, Warsh has struck a more speculative tone. “Our aim today is a humble one,” he mentioned yesterday, “to ask the right questions.”.

It has been revealed that warsh outlined multiple risks, for instance the threat posed to critical infrastructure if the technology falls into the wrong hands. He also remarked that widespread automation could increase unemployment. AI could also “disappoint,” he said, if expected returns fall flat, leading to an economic slowdown.

In a recent development, there’s also opportunity, he said: “SI leads to an increase in productivity and economic gains that are shared broadly across labor and the owners of capital. In that event, real GDP growth rises persistently above its long-run average, and the U.S. stays close to full employment.”.

Sources indicate that if contingency planning across a spectrum of outcomes sounds familiar, that’s because it’s a staple Wall Street habit. Warsh is a former Morgan Stanley vice president and executive director.

You don’t have to look far for examples: JPMorgan pulled together a war room in January last year following the re-election of President Trump, analyzing and evaluating the policies Trump had espoused while out on the campaign trail.

Bank of America and Citigroup reportedly set up similar internal functions to support investors.

Later that year, David Garfield, the co-CEO of consulting firm AlixPartners, told Fortune that his team was working with major companies across every industry to build tariff war rooms: mechanisms for responding to the shifting policy landscape navigated over the past two years.

According to recent reports, warsh’s planning is not a response to an immediate policy question, rather an issue of preparedness. “While I’m not here to offer predictions, I’m not exactly impartial about American leadership in a time so filled with both challenge and possibility,” Warsh remarked. His ultimate goal is to create a dynamic economy for future generations, and promote “human flourishing.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you find yourself walking around the Formula 1 track in Las Vegas this week, you’re likely to spot a mirror-chrome Airstream gleaming under the desert sun. Like an oasis, it’s serving Instagram-worthy drinks you won’t find anywhere else.

According to recent reports, the drinks are called DRIPS by Pepsi, and it’s the company’s answer to the dirty soda craze: classic sodas loaded with syrups, cold foam and popping boba. The trailer is how PepsiCo tests and markets them.

Even though PepsiCo is a nearly a $100 billion tech giant, the DRIPS team runs like a startup.

“We actually work as almost an intrapreneur within the company,” says Scott Finlow, chief marketing officer of PepsiCo Away From Home.

Here’s how it built a dirty soda brand from scratch, and what it’s learned along the way.

In a recent development, pepsi has been courting young drinkers for decades. In 1963, it invited them to “Come alive! You’re in the Pepsi Generation.” That pitch later became “The Choice of a New Generation.” DRIPS is a continuation of that playbook.

According to recent reports, this time, PepsiCo took its cue from Gen Z, who wanted drinks they could personalize with “a little bit of flair, a little bit of fun,” Finlow indicates. As Gen Z sees it, why should the root beer float be the only soda with personality?

That craving fueled the rise of dirty soda, popularized by Swig, a Utah drive-thru chain that coined the term. So PepsiCo built its own version. It developed a menu and a brand, then took DRIPS on the road in a converted Airstream. DRIPS has since popped up at festivals like Austin City Limits and landed on menus at Saucy, KFC’s chicken-tender chain, and Vail Resorts.

PepsiCo’s chefs are “the magicians behind these drinks,” Finlow claims. They start with a popular flavor trend, pair it with a cultural moment and build the drink on a PepsiCo brand, adding texture like boba or layers of cold foam.

For example, bananas are big this season (who knew?). For F1, the team created a banana float made with Mug root beer. “Very rapidly, we can take a flavor trend and then a big moment in culture like F1,” Finlow notes, “and we can then get in the kitchen with those chefs.”.

In a recent development, the menu spans what the team calls “vibe states,” from indulgent to refreshing. Buzzy brands like poppi and Celsius are now in the mix. Energy in particular is becoming “an increasingly notable base for crafted drinks as Gen Z shifts toward cold caffeinated drinks,” Finlow indicates.

Every recipe is also designed for the restaurants that serve DRIPS, down to the hand movements and the time it takes to make each drink. PepsiCo supplies operators with recipe kits, ingredients, marketing and help adding the drinks to their point-of-sale systems.

Now PepsiCo is packaging what it has learned for operators. Just today, it launched DRIPS by Pepsi Signature Mixes, its first standalone syrups, built on data from DRIPS pop-ups and customer feedback. Each of the five no-added-sugar syrups has several flavors in one pump, from Island Escape (mango, pineapple and coconut) to Mocha Mood (chocolate, caramel and warm spice). A new Lipton Green Tea concentrate mixes with still or sparkling water, so restaurants can make refreshers without new equipment.

Recent findings suggest that pepsiCo is also exploring standalone DRIPS stores in Austin and Upcoming York City. Finlow calls them “lab stores,” where the team can test prices, flavors and how fast staff can make each drink. Meanwhile, PepsiCo is piloting a DRIPS test kitchen in Manhattan that delivers six flavors.

Like any startup, the team is learning as they go and pivoting accordingly. Making sure the drinks work in busy restaurant kitchens is “the single biggest ongoing challenge,” Finlow indicates. There’s also pressure to grow fast, what he calls “a healthy tension” familiar to any founder going from early stage to scale.

Sources indicate that so far, DRIPS is more of a pour. Last month at the U.S. Grand Prix in Austin, there was a line of mostly Gen Zers waiting to get their dulche de leche and gochujang on. The trailer did close to $10,000 a day in sales and served up to 130 drinks an hour at peak, Finlow states. The top seller was a Pepsi mixed with peach, lime and lychee jelly called Pole Position.

It didn’t even exist a month earlier.

The drinks are called DRIPS by Pepsi, and it’s the manufacturer’s answer to the dirty soda craze: classic sodas loaded with syrups, cold foam and popping boba. The trailer is how PepsiCo tests and markets them.

The weak XRP predictions from Kalshi traders have come as XRP struggles to maintain momentum around its recent price levels, falling substantially below its local highs.

As of the time of writing, XRP is trading around $0.9892, representing a substantial decline of about 3.94% over the past 24 hours and an 11.3% drop over the last week.

It is important to note that the Kalshi data only reflects traders' positioning amid current market conditions and therefore does not guarantee XRP’s precise price movement in the future.

While XRP has continued to struggle below the major $1 level, it would need to stage a major recovery to reclaim the $1.30 level.
