Tech Report: SEC Targets Net Capital, Customer Protection and Recordkeeping Rules for Crypto Brokers

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1349 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The SEC's crypto broker-dealer proposal, RIN 3235-AN48, is under White House review with no public text.
  • According to recent reports, four rules written decades before Bitcoin existed are now sitting at the White House for a crypto rewrite, and nobody outside the SEC has seen a word of the draft.
  • In a recent development, the White House's regulatory review office logged the proposal on November 3.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The SEC's crypto broker-dealer proposal, RIN 3235-AN48, is under White House review with no public text. Here is what the four named rules require today and what review means.

According to recent reports, four rules written decades before Bitcoin existed are now sitting at the White House for a crypto rewrite, and nobody outside the SEC has seen a word of the draft. What is known is the list of rules the agency wants to change, and that list says a lot.

In a recent development, the White House's regulatory review office logged the proposal on November 3. According to the Unified Agenda entry for RIN 3235-AN48, the item is titled "Amendments to Broker-Dealer Financial Responsibility and Recordkeeping and Reporting Rules Regarding Crypto Assets." It sits at the proposed rule stage and carries an economically significant designation. The cited legal authority is Sections 15(c) and 17(a) of the Exchange Act, and the entry lists no legal deadline.

The abstract is short. The SEC's Division of Trading and Markets claims it is considering recommending that the Commission amend Rules 15c3-1 and 15c3-3 and other financial responsibility rules, along with Rules 17a-3 and 17a-4, to address how they apply to crypto assets. The CFR citation is listed as not yet determined. The entry's timetable also targeted a proposed rule in July 2026, so the package has run later than the agency planned.

That delay is worth a second look. It hints that the drafting proved harder than expected, which fits the subject, since these rules were built for a world of paper certificates and central clearing agents.

Industry observers note that review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs is not an approval. It is an interagency check on a draft the agency intends to propose, and it comes before the Commission votes to publish anything. The SEC, as an independent agency, now submits significant rules to that office under a 2025 executive order, which explains why a securities rule demonstrates up in a White House queue.

It has been revealed that "Economically significant" is a defined term. It generally covers a rule expected to have an annual economic effect of $100 million or more, or one that materially affects a sector of the economy. The label signals expected scale, not content or direction. After review, the process continues with a Commission vote, publication of a proposal, a public comment period and, only then, a final rule.

Industry observers note that nothing in the record notes what the rules would change. Anyone claiming the rewrite will loosen or tighten requirements is speculating.

It has been revealed that rule 15c3-1 is the net capital rule. It requires broker-dealers to hold a minimum level of liquid capital, and it applies haircuts to the value of proprietary positions so a firm can absorb losses and still meet its obligations to customers.

The SEC staff's FAQ on crypto asset activities already makes clear that broker-dealers can't ignore crypto. When a firm takes a proprietary position in crypto assets, that exposure must be counted in its net capital computation, and digital assets get no carve-out. The open question, and the likeliest subject of rulemaking, is how a volatile asset with no traditional ready market should be valued and haircut. That design choice carries real consequences for how much capital a crypto-active broker has to hold.

Sources indicate that rule 15c3-3 is the customer protection rule. It requires broker-dealers to promptly obtain and maintain physical possession or control of customers' fully paid and excess margin securities, and it calls for periodic reserve computations to safeguard customer cash. It applies only to securities, so crypto assets that aren't securities fall outside it, even when a broker-dealer holds them.

Existing staff guidance has tackled both prongs. The FAQ says a broker-dealer may establish "control" of a crypto asset security through a control location specified in paragraph (c) of the rule. A December 17, 2025 Division statement took up "physical possession," saying the staff wouldn't object if a firm deems itself to have possession under five conditions. Those conditions cover direct access and transfer capability, written policies assessing the underlying ledger, no custody where the firm knows of material security or operational weaknesses, protection of private keys, and contingency intends for events such as 51% attacks, hard forks and airdrops.

Commissioner Peirce's statement on that release urged the Division to move quickly on recommendations for amending Rule 15c3-3 to cover crypto custody. The OIRA package looks like the follow-up. Because staff statements are non-binding, a formal rule would give firms something sturdier to build on.

Sources indicate that rule 17a-3 lists the books and records a broker-dealer must make, including ledgers, blotters and customer account information. Rule 17a-4 governs how long records must be kept and in what form, with electronic records stored in a non-rewriteable, non-erasable format or under an audit-trail alternative.

In a recent development, crypto complicates both. A transaction's record lives on a public ledger the firm doesn't control, so a rule would need to settle whether onchain data counts as the firm's own record, how wallet addresses and key-custody events should be documented, and how reconciliation against the ledger should be preserved. The Division will likely address those practical points, given that recordkeeping failures rank among the most common triggers for enforcement actions.

The sequence is predictable even if the content isn't. The first signal would be the release of the draft text or a Commission vote to propose. A comment period follows, in which broker-dealers, custodians, exchanges and investor advocates weigh in, and then comes a possible final rule.

It has been revealed that the package matters less for any single provision than for what it signals. The SEC appears to be moving from staff FAQs and non-binding statements toward enforceable rules for the plumbing that crypto-active brokers depend on. Net capital, customer asset protection and recordkeeping determine whether a firm can safely hold customer assets, and they set the cost of doing so.

In a recent development, until the text appears, the useful questions are narrow ones. Will the SEC differentiate between crypto asset securities and other crypto assets? How will it treat custody through third parties? And will capital charges be calibrated to volatility or set conservatively? The answers will show whether broker-dealers become a practical route to crypto custody or remain a niche.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Charles Hoskinson has credited the underlying architecture for keeping Cardano (ADA) and Midnight (NIGHT) unaffected by the recent Binance hack, arguing that years of deliberate design decisions are now paying off.

The Cardano founder acknowledged that the network’s early focus on emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, liquid non-custodial staking, and the need for Layer-2 (L2) solutions built around its Extended UTXO (EUTXO) model, came in handy during the hacking incident.

In a recent development, hoskinson went further, saying these were not accidental advantages but deliberate choices based on anticipating the blockchain industry’s evolving needs. Furthermore, he suggested that the recent hacking demonstrated the importance of building networks with security and resilience at their core.

Cardano’s staking model continues to grow, with the Cardano Foundation reporting that 57.6% of ADA’s circulating supply is staked.

Notably, every delegated coin backs a stake pool that helps produce blocks and secure the network.

Unlike traditional staking models that lock up assets, Cardano’s liquid staking allows holders to delegate their ADA while retaining full control. As a result, they can spend, transfer, or move their funds without first having to unstake them.

According to recent reports, therefore, this approach is unique because it combines network participation with financial flexibility while supporting a decentralized pool ecosystem. Additionally, it reduces reliance on centralized custodians, boosting the network’s broader resilience.

Meanwhile, Cardano is expanding its real-world utility since police in Uttar Pradesh, India’s most populous state, recently began using its blockchain technology to track forensic evidence in active criminal investigations.

More importantly, the Cardano Foundation said evidence scans and laboratory results will be recorded on-chain, creating a tamper-resistant audit trail designed to strengthen the integrity of investigations.

What went wrong with Outlook: Microsoft blames ‘thundering herds’ and a bug unnoticed for months

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (824 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 7:31 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:31 am.
  • Microsoft’s own safety systems helped turn a dormant software flaw into last week’s global Outlook outage, rerouting traffic from failing servers onto healthy ones that had the same problem, until more than 80% of the servers in its Microsoft 365 networking gateway had stopped responding.
  • That phenomenon, known as a cascading failure, is one of the findings in Microsoft’s preliminary report on the outage, released overnight, dissecting the failure that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 7:31 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:31 am.

Microsoft’s own safety systems helped turn a dormant software flaw into last week’s global Outlook outage, rerouting traffic from failing servers onto healthy ones that had the same problem, until more than 80% of the servers in its Microsoft 365 networking gateway had stopped responding.

That phenomenon, known as a cascading failure, is one of the findings in Microsoft’s preliminary report on the outage, released overnight, dissecting the failure that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries.

According to the report, the attempts to recover were further complicated by a second problem: servers that engineers restarted were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and stopped responding again, a phenomenon known as a “thundering herd.”.

Industry observers note that microsoft says active service disruptions lasted nearly 24 hours. Delayed email continued to be delivered after service returned Friday morning, and the manufacturer posted its public all-clear on X late Friday night, nearly 38 hours after the outage began.

The underlying flaw dates to July, when Microsoft began rolling out a fix to the software that handles incoming connections on its networking gateway, the servers that sit in front of Outlook and many other Microsoft 365 services.

In a recent development, microsoft hasn’t stated what the fix was meant to address. It ran worldwide for more than three months without problems, according to the report.

Under heavy load, however, parts of that software could get stuck waiting on one another, using up the servers’ processing power and memory until they froze.

That’s what happened last week. About 15 hours before the outage, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved Teams traffic onto the same servers that handle Outlook email, adding to their load, according to the report. Microsoft called the switch part of normal operations but didn’t say what prompted it.

Complicating matters, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already out of service because of an unrelated problem, which also isn’t detailed in the report.

In a recent development, when traffic peaked during the U.S. workday, that was enough to trigger the outage.

Two things stand out as likely areas of scrutiny:.

Microsoft’s testing didn’t catch the bug. Its labs mostly used less powerful machines with fewer processing cores, running a different mix of traffic, while the problem was worst on the newer servers handling real customer load.

The fix also passed through Microsoft’s standard staged rollout, spreading worldwide over several weeks without any sign of trouble, according to the report.

The organization certainly has the means to test on the hardware it actually runs. It spent $45.2 billion on capital expenditures in its most recent quarter, much of it on AI infrastructure.

The safeguards meant to contain the damage didn’t hold. Walls between regions failed because of what the report calls “a separate concern,” which it doesn’t explain, so the outage went global.

In a recent development, the gateway is made up of thousands of “capacity units” grouped into regions, with walls between them meant to keep a failure in one place. Microsoft also runs a second, independent gateway so services can switch over during a disruption.

It has been revealed that teams, OneDrive, SharePoint and Office apps made that switch, which is why Teams chats and meetings mostly kept working. Exchange couldn’t, “for scale reasons,” as the tech giant put it, so email stayed down.

Industry observers note that microsoft’s own tools added to the problem. Its automated recovery “was not designed” for a fleet that was almost entirely unresponsive, according to the report, and its usual ways of rolling back a bad change couldn’t quickly undo one that was months old.

The organization’s systems automatically shifted traffic from unresponsive servers to healthy ones, and the extra load triggered the same bug on those servers, too. About 10 hours in, engineers turned off some of that automatic rerouting.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, posted an abridged version of the report on X late Sunday. “We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers and recognize the impact that this has on their normal business & operations,” he wrote.

Lamanna had previewed the findings Friday afternoon, blaming “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter” for the slow recovery, as GeekWire reported when Microsoft declared the outage over.

Microsoft claims it has rolled back the defective code, added server capacity and monitoring, and put upcoming limits on how traffic is redistributed to avoid another cascade. A final report with a full list of repairs is due Nov. 20.

According to recent reports, it may also answer the biggest question the preliminary report leaves open: why the walls between regions didn’t stop the outage from spreading worldwide. Microsoft blames that on “a separate matter,” apart from the July bug, but hasn’t remarked what it was.

Breaking: The 1 Skill AI Will Never Master — No Matter How Advanced It Gets

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1059 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • Sources indicate that everywhere we look, we’re confronted with latest things AI is doing, from making full-length movies to solving seemingly unsolvable math problems.
  • As AI reaches deeper into new corners of our personal and professional lives, there’s at least one thing it will never be able to do by itself: persuade.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Sources indicate that everywhere we look, we’re confronted with latest things AI is doing, from making full-length movies to solving seemingly unsolvable math problems. That makes automating marketing, sales and communications, among other things, seem all but certain. AI is truly everywhere, and it seems to be capable of just about anything — if not today, then tomorrow.

As AI reaches deeper into new corners of our personal and professional lives, there’s at least one thing it will never be able to do by itself: persuade. Persuasion — understood properly as “shared action” — will always require a uniquely human touch.

In a recent development, despite — or, indeed, because of AI’s many remarkable strengths — it will only ever be a supplemental tool for all of your persuasive endeavors, especially in business and leadership. Understanding AI’s limitations when it comes to persuasion will help you excel whenever you need to use it to engage others professionally and personally, whether you’re making the sale to a potential client or your spouse.

AI assistants like ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini have enormous strengths when it comes to communicating more persuasively.

Their ability to capture, analyze and synthesize massive amounts of information is unparalleled. AI can swiftly provide data on just about any subject. More than that, it can sort through the data, looking for trends and differences among viewpoints. AI’s ability to research exceeds the skills not just of interns, but of entry-level employees like Research Assistants and consultants, and even mid-level knowledge workers. Even teams of knowledge workers. That’s why many of these positions are being partially or entirely automated across many sectors, including at companies like McKinsey.

AI doesn’t stop at simply collecting information. It can make arguments for and against positions, too. It will structure those arguments logically and support them with facts. It can identify and respond to counterarguments to your position.

It will even make arguments against using AI itself. I asked ChatGPT if AI should be eliminated, and it rapidly answered, “Probably not.” Then it responded with many paragraphs nuancing the answer. Gemini responded, “Eliminating artificial intelligence entirely would mean losing transformative advancements.”.

AI can frame arguments for diverse audiences. I asked ChatGPT how it would frame advocating for zoning reform to progressives and conservatives (housing policy is one of my areas of expertise). It identified seven complications like equity and property rights and suggested thoughtful ways to navigate them with both groups.

Industry observers note that AI can even craft stories. I asked it for compelling stories to advance housing reform, and it offered 10. The first was about “The young couple who can afford the mortgage — but can’t afford the house.” Good place to start.

So, what’s missing from AI’s approach to persuasion? There are three areas where AI will continue to fall short.

First, getting what we want begins by adopting what I call “the persuader’s mindset”: It’s about them, not you. Which means you have to put them first. Only when you truly understand your counterpart, put their needs front and center, and show them how you can meet them (while also meeting yours), will they be eager to work with you not once but repeatedly.

Adopting this mindset requires you to be fully in tune with your audience. AI can offer general understandings of an audience. It cannot, however, do a few critical things. It cannot relate to someone interpersonally since, well, it’s not a person. Groups are comprised of individuals with nuanced views. Humans can poke, probe, dig and explore in ways AI can’t — with emotional intelligence.

Second, AI’s approach to persuasion is, unsurprisingly, logic-first. This is, in many ways, a virtue: AI can promptly bring an abundance of data to bear on any glitch.

Industry observers note that the trouble with this logic-first approach is that it’s not in accordance with how our brains work. All the neuroscience and all the psychology show that humans are wired to feel first, then reason. This means that you need to start with feelings before turning to logic.

Sources indicate that indeed, AI recognizes this limitation. When I asked Gemini what areas it would struggle with in persuading, it replied: “Gemini faces distinct limitations in persuasion whenever success relies entirely on deeply human emotional intelligence, physical presence or lived experience.” ChatGPT emphasized that it cannot experience any emotions it’d be responding to.

Industry observers note that AI’s logic-first approach will fall flat if it isn’t coupled with sufficient emotional intelligence. That’s where only humans can come in.

Third, AI can’t bring the human elements to interacting with others.

Recent findings suggest that humans listen not just to what others say, but how they say something. Were they excited or anxious? We watch for body language. She grimaced when I said that — uh oh! Maybe I shouldn’t have said it.

Recent findings suggest that humans can bring dynamism to how they share their ideas. They can be charismatic, warm and exciting. AI? Not so much.

Ultimately, the best way to leverage AI for all of your persuasive endeavors is to lean on its strengths — research, data, logic, arguments and the like — and then build a human-centered, emotionally intelligent edifice on top of it.

Everywhere we look, we’re confronted with upcoming things AI is doing, from making full-length movies to solving seemingly unsolvable math problems. That makes automating marketing, sales and communications, among other things, seem all but certain. AI is truly everywhere, and it seems to be capable of just about anything — if not today, then tomorrow.

In a recent development, as AI reaches deeper into new corners of our personal and professional lives, there’s at least one thing it will never be able to do by itself: persuade. Persuasion — understood properly as “shared action” — will always require a uniquely human touch.

Industry observers note that despite — or, indeed, because of AI’s many remarkable strengths — it will only ever be a supplemental tool for all of your persuasive endeavors, especially in business and leadership. Understanding AI’s limitations when it comes to persuasion will help you excel whenever you need to use it to engage others professionally and personally, whether you’re making the sale to a potential client or your spouse.

It’s impossible to predict the future of oil prices. Several factors determine the movement of oil, but it ultimately boils down to supply and demand. Again, when threats of economic downturn, war, etc. are high, the oil trajectory can turn rapidly.

When you pay for gas at the pump, you’re paying for more than just the crude oil itself; you’re also springing for links along the chain, such as the refineries and wholesalers—not to mention taxes and local gas station markups.

According to recent reports, still, the crude oil aspect affects the final price most dramatically, as it typically accounts for more than half the price per gallon. When oil prices spike, so do gas prices. And frustratingly, when oil prices drop, gas prices tend to take their time drifting down to the lower price (sometimes referred to as “rockets and feathers”).

Industry observers note that in case of emergency, the U.S. has a store of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its primary purpose is energy security in case of disaster (think sanctions, severe storm damage, even war). But it can also go a long way toward softening crippling price hikes during supply shocks.

It’s not a long-term answer—more of an immediate relief to assist the consumer and keep critical parts of the economy running, like key industries, emergency services, public transportation, etc.

Industry observers note that oil and natural gas are both major energy fuels. A big change in oil prices can affect natural gas by extension. For example, if oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible—which increases demand for natural gas.

When examining oil’s performance, there are generally two major benchmarks:.

In a recent development, between the two, Brent better represents global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. And, it’s often the best way to track historical oil performance. In fact, even the U.S. Energy Information Administration now uses Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook.

Looking at the Brent benchmark across several decades, oil has been anything but steady. It’s seen spikes due to factors such as wars and supply cuts, and it’s also seen crashes from global recessions and an oversupply (called a “glut”). For example:.

According to recent reports, all to say, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. Again, it’s hugely affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more.

Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage:.

The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic.

The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing.

In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply.

When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf.

Last year, Jeff Bezos asked social media, “Who’d you pick as the next Bond?” Amazon now has its own answer: Robert Pattinson.

The 40-year-old Pattinson — best known for “Twilight,” “The Batman” and this summer’s “The Odyssey” — becomes the seventh actor to play 007 in the official film series. He takes over from Daniel Craig, whose fifth and last Bond film, “No Time to Die,” came out in 2021.

In a recent development, amazon got a 50% stake in the Bond films when it bought MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022, and it took creative control last year in a joint venture with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson. Fans and bookmakers had been guessing about Craig’s successor since he remarked in 2019 he was leaving the role.

Over the years, the rumored contenders included Idris Elba, Tom Hardy, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Tom Holland and Henry Cavill. By the end, there were five finalists. Pattinson beat out Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner after screen tests in London in late October, according to The Upcoming York Times. Casting director Nina Gold ran the tests, which covered stunts, dialogue and camera presence.

Industry observers note that bond is one of the most valuable properties Amazon got in the MGM deal, its second-largest acquisition ever behind Whole Foods. The franchise has earned nearly $7 billion at the domestic box office, adjusted for inflation, since “Dr. No” in 1962. Now Amazon is running it without the Broccoli family, whose stewardship over six decades built it into one of Hollywood’s biggest moneymakers.

According to recent reports, pattinson’s casting is the most visible move yet in Amazon’s plans for Bond. As the Times noted, the 2025 deal followed years of behind-the-scenes friction over Amazon’s ambitions to expand the Bond universe beyond the films. The Times also pointed out that Amazon has to win over a generation of moviegoers who grew up during the franchise’s long hiatus and gravitated toward superheroes, horror movies and video game adaptations.

Industry observers note that amazon is already putting the back catalog to work. Alongside Monday’s announcement, it published a guide to streaming the 007 films on Prime Video.

Identity Confirmed pic.twitter.com/FCU5A9c1wk.

It has been revealed that to lead the next film, Amazon brought in producers Amy Pascal, the former Sony Pictures chairwoman, and David Heyman, who produced all eight “Harry Potter” movies. Denis Villeneuve (“Dune”) is directing from an original screenplay by “Peaky Blinders” creator Steven Knight. No release date has been set, and the Times reports that a theatrical release before 2028 is unlikely.

In a recent development, “Today marks a defining moment for our studio and a significant milestone in the history of James Bond,” Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, remarked in a statement. Hopkins said Pattinson’s “remarkable range, magnetic screen presence, and quiet intensity make him an exceptional choice” to carry on the 007 legacy.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said. “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.”.

According to recent reports, some longtime fans have worried that under Amazon, Bond will lose his distinctly British character and become more corporate and American, the Times reported. Pascal and Heyman, in a joint statement, called the English actor “the perfect Bond for our times.”.

Bezos had yet to weigh back in on social media about Amazon’s pick, but Amazon CEO Andy Jassy did in a LinkedIn post, writing that he was “excited” to have Pattinson in the role, calling him “one of the most versatile actors of his generation, who consistently makes fearless choices, and keeps surprising people with his performances.”.

Recent findings suggest that fans online were split. Some posted images of Elba or Cavill, calling Pattinson as 007 a “huge miss.” Others stated the actor was on a “generational run” right now with the roles he’s landing. Others shared GIFs of Sean Connery, saying there will only ever be one Bond.

I checked in with my mom, a longtime Bond lover and the biggest movie fan I know. She quickly responded via text.

Industry observers note that “No way … not sexy enough for me,” she wrote of Pattinson. “I really liked Daniel Craig, but Sean Connery has always been a favorite.”.

On a recent Tuesday, I sat down at my desk. The sun was just coming up, the air was crisp, my coffee was full. I blinked, and then, suddenly, it was night. I didn’t understand. Nearly 12 hours flew by, and I still had so much to do.

Recent findings suggest that to be clear, it’s not because I’m inefficient. My schedule is largely empty of busywork; I pride myself on a streamlined schedule and my ability to banish time-sucking tasks. I love testing out apps and finding new ways to clear my calendar for what matters most.

According to recent reports, but some days, no matter how many items I take off my plate or how little time I waste, the fact remains: I just have too much to do. A deadline gets pushed, a kid gets sick, a task takes longer than I thought it would. Life is like that sometimes. And when that happens, here’s what I do.

Industry observers note that perfectionism sounds good on paper. Who doesn’t want things to be perfect? But when you’ve got too much to do, it can be like quicksand, trapping you under work that could have been completed in a fraction of the time.

Sources indicate that there’s a reason why entrepreneurs should always build MVPs — minimum viable products — before getting too deep into an idea. You want to be agile enough to fix what’s broken and respond to user testing before wasting time creating something polished. When you have too much on your plate, embracing “good enough” as a mindset can make the difference between successfully doing what needs to be done, and not.

According to recent reports, there’s one surefire way to knock more items off your to-do list: Work more. As an entrepreneur, there will be some inevitable late nights, early mornings and weekends in front of your laptop. But you have to be careful to keep it from becoming the norm.

Sources indicate that despite all the science advising against it, the fact is that grinding is still very much embraced in startup culture. But it’s not worth it. Overwork causes high blood pressure, increasing your risk for stroke and heart disease. It also weakens your immune system — if you thought you had too much to do now, imagine trying to fight through your to-do list while battling the brain fog brought on by a virus.

You’re also risking burnout, which kills productivity — exactly what you don’t want. You might think it doesn’t apply to you, which is what The 5 Resets author and Harvard researcher Dr. Aditi Nerurkar thought, too — wrongly. “I thought: ‘Stress doesn’t happen to people like me; I’m resilient,’” she told The Guardian. “Now we know that that’s scientifically untrue — resilience, while protective, is by no means preventive for burnout.”.

Sources indicate that instead, go for a walk. Even a few minutes outside, away from your screen, can be enough to help your brain reset. Get enough sleep and eat well. These are the best protections you have against keeping your body and mind working at capacity — which, when you have too much to do, is critical.

It has been revealed that I hate flaking. It’s satisfying to be reliable and follow through on what I say I am going to do. Sometimes, though, there’s no other option.

In a recent development, when I really have too much to do, I take a hard look at my calendar and ask which commitments genuinely make sense. What items on there are “shoulds” rather than “musts”? What can be reshuffled to a less stressful time? What will happen if you ask to reschedule a podcast interview, or pass on a networking dinner? Will the world end if you miss a recurring weekly meeting, just this once? If the repercussions for canceling are minor, do it.

To avoid stepping on toes, it pays to be both honest and prompt. When you realize you’re in over your head, a short note that explains that you’re overcommitted and need to reschedule usually does the trick. People understand; they’ve been there, too. There’s no need to go into excessive detail — the most key thing is letting them know as soon as possible so they can adjust their plans accordingly.

It has been revealed that life gets hectic, and so much is outside of our control. Your schedule could be perfectly calibrated, and then your car breaks down. You’re preparing for a launch, and then a pipe bursts. You get called for jury duty, sending your week into chaos.

It has been revealed that when things happen, take a deep breath. Getting stressed won’t fix the situation, but it will make it worse. I try to remind myself that a derailed day isn’t a reflection of my discipline or capability. It’s just a day.

Being kind to yourself also has practical benefits. Researchers have found that self-compassion helps people recover from setbacks faster and stay motivated longer than self-criticism does. The energy you would expend replaying what went wrong can be used to make it go right tomorrow.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prominent market analyst and BitMine Immersion Technologies chairman Tom Lee has offered three potential explanations for the recent crypto market crash that has erased billions in market capitalization over the last few days.

Firstly, Lee points out that the recent crash in AI and semiconductor stocks, especially Nvidia, may have led to margin calls, particularly for retail investors in Asian markets.

According to the analyst, this scenario might have forced investors who needed more liquidity to cover their leveraged positions to sell other assets, including crypto.

Secondly, Lee explains that investors may be selling off their existing equity and crypto holdings to free up funds ahead of Anthropic’s upcoming IPO.

Lastly, the aftermath of the huge $6.3 billion Binance hack that occurred in late October may also be playing a role.

According to Lee, some account holders may be cashing out or converting their recovered funds into stablecoins, further contributing to the sell-off.

It has been revealed that aside from that, Lee has also cited potential risks posed by AI to existing cybersecurity systems and increased U.S. scrutiny of semiconductor sales to Asian markets, including China, as additional factors.

However, these are all just potential explanations rather than confirmed reasons for the downturn.

On Friday, Nov. 13, the world’s largest crypto asset, Bitcoin, fell below the psychological level of $70,000.

Further selling occurred on Saturday as BTC dropped below $66,000 and continued to decline to around $62,112 as of Sunday, its lowest level since July.

As for Ethereum, the losses are even worse, with ETH dropping to around $1,711, its lowest price since early July.

Major crypto assets like XRP and Solana (SOL) are also experiencing massive losses.

With such a sharp decline, there’s been another round of liquidations in the crypto market.

According to CoinGlass data, about $2 billion in leveraged crypto positions have been liquidated in the last 24 hours, with the majority involving bullish traders.

Additionally, this crypto crash has coincided with massive outflows from crypto exchange-traded funds (ETFs).

Recent findings suggest that from Oct. 30 to Nov. 13, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs saw nearly $3 billion in net outflows, indicating that institutional investors are also selling off.

SoftBank founder Masayoshi Son vowed tonight to “double down” on its investment in WeWork as he confirmed looks for a $9.5 billion rescue package that will provide up to $1.7 billion to WeWork cofounder Adam Neumann in exchange for cutting most ties with the company and will give SoftBank an 80 percent stake in the business. In a statement tonight in Fresh York, SoftBank said it would “accelerate” WeWork’s path to profitability and positive free cash flow. More here in the Financial Times.

According to recent reports, forty-six attorneys general have joined a Newly introduced York-led antitrust investigation of Facebook, officials announced this morning, raising the stakes in a sweeping bipartisan probe that could result in massive changes to the manufacturer’s business practices. The Washington Post has more here.

Recent findings suggest that limited partners or LPs  — the pension funds, the university endowments, the family offices that largely provide venture firms with their spending money — are receiving a lot of attention from venture capitalists, some of it unwanted. VCs have begun knocking down their doors with requests for fresh capital commitments so they’ll have money to invest if the market cools down.

Sources indicate that the problem is, many of these LPs are already over-allocated. LPs traditionally invest in many asset classes, such as public equities, and they allocate a small percentage of their portfolio to venture capital. Suddenly, they’re finding they’ve forked over more than they’d intended to VCs.

There are several reasons for this situation. First, VCs are returning to them ever faster for more capital  — sometimes in less than two years’ time  — because they are in vesting at such a furious pace.

Recent findings suggest that compounding the problem, not all LPs have received returns from their VC investments that they can recycle into latest venture capital allocations. In some cases, this capital is still tied up in startups that are raising much more money than in the past and staying private longer. “We have some large exposures to blue chip names where IPOs have been rumored to be coming for a long time already, and now it’s maybe 2021, maybe 2022,” states one manager who asked not to be named. In other cases where startups have gone public, falling prices have prompted VCs to hang on to their shares instead of distribute them.

The result is that LPs are having to cut back on the number of managers they can fund, and that could mean bad news for venture capitalists and startups alike. These LPs don’t have much choice. As the LP explains it, “We have a pretty structured allocation process, and we’re really trying to be creative,” she claims. One venture manager who reappeared too rapidly for more money was  “easy to walk away from,” says this person. “Others, we’re having to do financial backflips for them to remain strong partners.” Either way, this LP adds, “We can’t add any new relationships right now,” meaning new venture teams in particular are out of luck. “When [VCs] shorten their fundraising cycle by nine months to a year, you can only squeeze the balloon so much.”.

SoftBank’s $100 billion “Vision Fund” is one significant reason LPs find themselves in their current predicament. From the moment SoftBank began waving money around several years ago, it launched a vicious cycle. According to Chris Douvos, whose investment firm, Ahoy Capital, owns stakes in such venture funds as True Ventures and First Round Capital, “When Andreessen Horowitz hit the scene a decade ago, they changed the tempo of investing and everyone got more aggressive in their dealmaking as a response. Then SoftBank entered the picture in a big way, and it was like a16z on steroids.”.

Breaking: Study: 403 U.S. hyperscale data centers rival Denmark’s emissions; Oregon ranked No. 2 in power use

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (690 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 16, 2026 at 10:14 am.
  • A Harvard-led study estimates that electricity use at 403 U.S.
  • The research examined some of the nation’s largest and most powerful data center facilities operating between May 2024 and April 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 16, 2026 at 10:14 am.

A Harvard-led study estimates that electricity use at 403 U.S. hyperscale data centers was equal to roughly 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions — a volume roughly comparable to Denmark’s carbon footprint.

The research examined some of the nation’s largest and most powerful data center facilities operating between May 2024 and April 2025. Together, those facilities accounted for an estimated 1.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption.

“What we’re seeing is already striking, but it’s only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry,” Gianluca Guidi, the study’s lead author and a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, said in a statement.

Guidi noted that the data center boom has continued since the study period ended. “That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we’re reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026.”.

Industry observers note that the research, published in the journal Nature Sustainability, comes amid growing pushback and concerns about the facilities’ impacts on electric bills, water consumption, noise and carbon emissions. The authors also built a website about the report.

In the Pacific Northwest, government officials are enacting moratoriums and exploring legislation to regulate data center development. Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek in October directed a state agency to pause processing and issuing permits for fresh and expanding data centers until July 2027. In Washington, state Rep. Beth Doglio, D-Olympia, will propose data center rules in the legislative session that starts in January.

Hyperscale sites handle massive computing workloads and data storage, supporting operations including large language model training and AI deployment.

In a recent development, the researchers found that Oregon ranked second in electricity used by hyperscale data centers in the study, consuming about half as much as those in Virginia. Given Oregon’s access to clean hydropower, the state ranked sixth in carbon dioxide emissions attributed to the facilities’ electricity use. The publication highlighted data from the top 10 states for energy use, which does not include Washington.

According to recent reports, nationwide, roughly 54% of the electricity attributed to the facilities came from fossil fuels, primarily natural gas and coal. The estimates were based on regional power generation mixes, not individual operators’ clean energy purchases.

The study did not break out energy use by data center operator. Amazon, Microsoft and Google have the largest data center footprints worldwide and account for 57% of hyperscale data center capacity, according to Synergy Research Group.

All three have aggressive carbon reduction targets. While their emissions have all increased in recent years, the companies say they remain committed to their goals. Microsoft and Amazon point to their support for upcoming clean power projects and investments in low-carbon building materials for the facilities as positive steps towards reductions.

“We continue to really be focused around carbon negativity by 2030,” Melanie Nakagawa, Microsoft’s chief sustainability officer, told GeekWire in July.

Kara Hurst, Amazon’s chief sustainability officer, acknowledged that it will be difficult for the manufacturer to reach its target of net-zero emissions by 2040.

According to recent reports, “So that is a real challenge,” Hurst remarked in September, “and we’re here to meet the moment. I’m not saying that it’s going to be easy, and I’m not saying it’s going to be linear. But we’re going to put everything we have behind that.”.

At the same time, both tech giants are pursuing projects involving fossil fuel energy in Texas. Microsoft in June signed a 20-year deal to purchase power from a natural gas facility slated to come online in 2028. If it’s not — and that’s very possible, especially if it’s a newer brand — you have to consider which questions you could credibly own.

ACryptoS Loses $665K Across 77 Vaults on Five Chains After a Missing Input Check

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1324 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

💡 Key Takeaways
  • ACryptoS lost about $665,000 across 77 vaults on five chains after a missing input check let attackers mint most of a vault's shares with a tiny deposit.
  • ACryptoS, a DeFi yield aggregator, disclosed on November 9 that its vaults had been exploited for roughly $665,000 across 77 vaults on five chains.
  • It has been revealed that it then disabled deposits, left withdrawals open, remarked it can no longer maintain the project and offered the attacker a 10% bounty in exchange for returning the funds.The most specific technical account comes from SlowMist's hack database.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

ACryptoS lost about $665,000 across 77 vaults on five chains after a missing input check let attackers mint most of a vault's shares with a tiny deposit. Five exploiter addresses have been published.A vault is supposed to hand out shares in proportion to what you put in. ACryptoS's vaults handed out most of the pool for the price of one small token deposit, because a function never checked how many amounts it had been given.

ACryptoS, a DeFi yield aggregator, disclosed on November 9 that its vaults had been exploited for roughly $665,000 across 77 vaults on five chains. In its announcement on X, the project blamed a lack of input validation that let an attacker mint the majority of a vault's shares by depositing only a minimal amount of tokens.

It has been revealed that it then disabled deposits, left withdrawals open, remarked it can no longer maintain the project and offered the attacker a 10% bounty in exchange for returning the funds.The most specific technical account comes from SlowMist's hack database. It traces the bug to the `depositMulti` function, where the length of the amounts array was never verified against the number of tokens. An attacker could deposit a tiny amount of a single token, receive the vast majority of vault shares and then withdraw a proportional share of both tokens. SlowMist lists the affected chains as Arbitrum, BSC, Polygon, Base and Optimism.

Industry observers note that multi-token vaults, like those behind liquidity-pair strategies, take deposits in more than one asset. A function such as `depositMulti` receives a list of amounts, one for each token the vault holds. The contract then values that bundle against the pool and issues shares accordingly.The safeguard is basic: the number of amounts supplied must equal the number of tokens in the vault. When the two don't match, the contract is working from incomplete or mismatched input, and its valuation logic can behave in ways its authors never intended. According to SlowMist, that check was absent.How ordinary this flaw is deserves a mention. It isn't an oracle trick or a flash-loan puzzle. It's a missing `require` statement on a public function, exactly the kind of slip that audits and fuzzing exist to catch.

Recent findings suggest that A simplified illustration shows how the numbers work. ACryptoS's published analysis doesn't include the exact contract code, so what follows describes the mechanics of this class of bug, not a line-by-line reconstruction.In a healthy vault, shares are minted in proportion to the deposit's share of the pool. Suppose a vault holds $10,000 in assets and has issued 10,000 shares. A $1 deposit should mint about 1 share, or 0.01% of the supply, and redeeming those shares returns about $1.Now let mismatched inputs throw off the mint calculation. The ratio of deposit to pool collapses or inverts, and the contract might credit the attacker with 90,000 latest shares for that $1. The attacker then holds 90,000 of 100,000 shares, or 90% of the supply. Because withdrawals pay out pro rata, redeeming those shares returns about 90% of each token in the pool, roughly $9,000, for a $1 deposit.The reported total fits that scale. Spread across 77 vaults, $665,000 averages about $8,600 per vault, which points to relatively small pools drained repeatedly rather than a few large ones. It also explains why the attack could be repeated mechanically: each vault offered the same function and carried the same flaw.

Recent findings suggest that yield aggregators usually deploy vaults from a shared template, and each vault's strategy contract inherits the same logic. As a result, one unchecked function in that template turns into one exploit multiplied by every deployment. Seventy-seven vaults on five chains is what that multiplication looks like.The setup also keeps the cost of attack low. Once the flaw is understood, a script can walk through every vault on every chain, call the same function and withdraw. On top of that, ACryptoS indicates the stolen funds have been moved through several cross-chain protocols, a pattern that complicates recovery.

ACryptoS has asked exchanges and bridges to flag five exploiter addresses in a follow-up post on X:.

The request targets exit points. With the stolen funds hopping across chains, the places where they are most likely to be cashed out or bridged are the ones best placed to slow the attacker down. These are EVM addresses and the exploit spanned five networks, so anyone investigating should check each address on Arbitrum, BSC, Polygon, Base and Optimism.The rest of the response is blunt. Deposits are disabled and withdrawals remain open, with users urged to pull their assets rapidly. ACryptoS cited an inability to keep maintaining the protocol, so further patching is unlikely. Remaining users should assume vault pools may be thin, withdraw while the function still works and revoke token approvals granted to ACryptoS contracts afterward. A 10% bounty is a common offer in situations like this, but whether the attacker responds is unknown, and users shouldn't strategy around a recovery.

Sources indicate that for developers, the lessons are narrow and testable. Every public function that takes an array should check its length against the data it is supposed to match. Share-minting should be tested against an invariant: the value of shares issued can never exceed the value deposited. The ERC-4626 standard defines how vault share accounting should behave, and fuzz tests built on its rules would likely have flagged this.Sunsetting a protocol needs a plan as well. A deprecated vault that still holds funds and still exposes live deposit functions is an open target. Pausing deposits and migrating balances before the maintainers leave costs little compared with leaving an unmaintained contract holding user money.For customers, the story repeats a familiar warning. Small, older yield protocols with shrinking teams are the ones most likely to carry unpatched code. This incident has less to do with a clever attack than with maintenance running out before the code was safe, so the best protection is to treat vault deposits in aging projects as temporary.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:37 amNovember 16, 2026 at 12:14 pm.

Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin, two prominent AI researchers who spent years at the University of Washington before moving to Stanford, have raised $110 million for Noeri, a startup building AI systems that keep improving on a organization’s own work.

Menlo Ventures led the round, with participation from Seattle-based Madrona, Kindred Ventures, Wing Venture Capital and NEA. Cisco Investments, Nvidia and Snowflake also invested.

Bloomberg first reported the funding Monday; the valuation wasn’t disclosed.

Sources indicate that noeri’s software studies a manufacturer’s data and workflows, then proposes changes to the system around a specific task: the instructions, the tools, which model handles each step and, in some cases, the models themselves. Each change is explained and sent to a person for approval, much like a code review, the company mentioned.

In a recent development, it works with closed and open-weight models. Customers keep ownership of the workflows and models they develop, subject to third-party model licenses, the organization mentioned.

Industry observers note that the pitch is aimed at companies stuck choosing between paying for the most capable model and accepting weaker results from a cheaper one. The idea grew partly out of an effort to help a Stanford microbiology and immunology team use OpenAI’s models more cheaply, Bloomberg reported.

The small model they built learned to use older OpenAI models and, to the founders’ surprise, outperformed GPT-5 on that team’s research needs, Choi told Bloomberg.

The name Noeri means “intelligence, in the plural,” reflecting the founders’ argument against a future dominated by one powerful model. Guestrin said at Madrona’s IA40 Summit in late September that intelligence shouldn’t be controlled by one or two companies that own the models.

“Few companies would build their core operations on a single consultant who also advises every competitor, can change its terms at will, and can never be brought in-house,” Choi and Guestrin wrote in an essay posted with the launch. “A single, centralized AI offers exactly that arrangement.”.

Noeri isn’t alone in helping businesses tailor models. In a July report on Noeri’s fundraising, The Information cited Thinking Machines Lab’s Tinker, fine-tuning software that developers use through an API, and Applied Compute, which embeds engineers with its customers.

According to recent reports, guestrin helped develop XGBoost, a widely used machine learning tool, and co-founded Turi, the Seattle startup formerly known as GraphLab and Dato, which Apple acquired in 2016. He went on to lead Apple’s central machine learning and AI organization.

Choi, a 2022 MacArthur Fellow, led common-sense reasoning research at the Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) before she left UW and Ai2 in 2024 to join Nvidia as a distinguished scientist, a role she held until starting Noeri in May. She joined Stanford’s faculty in early 2025. The two are co-CEOs.

Industry observers note that noeri is based in Palo Alto with an office in Zurich. Madrona and NEA have backed Guestrin before: the two firms led a $6.75 million round in GraphLab, the startup that became Turi, in 2013.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Monero contributor has opened a pull request that changes how nodes relay transactions coming from Tor and I2P, according to the project's GitHub.
  • The patch addresses a privacy weakness that could allow an observer to connect a transaction to the anonymity network it came from due to the timing of its broadcast.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Monero contributor has opened a pull request that changes how nodes relay transactions coming from Tor and I2P, according to the project's GitHub.

The patch addresses a privacy weakness that could allow an observer to connect a transaction to the anonymity network it came from due to the timing of its broadcast.

PR 11743 was opened on November 13 and is right now pending review. It is an updated version of a PR opened on November 8 by contributor vtnerd. After receiving feedback from another Monero developer, vtnerd, the PR was updated.

The problem lies in a mechanism where a node receives a transaction over Tor or I2P and then passes it to the regular Monero network.

Currently, when a Monero node receives a transaction over Tor or I2P, it relays that transaction to the rest of the Monero network.

Industry observers note that while the transaction is technically private as it travels into the node, once it reaches Monero's public peers, the transaction is no longer private. This PR proposes that Monero nodes will only accept transactions from Tor and I2P peers over incoming connections. Transactions received over outgoing Tor and I2P connections would be ignored.

Once accepted, the transaction would be subject to a random delay before being relayed to the rest of the Monero network using Monero's existing transaction relay protocol, Dandelion++. Right now, a user can instruct their node to broadcast their transaction immediately.

Industry observers note that over Tor and I2P connections, this request would be ignored. No transaction would be exempt from the random delay.Being able to link a transaction's timing between the anonymity network and the Monero network is an easy way to deanonymize a user. If a transaction is broadcast to the Monero network immediately after being received from Tor, an observer watching both networks can link the two.

This is a similar concept to a previous PR from vtnerd that would have introduced a randomized delay when relaying transactions from Tor and I2P to the Monero network.

While the amount of code that would need to be modified is not particularly large, this does close a hole for consumers that rely on Tor and I2P to obscure their location.

It has been revealed that when the patch lands in a release is yet to be confirmed. The PR is also labeled for a backport, so it might reach the current release branch as well.

Latest Update: VCs Are Still Chasing Protein, Even As Fake Meat Falls Out Of Favor

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (899 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crunchbase

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that macronutrients don’t have popularity contests.
  • Sources indicate that for everything from sodas to snack bars to pasta, it’s now standard practice for food and drink makers to play up protein content whenever feasible.
  • According to recent reports, startups and their backers have been riding this trend too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that macronutrients don’t have popularity contests. But if they did, protein would surely be this era’s winner.

Sources indicate that for everything from sodas to snack bars to pasta, it’s now standard practice for food and drink makers to play up protein content whenever feasible. While we may cut carbs and fret over fat, most of us are still keen on protein.

According to recent reports, startups and their backers have been riding this trend too. Over the past decade, investors have poured billions into upstarts promising cheaper, tastier and more sustainable ways to meet our protein quotas.

Unfortunately, many of their earlier bets have fared poorly. Vast sums poured into lab-grown meat several years ago, for instance, have so far failed to produce a success story. Former high-flying plant-based meat startups Beyond (now public) and Impossible Foods have seen their valuations wither. Others have shuttered.

In response, more recent startup investment has shifted away from meat substitutes and toward stuffing more protein into other packaged foods and drinks. It’s a fad that’s obvious on supermarket shelves, where startups and established brands alike relentlessly tout the added protein in their noodles, pancakes, cereals, energy bars, popcorn and so on.

In startup circles, protein-related investment looks tiny in comparison to the billions bet on AI. Deal flow, however, remains fairly robust, with Crunchbase identifying a few dozen protein-focused startups funded in the past year. Moreover, some of these rounds are quite sizable, like a $250 million September Series B for Medici Brands, maker of David Protein snack bars.

To illustrate, we used Crunchbase data to put together sample sets of recently-funded protein-focused companies across several themes. These include packaged foods, drinks, ingredients and processes, and animal feed.

Snacks and packaged foods look like the largest fundraisers among protein startups, securing hundreds of millions in the past year.

For a sense of who’s raising, we put together a list of seven recently funded brands that are finding their way to store shelves.

The bulk of recent funding went to the aforementioned parent of David Protein. That brand, in addition to churning sweet-flavored bars with a protein content to rival cod, has been expanding into ice cream and milkshakes.

Sources indicate that wilde Brands, which makes crackers from chicken breasts, has also proven popular with investors, pulling in $40 million last month. Among early-stage startups, meanwhile, Frozen One has been off to a brisk start, raising over $8 million for a line of high-protein ice creams now selling at Target.

Startups and investors are also catering to people who want their high-protein diet in drinkable form. To illustrate, we put together six recently funded examples below.

Ripple Foods, which makes a vegan milk using pea protein, is the highest historical funding recipient, raising over $300 million in its 12-year-history, even though it hasn’t officially joined the unicorn club.

Clear protein drinks are also increasingly a thing, with multiple startups including protein soda brand Juuz and sports drink purveyor Protein2o.

Quite a few funded startups are focused more on novel, protein-rich ingredients rather than their own branded retail lineup. In many cases, they’re using precision fermentation to deliver.

We put together seven examples below.

In a recent development, the Every Co., which makes animal-free egg white proteins through fermentation, is the biggest funding recipient and one of the older names on our list. It’s raised nearly $300 million in the past 10 years, including a $55 million round a year ago.

Early stage is also seeing some action from startups including Edonia, which makes a high-protein cooking ingredient from spirulina,.

A number of funded protein startups are also focusing on pets and livestock — a target audience that’s not quite so overwhelmed by supermarket options.

To illustrate, we aggregated five such companies that raised funding in recent quarters.

In a recent development, notably, two of them — InnovaFeed and nextProtein — are bug-focused. InnovaFeed has raised over $500 million to raise insects for feeding livestock, pet food and aquaculture. NextProtein is using fly larvae for feedstock.

Others are focused on pets. Meatly, for instance, secured a Series A round this spring to build what it claims will be Europe’s largest cultivated meat facility. It looks to partner with pet food brands and sell its own branded lineup once production scales.

Recent findings suggest that if we were to encapsulate a broad trend across most of the protein-related financings it would be that startups aren’t trying to convince people that vegetables are meat. Rather, they’re focused largely on protein as an in-demand macronutrient that can be increasingly concentrated and stuffed into a bewildering variety of flavors and form factors.

That might not all taste as good as their more sugary, high-fat and carb-laden alternatives, but at least they’ve got protein.
